en: Composed by the venerable teacher Rājānakānandavardhana,
also known as the *Sahṛdayāloka*. (1) // The First Uddyota //

May the claws of the Enemy of Mura protect you— claws that are lions by their own will, which eclipse the moon with their perfectly clear luster, and which sever the suffering of those who have sought refuge in him.

That which has been traditionally declared by the wise as the soul of poetry—*dhvani*—others have denied its existence, while still others have said it is merely figurative (*bhākta*). Some have stated that its true nature resides in a realm beyond the reach of words. Therefore, for the pleasure of the minds of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*), we shall describe its essential nature. (Dhvanyāloka 1.1)
By the wise who know the essence of poetry, *dhvani* has been designated as the soul of poetry—
that which was previously handed down through tradition, properly and completely memorized, and revealed;
yet others have declared its non-existence, even though it shines forth in the minds of sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*).
And for those who maintain that [poetry] does not exist [as a distinct entity], these following alternatives are possible.
In this regard, some might say: "Poetry, first of all, has the word and its meaning as its body.
Among these, the causes of beauty residing in the words—such as alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and so forth—are indeed well known."
Furthermore, metaphors and the like pertaining to the meaning,
as well as those properties of phonemic arrangement such as sweetness (*mādhurya*) and so forth, are also perceived;
likewise, those modes of expression (*vṛtti*)— such as the *upanāgarikā* and others— which have been elucidated by some as being non-distinct from those [qualities], are also included.
Those [styles] as well, beginning with Vaidarbhī and the rest, have come within the range of hearing;
so what is this thing called "dhvani" apart from them?

Others might say: "Sound (dhvani) does not exist at all; for a type of poetry that deviates from the established systems would forfeit its status as poetry. The definition of poetry consists solely in being composed of words and meanings that delight the hearts of connoisseurs. And that is not possible for a path that transcends the aforementioned systems."

Nor does the designation "poetry" (kāvyavyapadeśa) applied to *dhvani*—even if it proceeds by virtue of its being established among certain sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*) whom one might imagine to fall within the scope of that [definition]—gain acceptance by the minds of all learned men.
Furthermore, others might otherwise assert its non-existence, saying: "There is no such unprecedented thing as *dhvani* at all."
For that which does not transcend what is desirable is already included within the very causes of beauty that have been mentioned;

or, if one were to provide a new name for any one of those [causes], it would be a mere triviality. Furthermore, since verbal distinctions are infinite, even if some [new quality] were possible, [it would still be redundant] by those who prescribe the definitions of poetry.

When even a mere fraction of the varieties [of poetry] has not been demonstrated by those who are renowned, these people—whose eyes are closed by the cultivation of a false sense of aesthetic sensitivity—dance about, crying "This is Dhvani! This is Dhvani!
We know not what the cause for this is;
for thousands of varieties of poetic ornaments have been revealed and continue to be revealed by other great souls.
And this condition of theirs is not heard of;
therefore, sound is a mere conventional report,
and it is impossible to demonstrate any reality in it that can withstand critical scrutiny.
And thus, another verse has been composed on this very point:
"That which contains not the slightest thing that gladdens the mind, though it be adorned; which is neither composed of refined words nor devoid of poetic turns of expression;"
Praising with delight that poetry is "endowed with dhvani," the dull-witted man does not know what he is saying when asked by a wise person about the true nature of dhvani.
Others say that [the soul of poetry] is figurative (bhākta);

others call it "suggestion" (dhvani), asserting that it is the soul of poetry through the function of poetic qualities (guṇa-vṛtti). And although no particular mode—whether figurative or otherwise—has been explicitly revealed by those who formulate the definition of poetry through the mention of the term "suggestion" (dhvani),...

Nevertheless, considering that the path of *dhvani*—though slightly touched upon by one who demonstrated its usage in poetry through a secondary (*amukhya*) function—was not yet clearly defined, it was stated thus: “Others call it metaphorical (*bhākta*).

However, others, whose intellects were confident in their mastery of defining [the nature of things], declared that the true essence of *dhvani* is beyond the reach of words and is to be experienced solely within the hearts of sensitive connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*).
Since such doubts persist, we shall describe the true nature of that *dhvani* for the delight of the hearts of the sensitive (*sahṛdaya*).

For the nature of this *dhvani*— which is the secret essence (*upaniṣad*) of all the poetry of great poets, exceedingly beautiful, and never before revealed even by the subtlest intellects of those who have formulated the definitions of ancient poetry—

is now being elucidated so that the joy of the sensitive readers, who perceive its well-established usage throughout the works of the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the *Mahābhārata*, and other such texts, may find firm footing in their minds.
In this regard, in order to prepare the ground for defining *dhvani* itself, the following is stated:

"That meaning which is praised by the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*) and established as the soul (*ātman*) of poetry—its two divisions are traditionally known as the expressed (*vācya*) and the implied (*pratīyamāna*). (Dhvanyāloka 1.2)

For in poetry—which is as beautiful as a body with its graceful and appropriate arrangement—there exists a meaning that, like the soul, abides as the essence and is worthy of praise by those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*). This [meaning] has two divisions: the expressed (*vācya*) and the suggested (*pratīyamāna*).
Among these, the expressed is well-known; it is [further divided] into types such as simile (*upamā*) and so forth.
It has been explained in many ways by others who have formulated the definitions of poetry.
Therefore, it is not elaborated upon here; rather, it is merely restated again as required for the purpose at hand. // DhvA_1.3 //

But there exists in the words of great poets another very distinct entity that is being perceived, which shines forth as something exceeding the well-known constituent parts, like the *lāvaṇya* (grace) in women. (Dhvanyāloka 1.4)

Furthermore, there exists in the compositions of great poets another reality entirely distinct from the expressed meaning (*vācya*); that which is well-known to connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*) manifests as something separate from the well-known, adorned, or perceived constituent parts, just like *lāvaṇya* (grace) in women. For just as in women, *lāvaṇya*—when observed separately—is something else entirely, distinct from all the individual limbs, an essence that is nectar for the eyes of connoisseurs; exactly so is that [suggested meaning].

For that [suggested] meaning will be shown to be divided into many varieties, consisting of the mere fact (vastu-mātra) implied by the power of the expressed meaning, as well as figures of speech (alaṅkāra), aesthetic flavors (rasa), and so forth.
And in all these modes, it possesses a distinctness from the expressed meaning;
for indeed, the first variety is far removed in its differentiation from the expressed.
For sometimes, when the expressed meaning is of a positive nature, it takes the form of a negation; as for example:
"O pious man, roam about with confidence!
That dog has been killed today by him who dwells in the thickets on the banks of the Godāvarī river, by one who has seen a lion. [3]
[*3] Verse 2.75, cited in the *Kāvyaprakāśa* (138):
"O pious man, wander with confidence; that dog has been killed today by the proud lion dwelling in the creeper-thicket on the bank of the Godāvarī river."
In some cases, where the expressed meaning is negative in form, it takes a positive form, as for example:
"The husband immerses himself here; I am here too. Look well for a day, O traveler! Do not immerse yourself in my bed tonight, blinded by the night. (4)
[*4] Verse 1.4. Quoted in the *Kāvyaprakāśa* 136 and the *Sāhityadarpaṇa* 1.2:
"The mother-in-law is bathing here."
"Look here even during the day; O traveler blind at night, do not plunge into my bed.
In some cases, when the expressed meaning is of the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*), there is that which is of neither nature (*anubhayarūpa*), as for example:
O cow, let there be only sighs and weeping for me alone;
let them not arise for you as well, O southern-faced one, without her.
(Gāthā 938)
"Let my sighs and weeping belong to me alone; let them not arise for you as well, who are already stricken by courtesy in her absence.
In some cases, when the expressed meaning takes the form of a prohibition, it may be of neither form (neither affirmation nor negation), as follows:
O goddess, be gracious and turn back; you have dispelled the mass of darkness with the moonlight of your face.
You are creating an obstacle for other female messengers as well, O destroyer of hope.
(Gāthā 962)
"O wretched one, having by fate seen the mass of darkness dispelled by the moonlight of your exceedingly beautiful face,
do you still create obstacles for other women going to meet their lovers?
In some cases, it is established as having a different scope from the literal meaning (vācya), as follows:

Whose anger would not arise upon seeing the wounded lip of his beloved, who, while smelling the lotus with its bee, acted with perverse disregard? Endure this now! Gāthā 880. Cited in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, verse 135.
"Or who would not feel anger upon seeing the wounded lower lip of his beloved—she who was forbidden yet perverse in her habit of smelling a lotus with bees? Suffer this now!
Other such varieties of the suggested meaning (pratīyamāna) exist that are distinct from the expressed meaning (vācya).
Only a mere indication of these has been shown here.
The second variety, which is distinct from the expressed meaning (*vācya*), will be demonstrated in detail later along with its elaborations.
The third variety, however, characterized by aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth, manifests as being suggested by the power of the expressed meaning (*vācya-sāmarthyākṣipta*).
But it is not the case that [the suggested meaning] is distinct from the expressed meaning simply because it is not the direct object of the operation of the word.
For its status as an expressed meaning would have to be either by virtue of being conveyed by its own specific word,
or by way of the presentation of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.
In the former position, there would follow the undesirable consequence that rasa and the other elements could not be perceived if they were not conveyed by their own specific words;
yet it is not the case that they are always conveyed by their own specific words. Even where such [specific words] exist, [the rasa is still understood].
Even there, their apprehension occurs only by way of the presentation of specific excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth;
it is merely restated by its own word [as "rasa"],
but it is not produced by that [word] itself, because such [apprehension] is not observed in other objects.

For indeed, there is not even the slightest perception of aesthetic flavor (*rasavattva*) in a poem that contains merely words such as "erotic" (*śṛṅgāra*) and the like, but lacks the presentation of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth;
since the perception of aesthetic flavors and the like arises from the specific determinants and so forth even when they are alone and without their own designations,
whereas it does not arise from their own designations alone.

Therefore, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is established that rasa and the like are merely implied by the power of the denotable meaning (*abhidheya-sāmarthya-ākṣiptatva*);
they are not in any way directly denotable (*abhidheyatva*).
Thus, it remains settled that even the third variety is indeed distinct from the expressed (*vācya*).
However, it will be shown later that its cognition occurs simultaneously with that of the expressed meaning.
That very meaning is the soul of poetry; likewise, in ancient times, the sorrow arising from the separation of the pair of Krauñca birds became embodied as a verse by the first poet.

Of poetry, which is beautiful through the manifold elaboration of various expressions and the expressed, that very meaning is the essential core. Even for the primordial poet Vālmīki, it was grief alone—born from the cry of a curlew distressed by the separation from its slain mate—that was transformed into verse. For grief is the stable emotional state (*sthāyibhāva*) of the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*).
And although other distinctions are perceived in that which is suggested, it is characterized primarily by way of rasa and bhāva alone. (Dhvanyāloka 1.5)
The Sarasvatī, flowing forth as the sweet essence of the subject matter of great poets, reveals a particular, throbbing intuition that is extraordinary to the world. (Dhvanyāloka 1.6)
The speech of great poets, flowing forth from that reality of things (*vastu-tattva*), manifests a particular genius (*pratibhā*) that is not common to the world;

by means of this, in this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) which carries on an exceedingly diverse succession of poets, only two or three, or five or six, such as Kālidāsa and others, are reckoned as "great poets" (*mahākavi*). (Dhvanyāloka 1.6)
And this is another means of proof for the existence of the suggested meaning:
"It is not perceived merely by one who possesses knowledge of the science of words and their meanings;
it is perceived only by those who know the true nature of the meaning of poetry. (Dhvanyāloka 1.7)
That meaning is such that it is understood only by those who know the true essence of poetic meaning (*kāvyārtha-tattva*).

If that meaning were merely of the nature of the expressed (*vācya*), then its comprehension would occur simply through a thorough knowledge of the forms of the expressed and the expressive (*vācya-vācaka*). However, for those whose efforts are limited solely to the characteristics of the expressed and the expressive, and who are averse to the cultivation of the true essence of poetry—

Just as the definition of musical notes, scales, and so forth is beyond the reach of those who know the definitions of music but do not sing, so too is this matter beyond the scope of those who know the definitions of poetry but have not sung it.
Having thus established the existence of the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) as distinct from the expressed meaning (vācya), he demonstrates that it alone possesses primacy:
"That meaning and that particular word, which possess the capacity for its manifestation—these two, the word and the meaning of a great poet, are to be recognized with effort. (Dhvanyāloka 1.8)
The suggested meaning and a certain word endowed with the capacity to manifest it—
this is not mere sound alone;
these two, the word and the meaning, are to be recognized as belonging to the great poet.
Great poets attain the status of "great poet" through the proper employment of the suggested (vyaṅgya) and the suggester (vyañjaka) alone,
and not merely by means of the composition of the expressed (vācya) and the expressive (vācaka).

Now, he states that it is likewise appropriate that poets first employ only the expressed meaning (vācya) and the expressive word (vācaka), even though the suggested (vyaṅgya) and the suggester (vyañjaka) are the primary elements:

"Just as a person seeking light exerts effort toward the flame of a lamp because it is the means to that end, so too [the poet] is intent upon the expressed meaning for the sake of the [suggested] sense. (Dhvanyāloka 1.9)
For just as a person, though desiring light, exerts effort toward the flame of a lamp because it is the means to that end—
since light cannot exist without the lamp's flame—
so too a person intent upon the meaning to be manifested exerts effort toward the expressed meaning.
By this, the operation of the poet as the communicator with respect to the suggested meaning has been shown. (Dhvanyāloka 1.9)
In order to demonstrate that [process] for the recipient as well, he says:
"Just as the meaning of a sentence is understood by means of the meanings of its words, so too the comprehension of the intended object is preceded by the expressed meaning. (DhvK 1.10)

For just as the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence occurs by way of the meanings of individual words, so too the apprehension of the suggested meaning is preceded by the cognition of the expressed meaning. (Dhvanyāloka 1.10)

Now, he demonstrates how the primacy of the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) is not compromised even though the cognition of that [suggested meaning] is preceded by the cognition of the expressed meaning (vācyārtha):

"Just as, while conveying the sentence-meaning solely through its own inherent power, the individual word-meanings are no longer perceived once the function [of conveying the sentence-meaning] has been accomplished. (Dhvanyāloka 1.11)

Just as the meaning of a word, even while manifesting the meaning of the sentence by the power of its own capacity, is not perceived as a distinct entity once the function has been accomplished. (Dhvanyāloka 1.11)
In the same way, for those with discerning minds whose nature is turned away from the literal meaning,
that [suggested] object suddenly flashes forth in the intellect that perceives the true reality.
Having thus established the existence of the suggested meaning (vyaṅgyārtha) which is distinct from the expressed (vācya), he applies it to the subject at hand and says:

"That particular type of poetry in which either the meaning or the word suggests that [suggested] meaning while subordinating their own primary meanings, is called 'dhvani' by the wise. (Dhvanyāloka 1.13)
Where a particular meaning or a particular expressive word manifests that meaning,
that specific type of poetry is *dhvani*.

By this, it is shown that the domain of *dhvani* is indeed distinct from the causes of beauty in the expressed and the expressive, such as metaphors (*upamā*) and so forth, as well as alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and so forth.
As for what was also said— that "there is no *dhvani* in poetry because it is a path that transgresses established conventions"—
that too is incorrect;
for it is simply not well-known only to the authors of the technical definitions (*lakṣaṇakṛt*).
But when the object of definition is examined, that alone is the essence of poetry (*kāvyatattva*) which brings delight to the hearts of connoisseurs;
anything other than that is merely "picturesque" (*citra*), as we shall demonstrate later.
As for what was said—that "since it does not transcend loveliness, it is included within the aforementioned varieties such as figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*) and so forth"—[that is incorrect].
That too is incorrect;

for how could *dhvani*, which is established by relying on the relationship between the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) and the suggester (*vyañjaka*), be included within a system that relies solely on the relationship between the expressed (*vācya*) and the expresser (*vācaka*)?
For the causes of beauty in the expressed and the expresser are merely subordinate members (*aṅga*) of that [system].
However, since it will be demonstrated that this [dhvani] is indeed of the nature of *aṅgin* (the primary element),
there are here some ancillary verses (*parikara-śloka*) regarding how *dhvani* is based upon the relationship between the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) and the suggester (*vyañjaka*).
How could there be inclusion within the causes of the beauty of the expressed and the expressive?
Now, it may be argued: let that indeed not be the domain of *dhvani* where the suggested meaning is not perceived with clarity;

however, where such perception does exist—as in the case of figures such as *samāsokti*, *ākṣepa*, *anuktanimitta*, *viśeṣokti*, *paryāyokta*, *apahnuti*, *dīpaka*, and *saṃkara*—[then it must be included].
In that regard, in order to refute [the objection] that "the inclusion of *dhvani* will occur therein" and so forth, it was stated: "those which have subordinated their own meanings.
Where a meaning has its own nature made subordinate, or a word has its denoted meaning made subordinate, such that it manifests another meaning—that is *dhvani*.
How is it included among those?
For *dhvani* occurs when the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is predominant;
and this [predominance] does not exist in cases such as *samāsokti* (synecdoche/metaphorical expression) and the like.
First, regarding *samāsokti* (synecdoche):
"The face of night was thus seized by the moon, whose passion had been aroused and whose pupils were tremulous."
Just as she did not perceive the entire dark garment fallen before her due to passion, so too she did not perceive [the truth].

In such cases, it is the expressed meaning (*vācya*) itself, accompanied by the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), that is primarily perceived, because the sentence-meaning consists precisely of the night and the moon, upon which the behaviors of the heroine and the hero have been superimposed.

Even in the figure of *ākṣepa* (paralipsis), although it suggests a particular suggested meaning, it is the beauty of the expressed meaning itself that is primarily the sentence-meaning; this is known from the very power of the statement of *ākṣepa*.

For instance, in that context, the *ākṣepa*—which takes the form of a negation based on words and intended to express a specific [unexpressed] qualification—is itself the primary body of poetry as it suggests the particular suggested meaning.

For the intention to emphasize either the expressed (*vācya*) or the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) meaning is based on the excellence of their respective beauty. As in the example: "The twilight is full of passion, and the day was its precursor;
oh, what a way fate has it! And yet, there is no union."

In this case, even though there is a perception of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), the beauty of the expressed meaning (*vācya*) alone possesses excellence; thus, it is that [expressed meaning] whose predominance is intended to be conveyed.

Just as in *dīpaka*, *apahnuti*, and so forth, although a simile (*upamā*) is perceived as being suggested, it is not designated by that [simile] because its predominance is not intended, so it should be understood here as well.
This also applies to the figure of speech "particularity" (*viśeṣokti*) where the cause is unstated (*anukta-nimitta*).
Even when called by his companions, even after saying "Om," and even though his sleep has been dispelled,
the traveler does not loosen his reluctance to depart.

In such cases, because of the power of the context, there is merely a cognition of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), but there is no production of any aesthetic charm (*cārutva*) caused by that cognition; therefore, it does not possess predominance (*prādhānya*).
Even in the case of *paryāyokta* (periphrasis), if the suggested meaning were predominant, let it indeed be included within *dhvani*; however, *dhvani* is not included therein.
This is because it will be established as having a vast scope and as being the primary element (*aṅgin*);
however, this is not a synonym for the case cited by Bhāmaha, where the suggested meaning alone possesses primacy.
For in that [latter] case, the expressed meaning is not intended to be present at all, as it lacks even the status of a subordinate element (*upasarjana*).

Furthermore, it is well known that in the figures of speech *apahnuti* (concealment) and *dīpaka* (illumination), the expressed meaning (*vācya*) is predominant while the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is subordinate. Even in the figure of speech *saṅkara* (commixture), when one figure of speech adopts the luster of another, it does not fall within the domain of *dhvani*, because the suggested meaning is not intended to be predominant.

However, when there is the possibility of two figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*), the expressed (*vācya*) and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) possess equal prominence. Alternatively, if the suggested meaning exists therein by being subordinate to the expressed, then that too must be the domain of *dhvani*;
it cannot be said that it is *dhvani* itself.
This follows the principle established by the figure *paryāyokta*.
Furthermore, even in the case of the figure *saṅkara* (commixture), the very mention of commixture in certain instances precludes the possibility of *dhvani* (suggestion).

This is also the case in *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), when the unstated subject (*aprastuta*)—whether through the relation of general and particular or through the relation of cause and effect—is what is actually being expressed.

When there is a connection with the suggested (pratīyamāna) which is the subject at hand (prastuta), then the expressed (abhidhīyamāna) and the suggested possess equal primacy. In that case, when there is a connection between the unmentioned general (sāmānya) which is being expressed and the contextual particular (viśeṣa) which is suggested, then— even though the particular is what is actually perceived— the general also possesses primacy because it is inseparably connected (avinābhāva) with that general as its primary element.
Even when the particular is grounded in the universal, if the universal is predominant, then because all particulars are included within the universal, the particular also possesses predominance.
This same logic applies to the relationship between the cause and the effect.

However, when in Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Praise of the Irrelevant) there is a connection between the irrelevant and the relevant based solely on similarity, even then, if there is no intention to emphasize the predominance of the irrelevant object that is being expressed through its similarity [to the relevant], [the figure remains Aprastutapraśaṃsā].
It is included within *dhvani* itself;
otherwise, however, it would be a distinct figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*).
Thus, this is the summary here:
Where the suggested meaning is subordinate and follows only the expressed meaning,
there figures of speech such as *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) and others are clearly figures of the expressed meaning (*vācyālaṅkāra*).
There is no *dhvani* where the suggested meaning exists merely as a flash of intuition (*pratibhā*) even while following upon the expressed meaning, or where its predominance is not perceived.
That alone should be considered the domain of Dhvani— free from any admixture of other figures— where the word and its meaning are directed solely toward the suggested sense.
Therefore, there is no inclusion of *dhvani* elsewhere; for this reason as well, there is no inclusion, because *dhvani* is declared to be the very essence (*aṅgin*) of a specific type of poetry.
Furthermore, its constituent parts—namely, ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), excellences (*guṇa*), and modes (*vṛtti*)—will be explained later.
It is not well known that a whole exists as something separate from its parts;
rather, it possesses the status of being their limb (*aṅga*) precisely because of its non-separateness from them.
But it is not reality itself;
or even where there is reality, because sound has a vast range of objects, it does not consist of that alone.
The phrase "stated by the wise" is a declaration of what was first conceived by the learned.
However, it is not established that [the tradition] proceeded in an arbitrary manner;
for, first of all, the grammarians are the learned ones, because all branches of knowledge have grammar as their foundation.

And when these [phonemes] are being heard, people employ the term "dhvani. In the very same way, other wise men who follow that doctrine and perceive the true nature of poetry have declared that the essence of sound (śabdātmā), which is a mixture of the signified and the signifier, should be designated as "poetry" (kāvyam), yet is called "dhvani" because of its similarity to the function of manifestation (vyañjakatva).

And for such a sound (dhvani), which possesses a vast scope through the synthesis of its various types and sub-types to be described hereafter, the illumination of it is by no means equivalent to the mere exposition of unestablished specific figures of speech; therefore, the enthusiasm of those whose minds are permeated by this [doctrine] is entirely justified.
Furthermore, one should not in any way manifest a state of mind defiled by envy toward them.
Thus, those who maintain that *dhvani* does not exist have been refuted;
*dhvani* indeed exists.

And that [suggested meaning] is generally of two kinds: that in which the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣita-vācya*) and that in which another meaning is intended (*vivakṣitānyapara-vācya*).
Of these, an example of the first is as follows:
"Three types of men gather the earth of golden flowers."
One who is brave, learned, and knows how to serve.
As for the second [verse] as well:
"On what mountain, indeed, for how long,
and under what name did he perform his ascetic penance?"
O young woman, by which [means] does the young parrot bite at your lip, as red as a bimba fruit?

As for what was stated—that *bhakti* is *dhvani*—that is answered as follows: "This *dhvani* does not possess identity with *bhakti*, because there is a difference in their essential natures. (DhvK 1.14a)
This aforementioned type of *dhvani* does not possess identity with *bhakti*, because their forms are distinct.

Where there is a manifestation, through the power of *tātparya* (intentional focus), of a meaning distinct from the expressed (*vācya*) by means of both the expressed and the expressive (*vācaka*), and where the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) is predominant, that is *dhvani*.
*Bhakti*, however, is merely a figurative application (*upacāra*).
Lest it be thought that devotion (*bhakti*) is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of suggestion (*dhvani*), he says:
"Because it is over-extensive (*ativyāpti*) or under-extensive (*avyāpti*), it is not perceived as such. (DhvK 1.14b)
Suggestive meaning (*dhvani*) is not indicated by figurative usage (*bhakti*) alone.
How so? Because of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) and under-extension (*avyāpti*).
Among these, there is over-extension because figurative usage is possible even in cases other than suggestive meaning.

For even where there is no great excellence produced by the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), poets are seen to employ figurative verbal functions (*upacarita-śabda-vṛtti*) and engage in usage driven by conformity to common renown (*prasiddhi*).
As in [Ratnāvalī 2.12]:
"Faded on both sides from contact with her full breasts and hips..."

This bed of lotus leaves, its greenness not yet reached by the friction within the middle of her body, speaks of the fever of the slender-limbed girl through the tossing and turning of her limp, vine-like arms in a disordered posture.
[*8] As it is said in Srk 709 and Rasārṇava 1.441:
"One may kiss her a thousand times, and one may embrace her a thousand times."
One may delight again and again in a beloved person; there is no such thing as repetition.
"He is embraced a hundred times, held fast a thousand times; having ceased, he is enjoyed again. There is no such thing as repetition for a beloved person.
Likewise—
With their necklaces dangling, their faces tear-stained yet smiling,
these women whose husbands have been slain carry away the heart just as they were seized.
[Whether angry, gracious, with tearful faces, or laughing—
just as they are grasped, so do these wanton women steal the heart.
Likewise—
A blow from a fresh vine given by her lover to the lady’s round breasts became unbearable to the hearts of her co-wives,
even though it was mild.
"A blow with a fresh creeper was given by her beloved to the surface of his wife's breast;
though gentle, it became as if unbearable to the hearts of the co-wives.
Likewise—

He who undergoes suffering for the sake of others, whose very breaking is sweet to everyone here, and whose transformation is indeed esteemed by all— if he does not reach full growth, it is because he has fallen upon barren soil.
Is this a fault of the sugarcane, and not rather a lack of quality in the desert land?
Thus, in this context, the word "experiences" (*anubhavati*) refers to the sugar-cane.
And such a thing has never been the object of the term *dhvani*. For:
"That which cannot be expressed by any other mode of speech, while manifesting its own beauty..."
Sound, assuming the state of a manifestor, becomes the object of the theory of Suggestion (dhvani).
In this cited instance, there is no word capable of manifesting a beauty that could not be expressed by another word.
Furthermore:
those words which are conventionally established in one sense, even when used in their own primary sense...
Those [qualities] such as *lāvaṇya* (loveliness) and so forth, when employed, do not become the locus (*pada*) of *dhvani*.
And since there exists a figurative application of the term [suggestion] to those cases,
even when the conventional usage of the term "suggestion" (dhvani) occurs in such a context, it proceeds by way of another mode,
not by way of such a literal expression.
Moreover:

"When the primary function is set aside and the meaning is perceived through a secondary function (guṇavṛtti), the word does not falter in its course toward that result which is aimed at. (Dhvanyāloka 1.17)

For in that case, when the purpose—which consists in the manifestation of a meaning distinguished by an excellence of beauty—is to be accomplished, if the word were not primary (amukhyatā), then its employment would indeed be defective.
But this is not so; therefore, the operation of poetic quality (guṇa-vṛtti) is established solely on the basis of its denotative power (vācakatva).
How could there be a definition of *dhvani*, whose sole root is the state of being a suggester? (DhvK 1.18)
Therefore, the sound is one thing and the function of secondary indication (guṇavṛtti) is another;
furthermore, this definition suffers from the fault of being under-extensive (avyāpti),
for a particular type of sound is not characterized by the expression of a sense other than what is intended.
Furthermore, many other varieties are pervaded by devotion;
therefore, devotion is not a defining characteristic [of poetry].
That [suggestion] might be a secondary indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of some particular variety of *dhvani*.
Furthermore, if that [suggestion] were to be conceived as a secondary indication of one or another of the varieties to be described hereafter;
and if it is said that *dhvani* is indicated solely through the function of metaphorical transfer (*guṇavṛtti*), then by means of the function of denotation (*abhidhāvyāpāra*), that other [variety]—
Since the entire class of poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) would thus be perceived [in the *dhvani* itself], it would follow that defining each individual figure is redundant.
Furthermore:
"And if the definition of this [dhvani] were already established by others, our own position would be proven. (DhvK 1.19a)
Or even if the definition of *dhvani* has already been formulated by others, our position is nonetheless fully established; for our position is simply that *dhvani* exists,
and since that was already established beforehand, we have achieved our desired objective without effort.
Even those who have declared that the soul of *dhvani* is indeed inexpressible—something to be experienced only by the hearts of the sensitive (*sahṛdaya*)—are not critical examiners of the matter;

for, even though the general and specific definitions of *dhvani* have been established through the logic already stated and that which is yet to be stated, if its inexpressibility were [absolute], it would follow that all things whatsoever are inexpressible.
However, if they describe the nature of *dhvani* as surpassing other poetry through this very hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), then they too are indeed speakers of what is consistent with reason.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Dhvanyāloka composed by the venerable teacher Rājānaka Ānandavardhana.
The Second Radiance.

Thus, *dhvani* has been shown to be of two kinds, according to whether its expressed meaning (*vācya*) is unintended (*avivakṣita*) or intended but subordinate to another meaning (*vivakṣitānyapara*).

Regarding that, in order to demonstrate the subdivisions of the type where the expressed meaning is unintended, this is stated: "The expressed meaning is either transmuted into another meaning or completely set aside."
In the case of suggestion where the expressed meaning is not intended to be conveyed (avivakṣitavācya), the expressed meaning is considered to be of two kinds.
And by those two [types of suggestion], there is a distinction specifically regarding the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
Among them, an example of that in which the expressed meaning is transmuted into another meaning (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya*) is as follows:
"The sky is smeared with the glossy, dark luster of clouds, and the clouds are filled with swaying cranes."
Let the winds be laden with spray, and let the sweet cries of the peacocks—the friends of the clouds—be full of joy; so be it! I am Rāma, firm and hard-hearted, and I shall endure all this.
But what will become of Vaidehī? Alas, alas, O Queen! Be steadfast.
In the passage from *Sadukti-karṇāmṛta* 978 and *Sāhityadarpaṇa* 2.17,
the word "Rāma" is used;
for by this, the designatum (*saṃjñin*) is conveyed as having been transformed into another suggested quality (*vyaṅgya-dharmāntara*).
It is not mere perception.
And as it is said by me in the *Viṣamabāṇalīlā*:
"Qualities arise from the *tāla* [rhythm] which are grasped by those who are capable."
The lotuses become truly lotuses when favored by the rays of the sun.
"In that case, virtues arise when they are perceived by those with sensitive hearts; lotuses become truly lotuses only when graced by the rays of the sun"—
in this instance, the second occurrence of the word *kamala* is [an example of *punarukta*].
An example of that in which the expressed meaning is completely set aside (atyanta-tiraskṛta-vācya) is by the ancient poet Vālmīki:
"The moon, its beauty transferred to the sun and its orb shrouded in frost, does not shine, like a mirror blinded by one's own breath. Thus.

In this context, there is the word "blind" (*andha*). For example: "The songs, the rutting elephants, the forests with *arjuna* trees dripping with streams [of sap], and the blue nights take away [the sorrow] of the deer who are free from ego."
"The sky with intoxicated clouds, forests where *arjuna* trees are drenched by rain-showers, and nights that are blue yet devoid of the moon—these captivate the heart.
Here, the words *matta* (intoxicated) and *nirahaṅkāra* (devoid of pride/self-consciousness) [are used]. (Dhvanyāloka 2.1)

The supreme self of *dhvani*, whose manifestation is beyond the perception of sequential stages, is considered to be twofold when manifested through sequence for the sake of the intended meaning. (Dhvanyāloka 2.2)
The suggested meaning (vyaṅgya-artha), which manifests primarily, is the soul of dhvani.

And that is considered to be of two kinds: some manifest with an imperceptible sequence [of the means of suggestion] in relation to the expressed meaning (vācyārtha), while others manifest through a sequence. (DhvA 2.2)
In that regard:

"The sequence consisting of rasa, bhāva, their semblances (ābhāsa), their pacification (praśānti), and so forth, is established as the soul of dhvani, appearing through the relationship of principal and subordinate. (Dhvanyāloka 2.3)
For an object such as rasa (aesthetic flavor) and the like manifests simultaneously with the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
And that [rasa], manifesting as the predominant element (*aṅgin*), is the very soul of dhvani.

Now, it is demonstrated that the domain of dhvani—which consists in the manifestation of the imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakramadyotana*)—is distinct from the figure of speech *rasavat* (which possesses rasa).
That in which the various types of causes for the beauty of the expressed and the expressive are subordinate to rasa and the like is considered the domain of dhvani. (DhvK 2.4)

Following the primary meaning characterized by rasa, bhāva, their semblances (ābhāsa), and their pacification (praśama), the figures of sound and sense, as well as the poetic qualities (guṇas), are established as having distinct forms in relation to one another and in relation to dhvani; it is for this reason that the designation "dhvani" is applied to that poetry. (DhvA 2.4)
In that poetry where rasa and the like are subordinate to another sentence-meaning, it is my view that rasa and the like constitute a mere figure of speech (alaṅkāra). (Dhvanyāloka 2.5)

Although the scope of the *rasavat* ornament has been shown by others in a different manner, my own position is this: in whatever poem another meaning constitutes the primary sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), those *rasas* and so forth that serve as its subordinate members (*aṅga*) constitute the scope of the *rasavat* ornament.

For example, in *cāṭu* (flattering verses), even though the figure of speech *preyaḥ* constitutes the primary meaning of the sentence, *rasa* and the like are seen to function as subordinate elements (*aṅga*).
And that *rasa*, etc., may be either pure (*śuddha*) or mixed (*saṅkīrṇa*).
Of these, the first is as follows:
"Why do you not return to me? Why have you appeared after such a long time?
O heartless one, what is this delight in living abroad? By whom have you been driven far away?"—thus speaking in his dreams, with his neck firmly clasped by his beloved.
The wives of the enemy weep loudly, their empty arms adorned with bracelets.

Thus, in this case, because the pure *karuṇa-rasa* (the sentiment of pathos) serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*), the presence of the *rasavad-alaṅkāra* (the poetic figure of "possessing rasa") is quite evident.
In such instances, the subordinate status of other *rasas* is likewise clearly established.
An example where a mixed *rasa* or similar element serves as a subordinate element is as follows:
Cast off when he clung to her hand, violently struck even as he seized the hem of her garment,
driven away as he grasped her hair, and not even looked upon with agitation as he fell at her feet—
he who was repulsed while embracing by the young women of Tripura, whose lotus-eyes were filled with tears.
May that fire from the arrow of Śambhu, like a lover who has recently committed an offense, burn away your misfortune.

Thus, in this instance, since the extraordinary power of the Enemy of Tripura constitutes the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), the *īrṣyā-vipralambha* (love-in-separation through jealousy), accompanied by *śleṣa*, functions as its subordinate element (*aṅga*).
Such indeed is the proper domain of figures such as *rasavat*.
For this very reason, because the *īrṣyā-vipralambha* and the *karuṇa* (pathetic) sentiments are established as subordinate elements, their coexistence does not constitute a fault.
For where rasa constitutes the meaning of the sentence (vākyārtha), how can it be an ornament (alaṅkāra)?
Indeed, an ornament is well known to be a cause of beauty; but this [rasa], being the very self [of the poem], cannot be the cause of its own beauty.
And thus, this is the summary here:
the establishment of the status of all poetic ornaments as ornaments is achieved by their being arranged based on their ultimate purpose, which consists of rasa, bhāva, and so forth.
Therefore, wherever rasa and the like constitute the meaning of the sentence, that entire domain is not the province of figures such as rasa; rather,
it is a variety of dhvani, while simile and other such figures belong to that [dhvani].

However, where the production of beauty is effected by rasa and the like through the primary realization of another meaning as the sentence-meaning, that is the domain of the status of rasa and so forth as an *alaṅkāra*.
In this way, there is a distinct separation of domains between *dhvani*, the *upamā* and other figures, and the *rasavat* *alaṅkāra*.

If, however, it is asserted that the state of being the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthībhāva*) of insentient things is the province of the *rasavat* and other such figures of speech, then it would follow that figures such as simile (*upamā*) have either an extremely restricted scope or no scope at all.
This is because, when the occurrence of an insentient object constitutes the sentence-meaning, there must somehow be the introduction of the narrative of a sentient object.
Alternatively, even if such an introduction occurs, if the state of being the sentence-meaning belongs to insentient things, it is said that this is not the province of the *rasavat* figure.
Otherwise, it would be said that this great poetic composition, which serves as a treasury of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), has become tasteless.
For example:
"With waves for the knitting of her eyebrows and the rows of agitated birds for her girdle..."
Dragging along foam like a garment loosened by passion,
she moves with many faltering steps as if pierced;
surely it is that impatient woman who has transformed into the form of this river.
Or for example:

"The slender maiden, with her sprouts moistened by the water of the clouds as if her lips were washed by tears; empty of ornaments due to the departure of her season, and with the emergence of her flowers at rest;"
Resorting to silence as if out of anxiety, she is perceived through the absence of the humming of bees; having cast me down at her feet, that fierce woman has become as if filled with remorse.
Or as it is said:

"O gentle one, is all well with those vine-cottages on the banks of the daughter of Mount Kalinda— cottages that were the companions of the amorous sports of the cowherd women and the witnesses to the secret trysts of Rādhā?"
Now that the use of soft earth for preparing your bed of love has been interrupted,
I know that your sprouts, their dark luster fading, are becoming withered.
Thus, in cases such as these, even though there is no status as a sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) for insentient things, there is nonetheless an application of the narrative of a sentient entity.
Now, where there is an application of the narrative of a sentient entity, there [the presence of] rasa and so forth constitutes an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
This being the case, figures such as simile (*upamā*) would either have no scope at all or have a very limited scope.

Since there is no such thing as a non-conscious entity where the application of the characteristics of a conscious entity is entirely absent—even in its state of dissolution—therefore, rasa and the like possess the status of *alaṃkāra* (ornament) by virtue of being subordinate members (*aṅga*).

Furthermore, that which is the primary subject (*aṅgin*), whether it be rasa or a *bhāva*, and which is the object to be ornamented in every respect, is the very soul (*ātman*) of *dhvani*. (DhvA 2.5)
Furthermore:
Those qualities which take that primary object as their support are known as *guṇas*;
however, those dependent upon the subordinate elements (*aṅga*) should be considered *alaṅkāras*, like bracelets and the like. (Dhvanyāloka 2.6)
Those qualities (*guṇa*) which support that primary element (*aṅgin*), namely the meaning characterized by rasa and so forth, are like bravery and other such traits.

On the other hand, those figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) which depend upon the subordinate elements (*aṅga*)—characterized as the expressed (*vācya*) and the expressive (*vācaka*)—are to be understood as being like bracelets and other such ornaments. (Dhvanyāloka 2.6)
And thus:
"The erotic sentiment alone is the supreme, sweet, and supremely gladdening rasa;
by relying on poetry composed of that [sentiment], sweetness is established. (Dhvanyāloka 2.7)
The erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) alone is "sweet" (*madhura*) in comparison to other sentiments because it is the cause of exhilaration.
Since poetry consists of words and meanings intended to manifest that [sentiment], it possesses the quality (*guṇa*) characterized as sweetness.
Furthermore, the quality of being pleasant to hear (*śravyatva*) is common even to the quality of vigor (*ojas*). (Dhvanyāloka 2.7)
In the erotic sentiment known as *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) and in the pathetic (*karuṇa*),
sweetness attains its highest degree of moisture, because the mind is more intensely engaged therein.

However, in the case of *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (love-in-separation) and *karuṇa* (pathos), sweetness alone is preeminent, because it is the cause for the supreme degree of captivating the hearts of those with aesthetic sensitivity. (Dhvanyāloka 2.8)
The sentiments (rasas) such as the Furious (raudra) and others residing in poetry are characterized by brilliance;
*ojas* (vigor) is established based upon the word and meaning that serve as the causes for their manifestation. (Dhvanyāloka 2.9)
For the sentiments (rasas) such as the Furious (raudra) and others produce supreme brilliance and luminosity; thus, by figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), they themselves are called "brilliance.
A sentence that is devoted to manifesting that [sentiment], adorned with long compounds and stylistic figures, is [the *dīpti*]. For example:
"The blow of the fierce mace whirled by his trembling arm..."
O Queen, Bhima, his hands stained crimson with the thick, congealed blood of Suyodhana whose pair of thighs has been crushed to pieces, shall bind your hair into a braid. (Veṇīsaṃhāra 1.21)
And the subject matter intended for its illumination is expressed through clear diction, avoiding the composition of long compounds; as for example:
"Whosoever among the armies of the Pāṇḍavas bears a weapon with pride heavy upon his own arms, whosoever is of the Pāñcāla lineage—whether a child, advanced in years, or even lying in the womb..."

"Whosoever acts as a witness to that deed, whoever moves against me in battle, and whosoever is hostile—blinded by rage—I myself shall be the end-maker even of him who is the end-maker of the worlds. (Veṇīsaṃhāra 3.32).
In such passages, there is the quality of *ojas* (vigorous intensity) in both [the speaker and the subject]. (Dhvanyāloka 2.9).

That quality of poetry which consists in its capacity to convey all aesthetic flavors (rasas) is to be known as the quality of *prasāda* (clarity), which performs the common function of making everything accessible.
Clarity (*prasāda*), however, is the transparency of both word and meaning.
It should be understood as a quality common to all *rasas* and common to all compositions, established primarily with respect to the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) alone. (Dhvanyāloka 2.10)
The defects such as those offensive to the sacred scriptures (śrutiduṣṭa) and others which have been shown to be occasional,
are declared to be avoidable specifically in the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), which is the very soul of suggestion (dhvani).

Furthermore, those defects such as *śrutiduṣṭa* (offensive to the ear) and others which have been indicated are not to be avoided when the sense is merely the denoted meaning (*vācya*), nor when the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) is not Śṛṅgāra (the erotic sentiment), which is not the very soul of Dhvani.
What then? They are cited as things to be abandoned only when they occur in the Śṛṅgāra that constitutes the soul of Dhvani, appearing as the predominant suggested element (*aṅgin*).
For otherwise, they would not even possess the defect of impermanence.
Thus, this nature of *dhvani*, which illuminates the sequence that cannot be perceived, has been demonstrated in general. (DhvA 2.11)

Regarding the various divisions of its constituent parts and the internal subdivisions belonging to each, their infinity is established through the conceptualization of their mutual relationships. (Dhvanyāloka 2.12)

The suggested meaning, such as *rasa* and so forth, which has been described as the single soul of *dhvani*— where the intended non-primary expressed meaning (*vivakṣitānyapara-vācya*) is the dominant factor (*aṅgin*)— possesses infinite varieties of its subordinate elements (*aṅga*).
These subordinate elements consist of the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) that follow the expressed meaning and the expressive words, as well as the internal varieties of that dominant meaning itself,

characterized by *rasa*, emotion (*bhāva*), their semblances (*tad-ābhāsa*), and their subsidence (*tat-praśama*), all accompanied by the presentation of the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*).

The particularities (*viśeṣas*) are infinite and limitless in relation to their own substrates; when one attempts to conceive of the mutual relationships among them, it is impossible to enumerate even the varieties of any single *rasa*, let alone all of them. For instance, regarding the principal *rasa* of *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic), there are first two primary divisions: *saṃbhoga* (union) and *vipralambha* (separation).

And for *sambhoga* [love], there are varieties characterized by mutual gazing with affection, sexual dalliance, and so forth; likewise, for *vipralambha* [love-in-separation], there are varieties such as longing, jealousy, separation due to absence, and separation due to travel.
Furthermore, each of these has its own distinctions based on the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāva*).

And since there is a distinction of their states based on differences of place, time, and so forth, that single [entity] is immeasurable even with respect to its own internal distinctions; how much more so when one considers the conceptualization of the distinctions of its constituent parts?
For if one were to postulate a connection between each of those constituent parts and the various distinctions of the whole, they would indeed result in infinity. (DhvA 2.12)
However, a mere indication is stated here, by which the intellect of those with cultivated minds will attain illumination regarding everything. (DhvK 2.13)

For by means of this mere indication, the intellect of those who are learned and sensitive— having attained its light through the thorough understanding of the relationship between the primary and subordinate elements (aṅga-aṅgi-bhāva) even in a single variety of rasa along with its ornaments— will everywhere [recognize] that in this [poetry],
the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), as the primary element, is characterized by a persistent uniformity of form through deliberate effort.
In all these varieties, alliteration is not the revealing factor.

For among all the varieties of the *śṛṅgāra* rasa that have been described as the "possessor of limbs" (*aṅgin*), alliteration (*anuprāsa*) occurring as a continuous sequence (*prabandha*) with a single uniform connection is not a suggester (*vyañjaka*).

By the term "of the possessor of limbs," he states that there is freedom of choice in employing alliteration connected in a single form for the *śṛṅgāra* that has become a subordinate limb (*aṅga*). (2.14)

The composition of *yamaka* and other such figures within the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), which is the very soul of suggestion (*dhvani*), constitutes negligence even when one possesses the requisite power; this is especially true in the case of the sentiment of separation (*vipralambha*).

Erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), which constitutes the very soul of the resonance (*dhvani*), being manifested through the primary intention by means of both the expressed and the expressive, [renders] the composition of *yamakas* and other such varieties of *yamaka*, as well as difficult verbal feats such as *bhaṅga* and *śleṣa*, an act of negligence—even if one possesses the capacity for them. By the term "negligence" (*pramāditva*), this is shown: although some single *yamaka* or similar figure might occasionally be produced by mere chance (*kākatālīya*), its composition as a constituent of *rasa* generally follows the pattern of other ornaments.

"It should not be done" means that by the phrase "especially in the case of deception," an extreme delicacy (*saukumāryātiśaya*) is indicated in that context; when that [delicacy] is to be manifested, the composition of subordinate elements such as *yamaka* (rhyme) must not be undertaken as a rule. (DhvA 2.15)
The reasoning for this is stated here:

That ornament whose composition can be accomplished by being drawn out by the aesthetic flavor (rasa), and which is produced without requiring a separate effort, is considered an ornament within Dhvani. (DhvK 2.16)

Even in the case of an ornament that would otherwise be marvelous upon its completion, if its composition becomes possible only because it is drawn forth by rasa (sentiment), that ornament is considered to belong to this *dhvani* where the suggested meaning has an imperceptible process (*alakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya*). The meaning is that for such an ornament, being a constituent part of rasa is its primary function. For example:
"The decorative leaf-design on her cheek was crushed by the pressure of her palm..."
This nectar-like essence of your lower lip has been drunk by my sighs; repeatedly clinging to my throat, it makes the slope of your tear-drenched breasts tremble.
O you who are indifferent to my entreaties, it is your beloved anger that has arisen, not I.

Furthermore, the definition of being an integral part of rasa (*rasāṅga*) is that it must be accomplished without a separate effort. Thus, that which is produced by a poet who, having abandoned the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of that ornament while dwelling among his kinsmen, applies a different effort, is not an integral part of rasa.

Furthermore, when a *yamaka* (paronomasia) is composed intentionally through a continuous sequence, it necessarily involves the undertaking of another effort consisting in the search for specific words.
If it is argued that this is equally true for other figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*), we say no;

for while other figures of speech may indeed be difficult to construct when analyzed, they nevertheless emerge spontaneously through a competitive impulse in the mind of an imaginative poet whose heart is absorbed in *rasa*.
As in the *Kādambarī* at the moment of seeing Kādambarī,
and as when Queen Sītā was overwhelmed by the sight of the illusory head of Rāma at the bridge;
and this is indeed appropriate.
Since rasas are to be suggested only by specific meanings [of words],
there are summary verses on this very point:
"For some subjects are possessed of rasa and endowed with ornaments..."
By a single effort alone, they are brought to completion by the great poet.
But in the composition of figures such as the *yamaka* (paronomasia), a separate effort is required for this [the rasa];
therefore, even for one who is capable, these [figures] do not possess the status of being subordinate members (*aṅga*) to the rasa.
The presence of a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa) as a subordinate element (aṅga) is not precluded in cases such as yamaka;
however, its status as a subordinate element is untenable when it occurs within the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), which constitutes the very soul of the suggested meaning (dhvani).

Now, the class of ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) which manifests *śṛṅgāra*—which is the very soul of suggestion (*dhvani*)—is being described: "The class of ornaments, such as metaphor (*rūpaka*) and the rest, attains its true significance when it is observed and applied within *śṛṅgāra*, which is the very soul of suggestion. (DhvK 2.17)
For an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is defined as the cause of beauty for the principal subject (*aṅgin*), by virtue of its similarity to external ornaments.
As for the entire class of verbal ornaments (*vācyālaṅkāra*) such as metaphor (*rūpaka*) and so forth— whatever has been mentioned and whatever will be mentioned by some [other authorities]—
this is because ornaments are infinite.

If all of that is arranged after due consideration, then it results in the cause of beauty for the entire *dhvani* whose suggested meaning has an imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakramavyaṅgya*), which is the primary element.
And this is his consideration regarding its placement:
it should never be subordinate (*aṅga*) due to being intent upon the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*);
rather, there should be the grasping and relinquishing [of it] at the proper time, and no excessive longing for the conclusion (*nirvahaṇa*). (Dhvanyāloka 2.18)

Even though their status as subordinate elements has been established, the careful examination [of them] with effort serves to prove the subordinate status of the class of ornaments such as *rūpaka* and the rest. (Dhvanyāloka 2.19)
When a poet, his mind intensely devoted to the bonds of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), intends to describe a particular ornament as being subordinate to that flavor, it is as follows [Śākuntala 1.20]:
“You touch the glance of the beautiful-eyed young cowherd girls, with its tremulous outer corners;
moving near their ears, you softly stroke them like one whispering a secret.”
While she shakes her hand, you drink from her lower lip—the very essence of pleasure.
O bee, we are ruined by our search for the truth; you alone are truly successful!
For here, the figure of speech (alaṅkāra) consisting of the description of the nature of the bee is in harmony with the aesthetic flavor (rasa);
it is said "not as the primary element" (nāṅgitvena), meaning not by way of predominance.
For sometimes an ornament, even when intended for the purpose of conveying rasa and so forth, is seen to be intended as the primary element itself. As, for example:

By the very force of his command, delivered through the impact of his discus, he rendered the festival of love for Rāhu’s wives devoid of the unrestrained pleasures of embracing, leaving only the act of kissing.
For here, there is the intention to treat *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) as the primary element (*aṅgin*), even though the focus remains on *rasa* (aesthetic flavor) and so forth.
Even when something is intended as a subordinate element (*aṅga*), one should grasp it at the appropriate occasion, not at an inappropriate one;
such is "grasping at the right time."

As it is said in the *Ratnāvalī* (2.4): "Beholding this garden creeper today— its buds full-blown, its luster pale, already beginning to yawn, and in an instant spreading its own exhaustion through incessant outbursts of sighing— like another woman possessed by passion, I shall surely cause the face of the Queen to take on a glow crimson with anger."

In this passage from the *Rasārṇava-sudhākara* (2.26), there is a simile (*upamā*) that subordinates the pun (*śleṣa*). Furthermore, even when a particular figure has been employed, one may abandon it at the appropriate moment for the sake of conforming to the prevailing aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), in preference for another figure of speech. For example:
You are red with fresh sprouts, and I too am red with the praiseworthy virtues of my beloved;
bees released from the bow of Love come to you, and likewise they come to me;
the kick from your beloved’s foot brings you joy, and so it does for me—thus our conditions are the same.
"Everything is equal, O Aśoka; I alone have been made sorrowful by the Creator.

[14] Herein, although the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) has been established throughout the composition, its abandonment for the sake of expressing *vyatireka* (contrast) nourishes a particular aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
If it is argued that there is no conjunction of two figures of speech here,
but rather another figure characterized by *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *vyatireka* (distinction), like the case of Narasimha— [we reply: no,
because that [figure] is established as a distinct variety.
For that very word which is the domain of *śleṣa* (punning) wherein a cognition of *vyatireka* (distinction) arises by another mode is its [the *vyatireka*’s] domain;
as for example, in such cases as: “That god is Hari by name, he is with Hari through his excellent multitude of horses.
For here, one word is the domain of *śleṣa*, and another is the domain of *vyatireka*.

If, in such a case, one were to postulate a separate figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*), then the scope of *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling) would be entirely deprived of its domain. If it is argued that this is not the domain of *saṃsṛṣṭi* because the essence of *vyatireka* (contrast) is obtained here solely through the medium of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), we say no; for *vyatireka* is seen even by way of another method. For example: [Example omitted in source] In this instance, the *vyatireka* is clearly perceived even without the presence of *śleṣa*. Therefore, it is not the case that *vyatireka* can never exist independently of *śleṣa*. Consequently, since the two figures coexist here without mutual dependence, they constitute a case of *saṃsṛṣṭi*. Thus, the objection that the scope of *saṃsṛṣṭi* would be lost is invalid. Furthermore, if one were to claim that *vyatireka* is merely a subordinate element (*guṇībhūta*) to *śleṣa*, that too would be incorrect; for the *vyatireka* is intended by the poet as the primary object of expression (*vācyatvena vivakṣita*). Hence, the two figures are indeed commingled. This is established. || 107 ||

May the brilliance of the sun— whose splendor is intensely emitted and radiant, which is not diminished by the wind of the eon’s destruction nor by the mountain shattered by its merciless force, which is never devoid of the collyrium of darkness during the day,
and which has attained birth from the wings of birds but never again returns to the thief-like heat of the sun— protect you.
May that very light, appearing in another form as a wick, bring happiness to the lamp of all continents.

For here, the distinction (vyatireka) is shown even without the demonstration of the elaboration of similarity (*sāmya*). Nor should it be said that "beauty is not perceived here from mere *śleṣa* alone, because *śleṣa* is intended merely as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *vyatireka*, and thus is not an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) in its own right. This is because, in such a case, beauty is indeed observed even from mere similarity when it is well-expressed. For example:
My cries are equal to the thunders [of the clouds], my tears to the ocean of unceasing rain-showers, and the flames of my grief during their intervals to the flickering of lightning;
within me is your beloved’s face, and for you the moon— our condition is exactly the same.
"O friend cloud, why then are you constantly intent on burning me? [15] Thus begins [the verse].
