And he whose heart is solely intent on carrying out the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), yet does not wish to carry it through to its ultimate conclusion, is as follows—
Bound firmly by her lover’s beloved with the noose of her soft, trembling vine-like arms out of anger, and led to the chamber of their dwelling at evening before her friends,
she signaled her misdeed with faltering, sweet-toned words, saying, "Never again like this!"
The fortunate man is indeed struck down by his beloved as she laughs while weeping, he who is intent on concealment.
For here, the metaphor is suggested but not fully developed, yet it serves to nourish the aesthetic flavor (rasa) to the highest degree.
Even that which one desires to develop with effort is regarded as a subordinate element, as in: "Her limbs are dark like those of a startled doe; her glance is like the cast of her eyes."
"I perceive the shadow of your cheek in the moon, your tresses in the heavy plumage of peacocks, and the play of your eyebrows in the slender ripples of the river;
alas, O timid one, there is not even a single likeness of yours found anywhere in one place. And so forth.
When employed in this manner, such an ornament becomes for the poet a cause for the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*);
however, if it deviates from the stated method, it invariably becomes a cause for the disruption of that flavor.
And such instances are frequently observed even within the compositions of great poets.

However, since proclaiming faults in great souls whose very selves are illuminated by thousands of elegant sayings (*sūkti*) results only in the defilement of oneself, this has not been demonstrated in detail. Rather, following the direction of the definition shown regarding the suggestive power of the class of ornaments such as metaphor (*rūpaka*) in relation to aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth, and while himself conceiving another definition, [the author] considers the case of that which was just mentioned, where the sequence is imperceptible (*alakṣyakrama-pratibha*).
When a skilled poet, with a concentrated mind, binds this very soul of sound (dhvani) [to his work], then its attainment becomes truly magnificent. // DhvA_2.18-19 //
The self that gradually manifests, which resembles an after-sound (anusvāna), is also established as being twofold, because it is rooted in the power of both word and meaning. (Dhvanyāloka 2.20)

Since this intended *dhvani*—which has another meaning as its expressed sense (*aparavācya*)—has a manifest sequence in its suggested meaning (*saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*), its nature, which resembles a resonance (*anuraṇanaprakhya*), is also of two kinds: that rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*) and that rooted in the power of meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*). (Dhvanyāloka 2.20)

Now, if that case where another meaning is manifested through the power of the word (*śabda-śakti*) is called a variety of *dhvani*, then would not the very domain of *śleṣa* (punning) be deprived [of its scope]? To this he replies:
"The figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*), though merely suggested (*ākṣipta*), is manifested by the power of the word."
For that [suggestion] which is not expressed by the word itself arises from the power of the word.

For our intended meaning is that *dhvani* arising from the power of words (*śabda-śakty-udbhava*) is that poetry in which an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), rather than a mere matter (*vastu-mātra*), is manifested through the power of the words.
Furthermore, when two matters are manifested through the power of the words, that is *śleṣa* (paronomasia). For example:
"By him, who destroyed Manobhava (the god of love), the body of Bali’s conqueror (Viṣṇu) was formerly made into a woman..."

May that Mādhava, the giver of all, protect you— he who wears as armlets and bracelets the serpent-garlands he has uprooted, who bore the Gaṅgā, whose head the gods call "the moon-possessing Hara," and who is praised by the immortals; may he himself, the destroyer of Andhaka, protect you.
Now, Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa has shown that even when there is the manifestation of another figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*), the designation of *śleṣa* (punning) still applies;
therefore, fearing that the *dhvani* based on the power of words (*śabda-śakti-mūla*) would again have no scope, he said "suggested" (*ākṣipta*).
This is the meaning: wherever another figure of speech appears directly as the expressed sense (*vācya*) through the power of the words, all that is the domain of *śleṣa*.

However, where another distinct ornament (*alaṅkāra*)—the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) alone, which is not the expressed meaning but is implied by the power of the word or by contextual force (*sāmarthya*)—is manifested, that is the domain of *dhvani*.
An example of the direct manifestation of another ornament through the power of the word is as follows:
"Her two breasts were naturally captivating even without a necklace..."
Whose wonder did those two breasts not inspire?

In this case, since the emotion (bhāva) called wonder—which is a transitory state (vyabhicāribhāva) of the erotic sentiment—and the figure of speech known as contradiction (virodha) appear directly, this is the domain of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) assisted by the shadow of contradiction;
it is not, however, the domain of *dhvani* whose suggested meaning is comparable to an echo (*anusvāna*).

But it is certainly the domain of *dhvani* with imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya*), whether that [suggested meaning] is manifested through the *śleṣa* of the expressed sense or through contradiction.
Whose wonder did her two breasts not inspire, which were naturally captivating even without a necklace?

In this case, since the transitory emotion (vyabhicāribhāva) called wonder (vismaya) belonging to the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) and the figure of speech known as contradiction (virodha) appear simultaneously, this is the province of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) which is favored by the shadow of contradiction;

it is not, however, the province of *dhvani* whose suggested meaning is comparable to an echo (*anusvāna*). But it is indeed the province of *dhvani* where the sequence [of suggestion] is imperceptible (*alakṣyakrama*), whether that *dhvani* is manifested by the expressed *śleṣa* or by the contradiction itself.
As it has been said by me:

"Hari, whose hand is the Sudarśana discus, who possesses a body entirely worthy of praise, and who with the graceful lotus of his feet— having conquered the three worlds with the playfulness of every limb— has pervaded the universe."

May that Rukmiṇī protect you—she whom Kṛṣṇa beheld as superior to his own body, bearing a face with the lovely luster of the moon and possessing eyes whose very essence was the moon; it was truly fitting that he saw her thus.
Here, the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is perceived as supporting the shadow of the *vyatireka* (contrast) precisely by way of being expressed. As for example:
"Whirling, restlessness, heaviness of heart, dissolution, fainting, darkness, and emaciation of the body..."
And the poison, forcibly making death its cloud, serpent, and elephant, brings about the end for women separated from their lovers.
Or as it is said:
"The elephants of his arms alone are like rutting tuskers; they possess the golden dust of great pride and fragrance, and their flow of generosity is uninterrupted."
"Whose arms, like lordly elephants, have crushed the fragrance of the golden lotuses of the hearts of his enemies, yet whose flow of generosity remains unbroken.
Here, the paronomasia (śleṣa), which is supported by the shadow of a metaphor (rūpaka), appears as a primary expressed meaning.

Furthermore, where that suggested figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) has its essential nature expressed by another word, there the designation "suggestion (*dhvani*) consisting of a resonance arising from the power of words" does not apply;
rather, there the designation applies only to the expressed figures of speech such as *vakrokti* (indirect expression) and the like. For example:
"O Keśava, because my gaze was captivated by the passion for the cowherd, nothing else was seen by me."
"O Lord, it was because of you that I stumbled; why do you not support me as I fall?
You alone are the refuge for all helpless women whose minds are distressed by adversity.
Thus addressed with a touch of reproach by Gopī, may Hari protect us for a long time in the cowherd settlement.
Let all such instances as these be, at will, the domain of *vācya-śleṣa* (punning on the expressed meaning).
However, wherever another poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*), though suggested by the power of the sense, is manifested through the power of the word (*śabda-śakti*), that is entirely the domain of *dhvani*.

For example: "In the meantime, bringing to an end the pair of seasons belonging to the time of flowers, there yawned the Great Time (*mahākāla*) named Summer, with the white smile of full-blown jasmine."
And as it is said:
"Whom did the heavy bosom of the slender maiden not fill with longing— that bosom which was elevated, with its shimmering necklace, and darkened by black aloe-paste?"
Or as it is said:
"The clouds, which bestow joy upon all creatures by means of waters released at the appropriate time,
having scattered in every direction during the forenoon, now gather together as the day comes to an end."
May the rays of the Sun— the boat for crossing the ocean of existence, which is the source of long-lasting suffering—
produce in you a supreme and boundless joy that purifies all.

In these examples, since another meaning—whether relevant or irrelevant—is manifested through the power of the words (*śabda-śakti*), one must, by the force of the context (*sāmarthyāt*), conceive of a relationship of subject and object of comparison (*upamānopameya-bhāva*) between the irrelevant and the relevant meanings, so that the sentence does not result in expressing an unrelated meaning.

Thus, this *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is implied by the sense (*arthākṣipta*) and is not based on the words themselves; therefore, the domain of *dhvani* where the suggested meaning is like an after-taste (*anusvānopama*) is indeed distinct from *śleṣa*.

Furthermore, other poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) also certainly occur within *dhvani* where the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) takes the form of a resonance rooted in the power of words (*śabda-śakti-mūlānusvāna-rūpa*). For instance, even the figure of contradiction (*virodha*) is seen in that form;
as in Bhaṭṭa Bāṇa’s description of the region called Sthāṇvīśvara:

And where there are women who walk like elephants yet are virtuous; who are fair (gaurī) yet devoted to wealth; who are dark-complexioned (śyāmā) yet possess the redness of lotuses; whose faces are as pure as white birds (swans) yet whose breath is fragrant with wine—here, it is impossible to say whether this is a case of expressed contradiction (*virodha*) or a paronomasia (*śleṣa*) that merely suggests the shadow of such a contradiction, because the figure of contradiction has not been manifested by the direct word itself.

For where the figure of contradiction (*virodhālaṅkāra*) is directly conveyed by the words themselves, there the scope belongs either to the expressed figure of contradiction or to the figure of paronomasia (*śleṣa*),
as in that very same [example]: "Like a collection of mutually contradictory categories..."
For instance, as in the passage beginning: "Even the form of the sun, though surrounded by the darkness of night," or likewise from my own work:
"Hari-Kṛṣṇa, the sole refuge of all, the imperishable sovereign, the lord of intellects."
Bow down to the fourfold self, the inactive one, the subduer of enemies, the wielder of the discus.
For here, a contradiction in the form of an *anusvāna* rooted in the power of words (*śabda-śakti*) is clearly perceived.
A similar kind of *vyatireka* (distinction) is also seen,
as in my own [work]:
Those which illuminate the sky, having dispelled the darkness; those which shine upon the nails;
those which nourish the beauty of the lotuses, surpassing even the splendor of cast-off blossoms;
those which shine upon the crests of mountains and those which rest upon the heads of immortals.
May those feet of the Lord of Day, which both [the gods and the demons] tread upon, be for your prosperity.

In this way, there are other varieties of *dhvani* based on the power of words (*śabda-śakti-mūla*) whose suggested form consists of resonance (*anusvāna-rūpa-vyaṅgya*); these should be pursued by the sensitive reader (*sahṛdaya*) himself.
However, for fear of making the book too voluminous, no detailed elaboration of them has been made here.
But another type arises from the power of meaning (*artha-śakty-udbhava*), wherein the meaning itself is manifested.
That which, by its own nature and without explicit statement, manifests another object through its primary intention (tātparya).

Where a meaning, by its own inherent power, manifests another meaning even without the operation of words, that is the suggestion (dhvani) known as "arising from the power of the meaning" (artha-śakty-udbhava), whose suggested sense is comparable to an echo.
As in [Kuṣasambhava 6.84]:
"While the divine sage was speaking thus, she stood by her father's side with her face cast downward..."
Pārvatī counted the petals of her play-lotus.

For here, the counting of the petals of the play-lotus—having subordinated its own literal nature—reveals another meaning characterized by a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāri-bhāva*) even without the operation of words.
Nor is this the domain solely of *dhvani* where the sequence [of suggestion] is imperceptible;

for where the realization of aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and so forth arises from the excitants (*vibhāva*), ensuants (*anubhāva*), and transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*) directly communicated by words, [that is a different case].
That is the path for that [type of poetry] alone;
as, for example, in the *Kumārasambhava*, the description of the Goddess’s arrival while wearing ornaments of spring flowers during the context of the honey-meadow,
up to the aiming of the arrows of the Mind-born (Cupid), and the description of the specific gestures of Śambhu whose fortitude had turned away.
This is explicitly indicated by the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*). Therefore, this is a different type of *dhvani*.
Furthermore, that case where an object, assisted by the operation of a word, is employed as the suggester (*vyañjaka*) of another object, does not fall within the scope of this *dhvani*. For example:
Perceiving that the lover’s mind was fixed on the time for their tryst, the clever woman closed her play-lotus, its intent communicated through eyes that were smiling.
In this case, the suggestiveness of the closing of the play-lotus has been communicated by the very statement [of the fact]. (Dhvanyāloka 2.22)

And likewise: "Where the suggested meaning, although already hinted at by the power of the word and its sense, is further revealed by the poet through his own explicit statement—that is another ornament distinct from Suggestion (dhvani). (DhvK 2.23)

Even when a suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) is implied by the power of the word, the power of the sense, or the power of both word and sense, if it is further brought to light by the poet’s own explicit statement, that is a distinct figure of speech (alaṅkāra) different from this Dhvani whose suggestion is like an after-sound (anusvāna). Or,
such another figure of speech exists as a possibility even within Dhvani where the sequence of suggestion is imperceptible (alakṣya-krama-vyaṅgya).
In that regard, by the power of the words (śabda-śakti), as follows:

"O child, do not fall into despair; abandon this upward-rushing breath of great speed; let whatever heavy trembling you may have be [dismissed]; go hence, for here [your goal] has been seized by the slayer of Bala."

May that ocean, which— under the pretext of quelling the fear of the gods— caused you to renounce [the churning], burning away your misfortune because of your pride in Lakṣmī, consume the wickedness of those who were deluded by the churning.
By the power of meaning (*artha-śakti*), as for example:
"The mother sleeps here; here is my father, the foremost among those advanced in years; and here is the slave-girl Kumbhadāsī, her body exhausted by the toil of all the household chores."
"In this [place], I alone am a sinner, for my lord of life has been away for only a few days"—
thus did the young woman speak to the traveler, under the pretext of a remark suited to the occasion.
By means of both powers, as for example in the verse beginning, “With her gaze stolen by the passion for Keśava and Gopa,” and so forth. (Dhvanyāloka 2.23)

The meaning that serves as an illuminator (dīpaka) of another matter is to be known as twofold: that which is possible by its own nature, and that whose body is produced solely through bold assertion (prauḍhokti). (Dhvanyāloka 2.24)

Regarding the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) in *dhvani* that arises from the power of the sense (*artha-śakti-udbhava*), which takes the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana-rūpa*), the suggester (*vyañjaka*) that has been described also has two types: first, that whose body is produced solely through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti-mātra*) of either the poet or a speaker composed by the poet;
and second, that which is inherently possible (*svataḥ-sambhavī*).
An example of that whose body is produced solely through the bold assertion of the poet is as follows:
Prepare yourself; the fragrant month of spring does not yet bestow the happiness of hundreds of thousands of young women upon the face of the fresh mango tree.
The fresh leaves are the arrows of the God of Love.
The fragrant month of spring prepares itself, yet it does not yet bestow those fresh mango blossoms capable of withstanding the glances of young women.
the nine-feathered arrows of the bodiless god of love.

An example of that whose body is produced solely through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of a speaker fashioned by a poet is the verse beginning with “*śikhariṇi*,” etc., as already cited; or for example:
“[The two breasts] rising up, having been given the hand-support of youth with respect...”
It is as if the very rising of the god of love has been bestowed by your two breasts.

That which is "possible in itself" (*svataḥ sambhavī*) is that whose existence is conceivable even in the external world by virtue of its propriety (*aucitya*), and whose form is not produced solely through the power of poetic expression.
As exemplified by the verse beginning with "When he spoke thus," or as in:
"The hunter's wife, proud and wearing an ornament of peacock feathers in her ear, wanders about."
In the midst of her co-wives, who were adorned with ornaments fashioned from pearls.

Where another ornament is perceived through the power of the meaning (*artha-śakti*), with its suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) being like a resonance (*anusvāna*), that is another variety of *dhvani*. (DhvK 2.25)

Where another figure of sense (artha-alaṅkāra), distinct from the expressed figures of speech (vācya-alaṅkāra), appears as being suggested by the power of the meaning (artha-sāmarthya), that is another type of *dhvani* called "arising from the power of the meaning" (*artha-śakty-udbhava*), which is characterized by suggestion in the form of a resonance (*anusvāna-rūpa-vyaṅgya*). Anticipating the objection that its scope might be too limited, this is said: "The group of figures of speech such as metaphor (*rūpaka*) and the like, which have resorted to the status of being expressed..."
All of that, possessing the state of being presently traversed, has been demonstrated by way of abundance.

Furthermore, those figures of speech such as *rūpaka* (metaphor) and others which are well-known elsewhere as being primarily expressed (*vācyatvena prasiddha*), have been shown by the venerable Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa and others to appear predominantly as suggested meanings (*pratīyamānatayā*) in other contexts.

Thus, in cases such as *sa-sandeha* (simile-in-doubt), the manifestation of *upamā*, *rūpaka*, and *atiśayokti* has been demonstrated; therefore, the fact that one figure of speech is suggested within another does not require a separate effort to establish, yet this much is indeed stated.
Where another poetic figure is also perceived, yet the expressed meaning does not appear as being subservient to that [figure], that is not considered the path of *dhvani*. (DhvK 2.27)

The night is made heavy by the moon, the lotus-pond by its lotuses, the vine by clusters of blossoms, the beauty of autumn by swans, and poetic discourse by the virtuous.

In such examples as "The night is made weighty by the moonbeams; the lotus-pond by its lotuses; the creeper by clusters of flowers; the autumnal splendor by swans; and poetic narrative by virtuous men," although there is an underlying simile (*upamā-garbha*), the aesthetic charm (*cārutva*) is established solely through the medium of the expressed ornament (*vācyālaṅkāra*), and not by virtue of the intended meaning of a suggested ornament (*vyaṅgyālaṅkāra*).
Therefore, in that case, it is logical to designate the work as poetry solely by way of its expressed ornament (*vācyālaṅkāra*).
However, where the expressed meaning is established solely for the sake of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), there it is proper to designate it by way of the suggested meaning alone. For example:
"Having now attained prosperity, why would he subject me again to that same toil of churning?"
I do not even imagine that he, whose mind was on fire, could have experienced sleep before;
and as you approached, followed by the lords of all the islands, the trembling of the ocean appears as if it were bearing these reflections: "Why does he build a bridge once again?"
Or as it was said by me alone:
"O lady with tremulous, long eyes, now that this face of yours is smiling, filling the quarters of the sky with the splendor of its loveliness— "
Since it does not undergo even the slightest agitation, I consider it quite evident that this mass of water is indeed the ocean.

In such a case, because the aesthetic excellence of the poetry is established by relying on a metaphor (*rūpaka*) in the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana*), the designation "suggested metaphor" (*rūpaka-dhvani*) is appropriate.
An example of "suggested simile" (*upamā-dhvani*) is as follows:
"For heroes, [the embrace] on the lap of their beloved’s breasts, red with saffron, is not [as pleasing] as [the embrace] on the lap of a lioness."
His gaze was like thick vermilion upon the frontal globes of a rival elephant.
"The eyes of heroes do not take such delight in the embrace of their beloved’s breasts, red with saffron, as they do upon the frontal globes of the enemy elephant, thickly smeared with vermilion.
Or, as in my own *Viṣamabāṇalīlā*, regarding the prowess of the Asuras against Kāmadeva:

The flower-arrowed god [Kāma], having fixed his heart— single-mindedly devoted— to that very shelter, the Bimba-lip of beloved women, which is an ornament of jewels that are siblings to Fortune (Śrī).
[Supplement 982 to the *Gāhāsattasaī*]
"Their hearts, which were single-mindedly intent on seizing the jewel that was the brother of Śrī, have been directed by the Flower-Arrowed One toward the bimba-like lips of their beloveds.
This is an example of *ākṣepa-dhvani* (the suggestion of prohibition).
He is capable of describing all the virtues residing in Hayagrīva,
just as one who is able to measure the great ocean with jars of water.

Here, by means of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), there is the manifestation of a *ākṣepa* (paralipsis), which consists in demonstrating the indescribability of Hayagrīva’s qualities and serves to illuminate his extraordinary particularity. There may exist both a suggestion based on the power of meaning (*artha-śakti-mūla*) and a suggestion in the form of a resonant after-effect (*anuraṇana-rūpa-vyaṅgya*) based on the power of words (*śabda-śakti-mūla*). Of these, the example of the former is as follows:
Since this fruit is so divine, what more can be done? Yet we say this much: the sprouts of the *kaṅkella* tree are not equal to other sprouts.
"When the fruit depends on fate, what can be done? We say this much more:
the sprouts of the red Aśoka are not equal to the sprouts of other trees.
And since this is a *dhvani* that illuminates the words, there is no contradiction even though the sentence has an intended meaning (*tātparya*) other than its literal sense.
An example of the second [type] is as follows:
"O you who know much, though I have offended you, it is not possible for you to remain angry with me, whose resentment is held in the heart and whose face is tearful, while you seek to appease me."

"O man of great learning, even though you have committed an offense, it is truly not possible for you to be angry with me— even one who has placed resentment in her heart and whose face is clouded by displeasure.

For here, through a specific statement (*vācyaviśeṣa*), another general principle (*sāmānya*) which supports it— that even for one who has committed an offense, anger cannot be directed toward a man of great learning— is revealed as the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
Suggestive expression based on contrast (*vyatireka-dhvani*) can also be of two types.
Among these, an example of the first has already been shown previously.
An example of the second is as follows:
One might grow in a forest region like a tree that is crooked, gnarled, and hollow; but one must not become a poor man in the world of men, whose every taste is for wealth alone.
"In a forest region, may I be born as a very crooked tree with fallen leaves;
may I never be born poor and devoted solely to renunciation in the world of men.
For here, the lack of welcome for birth as one who is poor and whose sole essence is renunciation, and the welcome for birth as a crooked tree with fallen leaves, are directly expressed by the words.

Even from such a tree, it reveals with intentional meaning (tātparya) the greater degree of pitiable state of such a man, preceded by the perception of the relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison.
An example of the suggestion of poetic fancy (utprekṣā-dhvani) is as follows:
"Intensified by the wind of the sighs of the serpents clinging to the sandalwood trees..."
In the spring, this Malaya breeze causes travelers to swoon.
For here, in this springtime, the Malaya breeze causes the fainting of travelers precisely by inflicting the torment of love;

and that [causality] is imagined as being due to its being fanned by the breath of serpents clinging to the sandalwood trees. Thus, although the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is not explicitly stated, it is perceived through the resonance (*anuraṇana*) of the power of the sentence-meaning.
Nor can it be said that in such a case there is mere incoherence in the absence of the use of words such as "as if" (*iva*).
Because it is indicative, even when it is not employed elsewhere, one observes the comprehension of its meaning; for example:
"Even though your face is clouded by jealousy, this full moon, having attained similarity to it today, does not fit upon your body as if it were your very limb."
Indeed, even though your face is clouded by jealousy, this full-moon night moon,
having attained a likeness to it today, simply cannot fit within your body alone.
Or as it is said:
"Agitated by fear, he fled in every direction from his dwelling,
yet he was not pursued by any archers whatsoever."
Nevertheless, the deer did not stop anywhere, its beauty of eye destroyed by the arrow drawn back to the ear by her whose navel is the center of her body.
In the conventional usage of words and their meanings, common consensus alone is the authority.
An example of the suggestion of double entendre (*śleṣa-dhvani*) is as follows: "Having obtained the banners, they are beautiful; being secluded, they increase passion."
In which the youths, together with their wives, frequented the balconies whose eaves were bent down.

In this case, immediately after the comprehension of the sentence-meaning—namely, that "the women enjoy the pleasure of the *valabhī* (pavilion)"—there arises the comprehension of the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) that "the *valabhīs* are like the women. Although this is not expressed by words (*aśabdā*), it functions as the primary meaning through the power of the sense (*artha-sāmarthyāt*). An example of *yathāsaṅkhyadhvani* (suggestion based on correspondence) is as follows:
The mango tree has sprouted, put forth leaves, formed buds, and blossomed;
likewise, passion has sprouted, put forth leaves, formed buds, and blossomed within my heart.

For here, in the subsequent enumeration following the initial statement, that beauty consisting of resonance (*anuraṇana*) residing in the words "sprouted" (*aṅkurita*) and so forth—which serve as qualifiers for Madana—is perceived as surpassing the expressed meaning characterized by *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing) and *samuccaya* (conjunction) regarding Madana and the mango tree (*sahakāra*).
In this same manner, other figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) are also to be applied according to their respective fitness. (Dhvanyāloka 2.27)

Having thus explained the path of the suggestion of figures (alaṅkāra-dhvani), this is said in order to demonstrate its utility: "Those figures of speech which, when established as the expressed meaning (vācya), do not possess a formal structure, attain a supreme splendor when they have entered into the state of being a limb of suggestion. (Dhvanyāloka 2.28)
And being a constituent of *dhvani* occurs through both modes: by way of being the suggester (*vyañjaka*) and by way of being the suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
In this context, it should be understood that [the ornament] is [a constituent] by way of being the suggested, due to the subject matter at hand.
Furthermore, even when an ornament is suggested, its inclusion within *dhvani* occurs only when there is an intention to emphasize its predominance.
Otherwise, however, it will be demonstrated that [the poem] possesses the quality of having a subordinate suggested meaning (guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya).

Even when they function as the primary element (*aṅgin*) in the process of suggestion (*vyaṅgyatā*), there are two possible ways for figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*): sometimes they are suggested by a mere fact (*vastu-mātra*), and sometimes by another figure of speech. Among these—
When figures of speech are manifested by the mere thing (vastumātra) through that [suggestion],
their status as a constituent of dhvani is certain.
The reason for this is:
The poetic function (kāvya-vṛtti) has that [suggestion] as its basis. (Dhvanyāloka 2.29)
For in that case, poetry proceeds precisely by being intent upon such suggested figures of speech;
otherwise, it would be merely a sentence. (Dhvanyāloka 2.29)
Furthermore, when those very ornaments function as the suggested meaning of another ornament... [etc.]...
again,
...it would become a subordinate element of suggestion (dhvani);
for if the predominance of the suggested meaning is perceived due to the excellence of its beauty, [then the word and its denotation are merely subordinate]. (DhvK 2.30)
For it has been said: “The intention to emphasize either the expressed or the suggested meaning is based on the excellence of their respective beauty.
Regarding the suggestion of mere facts (*vastumātra*), the scope [of this function] should be inferred from the very examples presented immediately above.

Thus, when another meaning—either in the form of a specific figure of speech or as a mere fact—is manifested by another meaning, whether that [manifesting] meaning be a mere fact or a specific figure of speech, [it constitutes suggestion].

When there is prominence based on the excellence of beauty, the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) in the form of a resonance arising from the power of the sense (artha-śakty-udbhava-anuraṇana-rūpa) is to be understood. // DhvA_2.30 //
Having thus explained the various divisions of *dhvani*, it is said in order to distinguish those cases that merely appear as such:
"Where the suggested meaning appears in a blurred manner, or where it serves merely as a subordinate element to the expressed meaning—that is not the province of *dhvani*. (Dhvanyāloka 2.31)
That which is perceived is also twofold: clear (*sphuṭa*) and unclear (*asphuṭa*).
Among these, only that which is clearly manifested through the power of words (*śabda-śakti*) or the power of meaning (*artha-śakti*) constitutes the path of *dhvani*, and not the other.

Furthermore, even that which is clearly perceived, if it appears as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*), is not within the domain of this *dhvani* whose suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) takes the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana*). For example:
The lotus clusters were not crushed, nor were the swans startled, nor even my aunt;
someone simply turned over a flat stone in the village pond.
"The lotuses have not been crushed, nor have the swans been driven away, O mother-in-law;
someone has merely stirred up the dust and thrown it into the village pond.
For here, the implied meaning—the young bride’s perception of the reflection of a cloud—is indeed subordinate to the expressed meaning.

In such a case, and in any other instance where the predominance of the expressed meaning (*vācya*) over the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is determined by the perception of a superior excellence in its beauty, there is no scope for *dhvani*, because the suggested meaning is perceived as subordinate. For example:
"Of her who was hearing the clamor of the birds flying up from the thicket..."
The limbs of the young woman, busy with household chores, grow cold.
[Supplement 868 to the *Gāhāsattasaī*:
Hearing the clamor of birds flying up from the thicket of reed-vines.]
"The limbs of the young wife, occupied with household chores, grow weary.
Indeed, a subject matter of this kind will generally be cited as an example of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion).

However, where the expressed meaning—its specific nature having been determined through context and other factors—appears once again solely as a subordinate element to the suggested meaning, that belongs to this very *dhvani* whose essence is resonance (*anuraṇana-rūpa*).
The Path: For example—"Gather the fallen flowers, but do not shake the *sehālika* plant, O daughter-in-law of the farmer!
Otherwise, the sound of your bangles will be heard as a discordant cry by your father-in-law."
"Pick up the fallen flower; do not shake the *śephālikā*, O daughter-in-law of the plowman!
Your bracelet has been heard by your father-in-law, and this will result in an unpleasant consequence for you.
Here, indeed, a female friend who is sporting with her husband in a state of immodesty is being warned by another friend who has heard the soft tinkling of her bracelets from outside.

This [second type] must be taken into account for the comprehension of the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*). And once the expressed meaning has been comprehended, because it is stated with the intent of concealing its lack of propriety (*avinaya*), it again functions solely as a subordinate element of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyāṅga*); thus, its inclusion occurs precisely within this *dhvani* consisting of resonance (*anuraṇana-rūpa-vyaṅgya-dhvani*).

Now, while the distinction between *dhvani* and its semblance (*tad-ābhāsa*) regarding *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is intended (*vivakṣita-vācya*) has been set forth, he speaks in order to establish that same distinction for *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is unintended (*avivakṣita-vācya*).
Furthermore, that which is a composition where the word falters due to lack of proficiency or incapacity is not to be understood by the wise as the domain of *dhvani*. (DhvK 2.32)
Furthermore, the composition of a figurative word that is either of faltering movement, unetymological, or incapable of expression is not the domain of *dhvani*. For it is said:
"In all its varieties, the clear manifestation of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), which has become the primary element (*aṅgin*), is the complete definition of *dhvani*. (DhvK 2.33)
And that [suggestion] has precisely the aforementioned objects as its domain.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Dhvanyāloka composed by the venerable teacher Rājānaka Ānandavardhana.

The Third Illumination: Thus, having demonstrated the nature of *dhvani* along with its varieties by way of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), it is now further elucidated by way of the suggester (*vyañjaka*):
"In the case of that where the literal meaning is not intended, there is manifestation through words and sentences."
And of that other *dhvani*, which consists of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) in the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana*).

In the variety where the expressed meaning is unintended (*avivakṣita-vācya*) and the expressed is entirely set aside (*atyanta-tiraskṛta-vācya*), manifestation through a single word (*pada-prakāśatā*) is as follows: from the great seer Vyāsa—"These seven are the fuel-sticks of prosperity";

or as in Kālidāsa's—"Who, when you are prepared for battle, would neglect his wife distressed by separation?"; or likewise—"For what indeed is not an ornament for beautiful forms?"* *Note: The final phrase is a common Sanskrit proverbial expression.*
In these examples, the words "samidhaḥ" (the fuel-sticks),
"sannaddhaḥ" (armed),
and "madhurāṇām" (of the sweet things) have been employed precisely with the intention of being suggestive.

An example of that same [type] where the expressed meaning is transferred to another sense (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya*) is as follows: "By Rāma, who holds his life dear, an act was done toward his beloved that was unbecoming of love.

Here, the word "by Rāma" (*rāmeṇa*) is the suggester (*vyañjaka*), its expressed meaning being transferred to suggest qualities such as his singular devotion to daring deeds (*samasāhasaika-rasatva*).
Or, for example:
People in this world may liken her cheek to the orb of the moon;
yet, in the investigation of ultimate reality, the moon is merely a wretched moon.
"In this very way, people attribute the lunar orb to her, who is like a cheek;
yet in ultimate analysis, the moon is merely a wretched moon.
Here, the second occurrence of the word *candra* (moon) is an instance of "the expressed meaning being transmuted into another" (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya*).

An example of sentence-level manifestation (*vākya-prakāśatā*) in the variety of "where the expressed meaning is not intended" (*avivakṣita-vācya*) and where the expressed meaning is completely set aside (*atyanta-tiraskṛta-vācya*) is as follows:
"That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled man keeps watch;
that wherein all beings keep watch is night for the sage who sees."
Indeed, by this sentence, neither the meaning of "night" nor any meaning of "waking" is intended to be expressed.

What then? It is established that the sage is intent upon the knowledge of reality and averse to what is unreal; thus, this sentence possesses suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) through its literal sense being set aside (*tiraskṛta-vācya*).
An example of that very same type of sentence where the literal sense is transferred to another meaning (*arthāntara-saṅkramita-vācya*) is as follows:
Time itself is uneven for some;
for some it flows like nectar, for some it is composed of poison, and for some it is free from poison.
"For some, Time acts as poison; for others, it becomes the creation of nectar.
For some, it consists of both poison and nectar; for others, it is neither poison nor nectar.

In this sentence, because the words "poison" (viṣa) and "nectar" (amṛta) have their literal meanings transferred to the forms of suffering (duḥkha) and happiness (sukha), there is usage through these terms; thus, there is the suggestiveness (vyañjakatva) of that in which the literal meaning is transferred to another sense (arthāntara-saṅkramita-vācya).

An example of the manifestation of a word (pada-prakāśatā) in the variety of suggestion arising from the power of words (*śabda-śakty-udbhava*), where the suggested meaning takes the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana*) of the intended subject matter, is as follows: "If indeed I was not created by fate to satisfy the desires of supplicants with wealth..."
On this path, there is a lake with clear waters or perhaps a well; why then have I been made so dull?

For here, the word *jaḍa* (dull/water), used by the despondent speaker as being coreferential with himself (*vaktr-ātman*), attains through its own power a state of coreferentiality with the well (*kūpa*) by way of resonance (*anuraṇana-rūpatayā*).

This is precisely what constitutes the manifestation of the sentence, as in the lion’s roar in the *Harṣacarita*: “Now that this great dissolution has occurred, you alone remain as the serpent Śeṣa to support the earth.
For this sentence clearly manifests another meaning through the power of the words (*śabda-śakti*) by means of resonance.

Of this very [suggestion] whose body is produced solely through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet, there is a variety arising from the power of the meaning (*artha-śakty-udbhava*) by way of being manifested by a word (*pada-prakāśatayā*), as in the *Harivijaya*: "The mango sprout... (*cūaṅkurāvaasaṃ chaṇapasara-*).
The face of the Goddess of the Month of Madhu, though not yet bestowed, was seized by the Flower-Arrowed One— priceless, heart-stealing, and intoxicating like wine.
[The flower]— adorned with mango sprouts, possessing a momentary, spreading, highly precious, and captivating fragrance of wine—
was taken even though it had not been offered.
[...the face of the Fortune of the month of Madhu by means of an arrow.

For here, although it was not actually surrendered, the face of the Fortune of the month of Madhu was seized by the Flower-Arrowed One (Kusumaśara). Thus, the phrase "although not surrendered"—which denotes a state of affairs—by the power of its own meaning (*artha-śakti*), reveals the forceful compulsion of the Flower-Arrowed One.

Within this very same classification, there is "manifestation through the sentence" (*vākya-prakāśatā*), as previously illustrated by the example beginning with "The fragrant month prepares [the world]" (*sajjayati surabhimāsaḥ*). Here, the sentence-meaning—"The fragrant month prepares [the world], yet does not yet discharge arrows at the bodiless god of love"—has its body produced solely through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet; it indicates the state of the spring season being afflicted by the torment of the god of love.

Regarding the manifestation of power over the meaning of the body [of the sentence] arising from itself, the illumination of the word is as follows: "O merchant, where could we have elephant tusks, or even the fame of a tiger,
so long as my daughter-in-law with her disheveled locks wanders about the house?"
[“O merchant, where are our elephant tusks and tiger skins? For here in the house is the daughter-in-law with her face and locks disheveled, embracing me.

Here, the phrase “with her face and locks disheveled” (*lulitālaka-mukhī*), by means of the inherent power of the meaning of the hunter’s wife’s own body, suggests her addiction to the play of sexual union, thereby indicating the constant exhaustion resulting from the enjoyment of her husband.
It illuminates;
it is the very luminosity of that sentence, as in:
"The young woman with ears adorned by peacock feathers and heavy breasts wanders about."
In the midst of all the queens adorned with ornaments of pearls and gems.
"Adorned with peacock-feather earrings, the haughty wife of a hunter wanders amidst her co-wives who are decorated with ornaments made of pearls.
By this verse as well, the extraordinary good fortune of a certain recently married hunter's wife, wearing peacock-feather earrings, is revealed.

The meaning is revealed that her husband has become one who delights solely in her company and is capable of killing even a peacock; by this revelation of the sense, the extreme misfortune of the other wives—those long-married women adorned with ornaments of pearls—is proclaimed.
Furthermore, by revealing the sense that at the time of their sexual union, that very same hunter was capable of the act of slaying a noble elephant, [the same point is made].
Now, it has been stated that *dhvani* is a specific type of poetry; how then can it be manifested by individual words (*pada*)?

For a specific type of poetry is a particular arrangement of words that serves as the cause for the comprehension of a distinguished meaning. And the existence of such a thing [as a whole] is not possible if it were manifested by individual words.
Because words function as mere reminders and are not expressive [of meaning], it is said:
"This fault would arise if expressiveness were the determining factor in the linguistic usage of sound (dhvani). But this is not so; for sound is established as being a manifestor (vyañjaka)."
Furthermore, although the perception of beauty in poetic compositions— like that in physical bodies— is accomplished by the whole as delimited by its specific configuration,

it is nevertheless attributed to the individual parts through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Thus, the application of the term *dhvani* (suggestion), which is established on the basis of the suggestive power of words, is not contradictory.
Just as hearing something undesirable brings about a sense of defectiveness,
so too, in the case of those [words] with defective audition and the like, the recollection of what is desired clearly brings about a sense of excellence.
Even though words function as reminders, they appear as mere phonemes;
therefore, there is aesthetic delight in all the various varieties of sound.
Like a passionate woman graced by a single ornament that shines with exquisite artistry,
the speech of a skilled poet gleams through its suggestive resonance (dhvani) manifested in the words.
Thus are the ancillary verses. (Dhvanyāloka 3.1)
But that suggestion (dhvani) whose manifestation is of imperceptible sequence, which exists in phonemes, words, and so forth,
shines forth also in sentences, in composition, and even in entire literary works.
In this regard, having raised the objection that since phonemes (varṇas) lack inherent meaning, their capacity to suggest [meaning] is impossible, it is said:

"The letters *śa*, *ṣa*, the conjunct *s-ra* (sra), and also the letter *ḍha*—these are generally opposed to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*); yet they do not fall away from being aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). (Dhvanyāloka 3.3)
But when those very same [sounds] are employed in a sentiment such as the loathsome (bībhatsa) and others, then they indeed intensify that sentiment; they are not devoid of aesthetic flavor (rasa).

By means of these two verses, through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the expressive capacity of phonemes (*varṇa*) is demonstrated. Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of that whose sequence is imperceptible (*alakṣya-krama-vyaṅgya*) within a word, it is as follows:
"Trembling, her garment slipping away in fear..."
Casting those distressed eyes in every direction,
you were not seen by the cruel fire, which, blinded by its own smoke, suddenly consumed you with its ferocity.
For here, the word *atra* (here) clearly manifests as being composed of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) to those of sensitive hearts (*sahṛdaya*). Or, for example:
"At the sight of that deer, variegated with gold, the sudden, playful glances of my beloved fell upon me with impetuous grace."
Scattering like a mass of petals from blue lotuses tossed by the wind, they burn when remembered.
An illustration of suggestion by means of a single word-part (padāvayava) is as follows:
"In the presence of her elders, with her face cast down due to bashfulness, suppressing within her heart the anger [arising] from the violent trembling of her jar-like breasts..."
Why did she not say "Stay"? For that three-quarters of her glance, as lovely as a startled doe's eye, abandoned its tears and became fixed upon me.

Thus, here the word "tribhāga" [is used]. Furthermore, suggestion (*dhvani*) in the form of a sentence is considered to be of two kinds: pure (*śuddha*) and mixed with a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra-saṅkīrṇa*). Among these, an example of the pure kind is the verse beginning with "kṛtaka-kupitaiḥ" from the *Rāmābhyudaya*.
For this sentence, by demonstrating a mutual passion that has reached full development, reveals the supreme essence of aesthetic flavor (*rasatattva*) in every respect;
it is intermingled with other figures of speech, as in the verse beginning: “Carried away by the fresh flood of the river of Love,” and so forth.
For here, the aesthetic flavor (rasa), established by means of the metaphor which conforms to the aforementioned characteristics of the suggestor, is manifested all the more clearly. (DhvA 3.3–4)

It has been stated that *dhvani* whose suggestiveness is characterized by imperceptible sequence (*alakṣya-krama-vyaṅgya*) manifests in composition (*saṅghaṭanā*). In that regard, the nature of composition itself is first defined: "Composition is said to be threefold: that which is free from compounds (*asamāsā*), that which is adorned with middling compounds (*madhyama-samāsa*), and likewise that which consists of long compounds (*dīrgha-samāsa*). (DhvK 3.5)
By some [it is said]:
having merely restated that [position], this is stated:
"Residing by depending upon the qualities, it manifests sweetness and the other [qualities]."
The aesthetic flavors (rasas) ... [Dhvanyāloka 3.6a]
That configuration manifests the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and other qualities by depending upon them; it exists as something that subsists by relying on the qualities.
In this regard, one must consider whether there is identity or distinction between the qualities and the configuration.
Even if there is distinction, there are two possible courses.
The composition is the locus of the qualities, or the qualities are the locus of the composition.

In that regard, according to the position of their identity, and according to the position that the qualities have the composition as their locus, the meaning is this: the composition—which exists by depending on the qualities, whether those qualities are not identical with it or are its substrates—manifests the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and so forth.

But when, in the view of manifoldness (*nānātva-pakṣa*), there is the position that the qualities (*guṇa*) are the substratum of the configuration (*saṅghaṭanā*), then the meaning is that [the substance] exists by depending on the qualities, having a nature dependent on the qualities, and not being of the very form of the qualities themselves.
What, then, is the purpose of such an alternative analysis?
It is stated: if the qualities and the configuration are one single reality, or if the qualities are the substrata of the configuration...
In that case, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the qualities, like the structural arrangement, would have no fixed scope.
For the excellence of sweetness (*mādhurya*) and clarity (*prasāda*) belongs exclusively to the domains of pathos (*karuṇa*), love-in-separation (*vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*), and the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*);
whereas *ojas* (vigour) has as its domain the furious (*raudra*), the marvelous (*adbhuta*), and so forth.

The restriction of scope is established such that sweetness (*mādhurya*) and clarity (*prasāda*) have as their objects only the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*), the transitory emotions (*bhāva*), and their semblances (*tad-ābhāsa*); however, this restriction does not apply to structural composition (*saṅghaṭanā*). For instance, even in the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) flavor, long compounds are observed, whereas in the furious (*raudra*) and other flavors, there are no compounds.
In that regard, long compounds (dīrgha-samāsa) are used in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), as for example: “her locks were turned golden-brown by the pollen of mandāra flowers”; or as in:
“your [face], whose decorative leaf-patterns have been washed away by the incessant falling of drops of tears from the eyes.”
"O frail one, whom does this face resting upon the palm of the hand not torment?"—
in such instances as these, even in the *raudra* (furious) and other rasas, the absence of compound words (*asamāsa*) is observed.
As in the example: “Whosoever, heavy with pride in his own arms, bears a weapon,” and so forth.
Therefore, the qualities (guṇas) do not have the nature of the composition itself, nor do they reside in the composition.
Now, if the collection of qualities has no substratum, upon what basis are these qualities imagined?
It is said: their basis has indeed been explained. Those which depend upon that object as the possessor of qualities (aṅgin) are remembered as "qualities" (guṇas).
"However, the ornaments (alaṅkāras) should be understood as depending on the constituent parts [of speech], like bracelets and so forth.
Alternatively, let the qualities (guṇas) indeed depend solely on the words; yet they do not possess the same nature as alliteration (anuprāsa) and the like.
For alliteration and the like have been explained as being properties of words and meanings that are independent [of any specific suggested sense],
whereas the *guṇas* (poetic excellences) are indeed properties of words capable of conveying a denoted meaning (*vācya*) that manifests a particular suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*).

And their status as properties of words, even though they depend on something else, is like the status of bravery and other qualities which, though residing in the body, are considered properties of the person.
Now, if the *guṇas* have sound as their substratum, then it follows that they must either consist of the arrangement of those sounds or have them as their substratum.

For unarranged sounds cannot serve as the substratum for *guṇas* which depend on *rasa* and so forth—since [unarranged sounds] do not express specific meanings and thus cannot support what depends upon them.
This is not so.
Since it has been established that rasa and the other elements are suggested by phonemes (varṇa), words (pada), and [sentences],

or even if it is granted that rasa and the others are suggested by sentences, no fixed structural arrangement (saṅghaṭanā) can be established as their substratum. Therefore, it is the words themselves— possessing unfixed arrangements and following specific suggested meanings— that are the substrata of the qualities (guṇas).
Now, if it is indeed said that sweetness (*mādhurya*) is thus [dependent on specific arrangements], let that be so;
but how can vigor (*ojas*) have as its basis words with unrestricted composition?
For a composition that is devoid of compounds never attains the status of being a basis for vigor.
It is said: if the mind is not corrupted by the mere grasping of conventional renown, then we do not deny this here either.
How could a composition free of compounds not be the locus of *ojas* (vigor)?
For it was previously established that the brilliance (*dīpti*) of poetry manifesting the Furious (*raudra*) and other sentiments is indeed *ojas*.
And if that *ojas* were to exist even in a composition that is not compound-heavy (*asamāsa*), what fault would there be?
Nor is there any lack of aesthetic beauty (*ācārutva*) perceptible to the hearts of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*).
Therefore, there is no harm whatsoever in the fact that the *guṇas* depend upon words arranged in an unrestricted manner.
However, for these [qualities], just as in the case of the eye and so forth, there is never any deviation from their own nature as it is restricted to its respective object.

As for what was said— "Like a configuration (*saṅghaṭanā*), the qualities also result in having unrestricted objects, because deviation is observed in the case of the defined characteristics (*lakṣya*)"— [that is not so].
Regarding this, it is said: even in that case, let it be admitted that where there is a deviation from the intended object in the poetic figure (*lakṣya*), it is indeed unseemly (*virūpa*).
If it is asked, "How is it that such unloveliness (*acārutva*) does not appear to connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*) in such an instance?
[the answer is: because it is concealed by the poet's power (*kavi-śakti*).
For defect is of two kinds: that caused by a poet’s lack of learning (*avyutpatti*) and that caused by his incapacity (*aśakti*).
Among these, a defect caused by lack of learning is sometimes not perceived because it is eclipsed by [the poet's] power of expression;
however, a defect caused by incapacity is immediately recognized.
And there is a supplementary verse on this point: "A defect caused by lack of proficiency is concealed by the poet's power;
however, that which is caused by incapacity manifests itself instantly."

For instance, even among great poets, an impropriety— such as the depiction of erotic love (*śṛṅgāra*) involving well-known enjoyments with a supreme deity— is not perceived as vulgar because it is eclipsed by their poetic power, as in the description of the Goddess’s union in the *Kumārasambhava*.
And how such a departure from propriety occurs in such subjects has already been demonstrated further on.
That [the effect] is produced by capacity (*śakti*) is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
For indeed, when a poet devoid of such capacity composes the *śṛṅgāra* rasa in such a context, it clearly appears as a defect.
Now, in this view, what lack of beauty (*acārutva*) is there in such passages as "Whoever bears a weapon" (*yo yaḥ śastraṃ bibharti*)?
We are merely superimposing something that is not actually perceived.

Therefore, it is said that if *saṅghaṭanā* (structural arrangement) is distinct from the *guṇas* (poetic qualities) or if it is identical in nature to them, some other cause for its restriction must be stated:
"...The cause for that restriction is the *aucitya* (appropriateness) of the speaker and the subject matter. (Dhvanyāloka 3.6b)
In that regard, the speaker may be a poet himself or one composed by a poet;
and the one composed by a poet may either be devoid of rasa and bhāva or endowed with rasa and bhāva.
Furthermore, the rasa may reside in the protagonist of the narrative or in his adversary.

Furthermore, there are alternatives regarding the protagonist of the narrative: whether he is divided into types such as the *dhīrodātta* (noble and self-controlled) and so forth, and whether he appears at the beginning or immediately thereafter.
Moreover, the subject matter (*vācya*) may be a constituent of *rasa* whose essence is suggestion (*dhvani*), or a constituent of a semblance of *rasa* (*rasābhāsa*);
it may be intended for dramatic performance (*abhineyārtha*) or not intended for performance (*anabhineyārtha*).
It may be based on an excellent nature or on something other than that, and thus it is of many kinds.
In this regard, when the speaker is a poet who is devoid of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and emotion (*bhāva*), then there is freedom of composition;
likewise, when the speaker is one created by the poet and is himself devoid of *rasa* and *bhāva*, then it is the same.

But when the poet, or the speaker composed by the poet, is imbued with *rasa* and *bhāva*, and *rasa*— being the soul of *dhvani* because it rests upon the primary element— is predominant, then the composition must necessarily consist of either no compounds at all or only middle-sized compounds.
However, in the cases of *karuṇa* (pathos) and *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (love-in-separation), the composition should consist exclusively of uncompounded words.
If it is asked how this is so, it is said: when Rasa is to be presented as the primary element, then everything that obstructs or contradicts its apprehension must be avoided in every respect.

Thus, since a composition with long compounds—given the possibility of various types of compounds—might at times obstruct the apprehension of Rasa, excessive attachment to such [compounds] is not appropriate, especially in poetry intended for dramatic performance.
Furthermore, this is especially true in the case of *karuṇa* (pathos) and *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (love-in-separation),
for because these two are so exceedingly delicate, even a slight lack of clarity in word and meaning causes their comprehension to become sluggish.

However, when another rasa such as *raudra* (the furious) is to be conveyed, a composition with a moderate number of compounds may occasionally be employed through its connection with the activities of a hero who is firm and haughty (*dhīroddhata*).

Even a long compound is not devoid of merit when considered in relation to the expressed meaning that is appropriate to the sentiment (rasa) and is invariably connected with its suggestion; therefore, it too should not be entirely avoided. Furthermore, the quality known as clarity (prasāda) pervades all modes of composition.
For it has been stated that this [quality of clarity] is common to all rasas and common to all compositions (*saṅghaṭanā*).
Indeed, if clarity is transgressed, even a composition free of compounds (*asamāsa*) does not manifest the *karuṇa*, *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*, or *śṛṅgāra* rasas;
yet, when that [clarity] is not abandoned, even a composition with moderate compounds (*madhyama-samāsa*) does not fail to reveal them.
Therefore, clarity (*prasāda*) should be pursued everywhere.

For this very reason, in passages such as "Whoever bears a weapon," if the presence of vigor (*ojas*) is not intended, then the quality present is indeed called clarity (*prasāda*), not sweetness (*mādhurya*);
nor is there any lack of beauty.

Because it reveals the intended aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), whether the *saṅghaṭanā* (structural arrangement) is non-different from the qualities (*guṇa*) or different from them, there exists a restriction of its scope based on the aforementioned propriety (*aucitya*). Thus, it too possesses the capacity to manifest *rasa*.

Furthermore, since this very cause of restriction—which was just mentioned—is the factor that serves as the occasion for the manifestation of *rasa*, it is not contradictory to establish the qualities as having a fixed scope by means of that [arrangement] as their substratum.
Another propriety, which depends on the subject matter, also regulates that [poetic sentiment];
for it exists in various forms, established according to the different types of poetry.

Even when there is propriety pertaining to the speaker and the subject matter, another kind of propriety based on the specific context governs the composition (*saṅghaṭanā*). For this reason, the divisions of poetry include the *muktaka* (stanza standing alone), as well as those composed in Sanskrit, Prākṛit, and Apabhraṃśa;
and the *sandānitaka*, *viśeṣaka*, *kalāpaka*, and *kulaka*.
Paryāya-bandha, parikathā, khaṇḍakathā, sakalakathā, sargabandha, abhineyārtha, ākhyāyikā, kathā, and so forth—
by means of these as well, the composition becomes characterized by specific distinctions.
Among these, in the case of *muktakas*, the propriety based on them belongs to the poet who is intent upon the arrangement of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

And that has already been demonstrated elsewhere: there is freedom of action [in this regard]. For poets devoted to the composition of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) are seen even in prose compositions, as if they were working in verse.
For it is well known that the *muktaka* verses of the poet Amaruka, which overflow with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), function as a continuous composition.
However, in the case of *sandānitaka* and other such forms, because of the propriety of a grand style of composition, the construction should employ either a medium compound or a long compound.
Regarding compositions based on a larger work (*prabandha*), one must follow the propriety of the specific type of composition as previously described.
Furthermore, in the *paryāya-bandha* (successive composition), the *saṅghaṭanā* (composition) consists only of non-compound or middle-length compounds.

Occasionally, however, depending on the suitability of the meaning, even when the *saṅghaṭanā* involves long compounds, the *vṛtti* (mode of expression) must avoid being harsh (*paruṣā*) or vulgar (*grāmyā*).
In the *parikathā* (narrative), there is freedom of choice.
In that regard, because there is no excessive preoccupation with the binding of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) through the mere presentation of the plot (*itivṛtta*),
there is no contradiction even in the presence of long compounds in *khaṇḍakathā* and *sakalakathā*, which are well-known among common people and consist largely of compositions such as *kulaka*s;
however, the appropriateness of the poetic style (*vṛtti*) should be followed according to the specific *rasa*.
In the composition of a *sarga* (cantos), however, when the primary aim is *rasa*, propriety (*aucitya*) must correspond to that *rasa*; otherwise, there is freedom of choice.
Since we observe practitioners of both paths composing *sargas*, the aim of *rasa* is superior.
But in the case of works intended for performance (*abhineyārtha*), one must by all means apply oneself to the composition of *rasa*.

Since narrative tales (*ākhyāyikā*) and stories (*kathā*) consist largely of prose composition, and since prose differs from metrical verse in its structural principles, a reason for the restriction [of poetic figures] is here briefly provided, even though it has not been established before:
"It is precisely this aforementioned propriety (*aucitya*) that is the regulator of that [prose], even in all prose compositions that are devoid of metrical restriction. (Dhvanyāloka 3.8)

This very appropriateness (*aucitya*), residing in the speaker and the subject matter, which was stated to be the regulator of composition, is itself the cause of regulation even in prose (*gadya*), despite its lack of metrical constraints, depending upon the context.
For even here, when the poet or the speaker composed by the poet is devoid of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and emotion (*bhāva*), there is freedom of action;
however, when the speaker is endowed with *rasa* and *bhāva*, one must follow exactly what was previously stated.
In that case as well, it is simply a matter of suitability regarding the subject matter.
In the *ākhyāyikā*, however, the composition generally consists of middling compounds and long compounds,
because the prose possesses a certain luster by relying on a rugged style of composition.

And because that [prose] is being drawn out there, even when there is an abundance of complex structures in the composition, one must follow the propriety described for the construction of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in prose. // DhvA_3.8 //

The propriety described in the context of the binding of aesthetic flavor (rasa-bandha) shines forth as that which is relied upon everywhere; however, that stylistic arrangement (racanā) possesses some slight variation depending on the subject matter.
Alternatively, even in prose composition, the construction follows the propriety (*aucitya*) described for the construction of *rasa* throughout;
however, that [propriety] varies slightly depending on the subject matter,
but not in every respect.

For instance, even in prose composition, a construction with excessively long compounds does not shine in the *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (love-in-separation), *karuṇa* (pathetic), or *ākhyāyikā* (narrative) genres;
nor does a lack of compounds shine in dramas and the like when describing the *raudra* (furious) or *vīra* (heroic) sentiments.
However, propriety (*aucitya*) is either diminished or enhanced according to the requirements of the subject matter and its formal measure.

For thus, in the narrative (ākhyāyikā), there is no absolute absence of compounds even within its own domain; likewise, in the drama (nāṭaka) and other forms, there are no excessively long compounds. This is the direction one must follow regarding stylistic composition (saṅghaṭanā). (DhvA 3.9)
Now, the suggestion (*dhvani*) whose sequence is imperceptible (*alakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya*), which consists of entire compositions such as the *Rāmāyaṇa* and the *Mahābhārata*, is indeed well known.
However, the manner in which it is manifested is now set forth:
[it is manifested] through the beauty of the propriety (*aucitya*) of the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), and the transitory emotions (*sañcārin*).
The "method" (vidhi) refers to the body of the narrative, whether it be based on an actual event or imagined.

Having abandoned a mode of expression that is inconsistent with the requirements of the narrative, one may even, through creative imagination, construct a description of events suited to the intended aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) within the work. (Dhvanyāloka 3.11)
The joining of the junctures and their constituent parts is for the sake of manifesting aesthetic flavor (rasa),
and not merely out of a desire to fulfill the formal requirements of the treatises.
The reconnection of the principal rasa—which had begun but not yet reached its rest—occurs at appropriate intervals during its intensification and pacification. (Dhvanyāloka 3.13)

Even when the poetic figures possess the capacity [to suggest], their employment in accordance with propriety is the basis for the manifestation of rasa and the other elements within a literary composition. (Dhvanyāloka 3.14)
It has been stated that the plot (*prabandha*) is also a suggester (*vyañjaka*) of rasa and the other elements; now, the basis for its suggestiveness is explained.

First, there is the composition of the body of the narrative (*kathā-śarīra*), which is beautiful through the propriety (*aucitya*) of the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), and the transitory states (*sañcārī-bhāva*).
This composition must be arranged according to the specific determinants, consequents, and transitory states required by the particular rasa or bhāva one intends to convey.
Alternatively, the arrangement of the body of the narrative—which is made beautiful by the propriety of those [emotions] as transitory states—is one basis for suggestiveness.
Among these, the propriety of the determinants (*vibhāva*) is well known;
however, the propriety of the emotions (*bhāva*) arises from the propriety of their inherent nature (*prakṛti*).
For nature (*prakṛti*) is differentiated by way of superior, middling, and inferior states, as well as by divine, human, and other conditions.
When the stable emotion (*sthāyī bhāva*) is portrayed in accordance with that [nature] without confusion, it partakes in propriety (*aucitya*).

Otherwise, however, if the energy (*utsāha*) and other emotions of a divine being are portrayed based solely on a human basis, or those of a purely human being based solely on a divine basis, they become improper.

And likewise, when describing a mere mortal such as a king and so forth, activities characterized by the crossing of the seven oceans and the like, even if composed with elegance, invariably become devoid of aesthetic flavor;
in that case, the cause is simply impropriety (*anaucitya*).
But surely, journeys to the world of the *nāgas* and other such feats are heard of in the cases of Sātavāhana and others?
What impropriety is there in describing the extraordinary excellence of the power of that light for those rulers of the earth who are capable of sustaining the entire world?
There is none. We do not say that it is improper to describe the extraordinary excellence of the power of kings;
rather, we maintain that in a narrative concerning a product created based solely on a human basis, divine propriety should not be applied.
However, in the case of stories concerning divine or human beings, the application of both types of propriety is entirely uncontradicted,
as in the story of Pāṇḍu and others.
But regarding figures such as Sātavāhana and others, only as much of their life-story (apadāna) as is heard is to be followed, and that much appears appropriate.
However, to describe [an emotion] as distinct from those very [stable emotions] is improper.
Therefore, this is the ultimate truth here: apart from impropriety (*anaucitya*), there is no other cause for the disruption of aesthetic flavor (*rasabhaṅga*).
But the composition of well-known propriety is the supreme secret of rasa.
For this very reason, Bharata has presented the requirement that a *nāṭaka* must have a well-known subject matter and a well-known, noble protagonist as an essential duty.
By means of this, the poet does not become confused regarding the propriety or impropriety of the protagonist's character.
However, for one who would compose a *nāṭaka* or similar work with an invented plot, there is a great risk of error in describing the nature of an unestablished or unsuitable protagonist.

Now, if an examination of the propriety of divine, human, and other characters is somehow to be conducted when describing emotions such as energy (*utsāha*), let it be done; but what is the use of it in the case of love (*rati*) and the like?
For it is an established rule that even for divine beings, love must be described through conduct appropriate only to the land of Bhārata.
It is not so;
in that case, there is an even greater fault due to the transgression of propriety.
For instance, what laughter would there not be if the erotic sentiment were depicted for a character of superior nature according to the propriety of an inferior nature?
If it is argued that while the threefold propriety (*aucitya*) pertaining to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) exists even in Bhārata-varṣa, divine propriety is of no assistance there—[we reply:
we do not say that there is some other divine propriety pertaining to the erotic;

rather, just as the composition of the erotic sentiment among excellent heroes such as kings and others is appropriate in the context of Bhārata-varṣa, so too does it shine when based on divine beings.
Furthermore, it is well known that in works such as the *nāṭaka*, there is the composition of the popular *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment) as established among kings and others;
likewise, that [sentiment] must be avoided in relation to the gods.

If it is argued that there is an avoidance of it in that case because the *nāṭaka* and similar works are intended for performance (*abhineya*), and because the performance of the subject matter of *sambhoga-śṛṅgāra* is indecorous—[we reply: no.
If indecorousness belongs to drama when it has such a subject matter, by what means can it be prevented from belonging to poetry with such a subject matter?

Therefore, whether in a dramatic work or in a poetic one that is not intended for performance, the description of vulgar sexual union between a person of high character, such as a king, and heroines of high character is exceedingly indecorous, like a description of the sexual union of parents.
The same applies to objects such as supreme deities and so forth.

Furthermore, the erotic sentiment of enjoyment (*sambhoga-śṛṅgāra*) does not consist solely of the single mode characterized by sexual union; rather, other varieties are also possible, such as the mutual manifestation of love and so on.
Why, then, are they not described as belonging to the highest nature?
Therefore, just as with energy (*utsāha*), propriety of nature must be observed even in the case of love (*rati*);
and likewise in the case of wonder (*vismaya*) and the rest.
However, if even in such a matter, the lack of circumspection seen in the works of great poets (*mahākavi*) is observed in their actual compositions, that is indeed a fault;
yet it has already been stated that this fault is not perceived in them because it is eclipsed by their poetic power (*śakti*).
The propriety of the *anubhāvas* (consequent emotions), however, is well-established in the works of Bharata and others.

This much is said: a poet, while conforming to the conventions established by Bharata and others, while thoroughly examining the works of great poets, and while following his own creative intuition, must— with a concentrated mind— exert the greatest effort to avoid any lapse in the propriety of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and other elements.
By the statement, "The apprehension of the body of a story— whether factual or imagined— that possesses propriety (*aucitya*) is the suggestor," he demonstrates this:

even though there exist various stories in the *itihāsas* and other works that are rich in aesthetic flavor (*rasavat*), only that body of the story which possesses the propriety of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth is to be grasped, and nothing else.
Furthermore, one must be especially diligent when composing a narrative body that is based upon an existing work;
for in such cases, there is a great risk of the poet being perceived as lacking learning if he falters through lack of attention.
And regarding this, there is a verse of praise:
Having established the body of the narrative, the subject matter to be developed should be treated in such a way that the entire work appears as consisting of aesthetic flavor (rasa).
And the means for that is the proper pursuit of the suitability of the vibhāvas and so forth;
and that has already been shown. Furthermore:
there exist works such as the Rāmāyaṇa and others, which are renowned for their perfected aesthetic flavor (rasa).
One should not employ one's own arbitrary whims, which contradict the aesthetic flavor (rasa), as the basis for the narrative.
For regarding those very bases of discourse, one's own whim alone should not be applied;
as it has been said: "There is no transgression on the path of discourse.
Even if one's own whim is to be applied, it must not be applied in a way that contradicts the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of that [discourse].

This is another basis for the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in a composition: having abandoned a situation that, though arrived at by the force of the plot (*itivṛtta*), is somehow incompatible with the *rasa*, one should—by means of creative imagination (*utprekṣā*)—construct an intervening narrative suited to the intended *rasa*. This is seen, for example, in the compositions of Kālidāsa and in the *Harivijaya* composed by Sarvasena.
And as it is stated in my own epic poem, the *Arjunacarita*:

"A poet composing a literary work must be devoted to aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) with his whole being. If, within that plot, he perceives a situation inconsistent with the flavor, he should, even by breaking that [plot], independently create another narrative that is consistent with the flavor."
For there is no purpose for a poet in merely concluding the historical narrative, since that is already established by history itself; rather,
this is another primary basis for the composition of a literary work when its function is to manifest aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth.

The arrangement of the junctures— known as the opening (*mukha*), the development (*pratimukha*), the middle (*garbha*), the pause (*avamarśa*), and the conclusion (*nirvahaṇa*)— as well as their constituent parts (*aṅga*) such as the introduction (*upakṣepa*) and so forth, is made with a view toward the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), as in the *Ratnāvalī*,
and not merely out of a desire to fulfill the requirements of the technical treatises.
