For example, in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, the inclusion of the *vilāsa*— a limb of the *pratimukha-sandhi*— in the second act is a construction that, although inconsistent with the development of the primary sentiment (*rasa*), is intended merely to follow the authority of Bharata’s treatise.
Furthermore, another cause for the manifestation of *rasa* in a composition is the occasional interruption of the *rasa* between its intensification (*uddīpana*) and its pacification (*praśamana*).
As in the *Ratnāvalī* itself;
and furthermore, the reconnection of the principal sentiment (*rasa*) after it has been interrupted by a new beginning,
as in the *Tāpasavatsarāja*.

Furthermore, this other point must be understood regarding the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in specific compositions such as dramas: that even when figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) possess the capacity [to evoke flavor], they should be employed with appropriateness.

For a poet, being capable [of composing], might sometimes begin a composition by focusing solely on the construction of figures of speech, thereby neglecting the binding of aesthetic flavor due to being preoccupied with them; it is for the purpose of instructing him [against this] that this was stated.
Indeed, poets are seen who, in their compositions, focus exclusively on the construction of figures of speech while disregarding aesthetic flavor.
Furthermore:
Even that variety which has been described as being like a nasalization (anusvāra) also appears in certain compositions within this [sound] of resonance (dhvani). (DhvK 3.15)

Furthermore, that two-fold division of *dhvani*—which has another suggested meaning (*aparavācya*) as its intended sense and whose suggested element (*vyaṅgya*) takes the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana*)—is also manifested in certain compositions.
For example, in the *Madhumathanavijaya* within the utterances of Pāñcajanya;
or likewise, in my own *Viṣamabāṇalīlā*, in the meeting of Kāmadeva with his companions.
And as in the dialogue between the vulture and the jackal and so forth in the Mahābhārata.

It is manifested through the connection of nominal and verbal suffixes, as well as by the powers of the grammatical factors (kārakas), and by primary (kṛt), secondary (taddhita), and compound formations; in some cases, its sequence is imperceptible.

The soul of *dhvani*, consisting of rasa and so forth, is characterized by an imperceptible sequence; it is seen to be manifested when employed through specific nominal suffixes (*sub*), specific verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), specific numbers (*vacana*), specific relations (*sambandha*), the capacities of the grammatical factors (*kāraka-śakti*), specific primary derivatives (*kṛt*), specific secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*).
By the word "and" (*ca*), it is understood that it is also manifested by particles (*nipāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), tenses (*kāla*), and so forth.
For this is indeed an insult to me—that my enemies are there; and that ascetic is also right here, slaughtering the race of Rākṣasas! Oh, yet Rāvaṇa still lives!
Shame, shame on Rāvaṇa, who was defeated by a mere discus! And what is the use of Kumbhakarṇa, who was merely awakened?
What is the use of these arms, puffed up in vain for the purpose of plundering the petty village that is heaven?
For in this verse, the suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) of almost all these elements is clearly observed.
Among them, by the phrase "me yad arayaḥ" (my enemies), there is the suggestiveness of case-endings (*sup*), relations (*sambandha*), and verbal forms (*vacana*).
By the phrase "tatrāpy asau tāpasaḥ" (even there, that ascetic), there is the suggestiveness of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) and particles (*nipāta*).

In the verse, “So too he slays the race of Rākṣasas right here; oh, Rāvaṇa still lives!”, there is [the excellence] of the finite verb (tiṅ), the case-role (kāraka), and the verbal capacities (śakti).

In the half-verse beginning with “Fie, fie on the conqueror of Cakrin,” there is [the excellence] of the primary derivative (kṛt), secondary derivative (taddhita), compound (samāsa), and prefix (upasarga).
And when such a multiplicity of suggestors (vyañjaka) comes together, the splendor of the composition (bandha-chāyā) of the poem unfolds, surpassing all others.

For even where there is the manifestation of a single word that reveals the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), there is a certain beauty of composition in poetry; how much more so where there is a convergence of many such words?
As in the verse just mentioned.

For here, although the word "Rāvaṇa" is adorned by a variety of suggestion (*dhvani*) in which the literal sense is transmuted into another meaning (*arthāntara-saṃkramita-vācya*), there further arises the manifestation of the types of suggestors (*vyañjaka*) described immediately above.
Furthermore, such types of poetic compositions are frequently seen among great souls endowed with exceptional genius,
as in the case of the great seer Vyāsa: "Times have passed in which happiness was transcended, and now dreadful times have arrived."
Day by day the days become more evil; the earth has lost its youth.
For here, by means of primary derivatives (*kṛt*) and secondary nominal derivatives (*taddhita*), the suggestion of the non-discernible sequence (*alakṣyakramavyaṅgya*) is manifested;
and by the phrase "the earth has lost its youth," the suggestion in which the literal meaning is completely set aside (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*) is revealed.
Furthermore, the suggestiveness of these elements—beginning with the case endings (*sub*)—is observed almost invariably in the compositions of great poets, whether individually or in combination.
The manner in which a subordinate element acts as a suggester (*vyañjaka*) is as follows:
"By my beloved, who was made to dance to the rhythm of her bracelets jingling with beauty,
[that place] where your friend, the peacock, dwells at the close of day."
[The verb form is used as follows:
"It was surely created by fate that my eyes were made of stone;
for though they pierced your heart at the mere sight of you, your heart was not known to them."
"Go away! Do not even weep for one who was merely created; do not destroy my eyes, which were maddened by the mere sight of you, yet by which your heart was not recognized as being of such a nature.
Or, for example:
Do not block the path; go away, you shameless boy!
We are without desire; we must guard this empty house. (Gāthā-saptasatī, Suppl.
"Do not block the path; go away, you child, you immature one! Oh, how shameless you are!
We are dependent on others, since my empty house must be guarded.
As for an example of this in relation to a kinsman:
Go elsewhere, young man! Why do you gaze at me while I am bathing?
O, for those who are afraid of their wives, this [freedom] does not exist, just as it does not exist on a riverbank.
"Go elsewhere, O boy; why do you gaze at me as I am bathing? Listen! For those who are afraid of their wives, even the riverbank does not exist.
In artificial Prakrit compositions, this suggestive power (*vyañjakatva*) regarding the welfare of others is indeed made manifest.
What is the excellence of contempt?
And regarding the employment of compounds according to the propriety of their function,
the suggestiveness of particles is as follows:
This sudden separation from my beloved, brought upon me all at once, is exceedingly difficult for me to bear,
as are the days following the rising of the fresh rain-clouds.
And it must be delightful with half-shaded areas free from the heat.
And here, the word "ca" (and) is used; or as in:
"Her lower lip repeatedly covered by her fingers, charming yet faltering in its refusal to utter words of denial..."
The face of the long-lashed-eyed woman was turned toward her shoulder;
though it was somehow raised, it was not kissed.
In this context,
however, it should be understood that although the indicative function (*dyotakatva*) of particles is well known, it is mentioned here with reference to aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
As for the suggestive power (*vyañjakatva*) of prefixes (*upasarga*), it is as follows:
Beneath the trees, there are grains of wild rice fallen from the openings of hollows inhabited by parrots;
in some places, stones are visible, polished smooth by the rubbing of *iṅgudī* fruits;
and the deer, having gained confidence and moving without fear, endure the sound [of our approach].
And water-reservoir paths marked by lines of oozing sap from bark-garments, and so forth.
Furthermore, the employment of two or three prefixes within a single word is also faultless provided it is conducive to the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
For example: “Beholding the creatures whose coverings were suddenly stripped away as the darkness, possessing the luster of falling upper garments, [dispersed]. And so on.
Or as in: “acting in accordance with human conduct,” and so forth; likewise for indeclinables (*nipāta*), as in:
“O, how enviable is your vigor! and so forth; or as in: [further examples].

Alas, what a pity! Oh, where shall I go for refuge for the sake of those people who live yet cannot contain themselves within their bodies, who dance with joy upon seeing a virtuous and exalted man, their tears flowing as they weep with delight and their hair standing on end? Alas, what a tragedy! Where shall I find shelter for them?
"...may the enemy of the virtuous, who is nourishing the destruction brought about by the deceitful Fate... and so forth.
Furthermore, the repetition of words (*pada-paunaruktya*), when employed occasionally with a view toward suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*), brings beauty;
as for example:
When a wicked person, intent on his own ends, speaks with feigned words full of much flattery and a mind set on deception,
the virtuous do not fail to recognize it; indeed, they recognize it.
"They are unable to feign affection for him"—thus it begins.
An example of time acting as a suggester (*vyañjaka*) is as follows:
"Indistinguishable whether on level or uneven ground, moving very slowly in every direction..."
Before long, even those paths that are difficult to traverse will become accessible to one's desires.

For here, in the phrase "paths will soon come into being," the suffix in the word *bhaviṣyanti* (will be), which denotes a specific time, shines forth as the cause for the nourishment of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Indeed, this meaning of the verse becomes possessed of flavor when it is perceived as a determinant (*vibhāva*) of the erotic sentiment of separation caused by travel. Just as the suffixal portion is a suggester (*vyañjaka*) in this case, so too the verbal root portion is sometimes seen to be so; for example:
That was a house with low walls; this is a palace that has gained entry from heaven.
That was an old cow; these are herds of elephants with the hue of clouds wandering about.
That was the dull sound of pestles; this is the sweet music of women.
It is a marvel that in so few days this twice-born man has been raised to such a height!
In this verse, even the nominal stem (*prakṛti*) in the word *divasaiḥ* is suggestive;
and the suggestiveness of pronouns is as seen in the verse just mentioned.
Furthermore, having established in his mind that suggestiveness belongs exclusively to pronouns, the poet did not employ words such as *kva* (where).
Following this direction, other specific types of suggestors (*vyañjaka*) should also be inferred by those with sensitive hearts (*sahṛdaya*) on their own.

And although all of this has already been understood through the very statement regarding the manifestation of word, sentence, and composition, it is stated again for the sake of proficiency due to its variety.
Now, it was indeed said that the aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) and so forth are suggested by the power of the meaning (*artha-sāmarthya*).
And thus, the statement regarding the diversity of the suggestive power (*vyañjakatva*) of words such as *sub* and so forth would be entirely incoherent.
This has been stated here on the occasion of discussing the suggestiveness of words.

Furthermore, even though aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and the like are implied by specific meanings, because those specific meanings are invariably concomitant with the suggestive words, the thorough understanding of the nature of the suggester as it has been demonstrated is useful when analyzed.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the aesthetic beauty (*cārutva*) of specific words—which has been demonstrated through various classifications both here and elsewhere—is also established solely by way of their being *vyañjaka* (suggestive). Even in cases where that beauty does not manifest, one must recognize that it is precisely that excellence (*sauṣṭhava*), previously unperceived in other compositions acting as suggestors, which belongs to those words when they fall into a particular sequence; and this very quality remains present even when they are extracted [from that context] through practice.
It should be understood that [beauty] shines forth;
otherwise, if the capacity to denote meaning were equal for all words, what specific distinction regarding loveliness could there be?
If it is argued that this [distinction] is something entirely different, perceivable only by those with aesthetic sensitivity (sahṛdaya), [we reply:]...
What is this so-called "sensitivity" (sahṛdayatva)?

Is it proficiency in knowing specific conventions based on poetry that is independent of rasa and bhāva, or is it skill in thoroughly understanding the very nature of poetry consisting of rasa, bhāva, and so forth?
In the first position, there would be no fixed rule for the aesthetic charm of specific words established by such connoisseurs,
because it is possible that at another time they might establish them differently.
In the second position, however, being a connoisseur (*sahṛdaya*) consists precisely in being a knower of aesthetic flavor (*rasajña*).

For words, their innate excellence consists precisely in that capacity to impart rasa and so forth which is to be experienced by such connoisseurs; thus, their primary beauty resides solely in their power of suggestion (*vyañjakatva*).

However, for those [words] based on denotation (*vācakatva*), their specific quality is clarity (*prasāda*) when there is a dependence on the meaning, whereas when there is no dependence on the meaning, it is simply alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and the like. (Dhvanyāloka 3.15–16)
Having thus described the nature of that which manifests rasa and the other elements, this [verse] is commenced in order to define their contrary forms:

"Whether in a continuous composition (prabandha) or in an isolated verse (muktaka), one who desires to bind together rasa and the rest must exert effort, with a keen intellect, in the avoidance of their contraries. (Dhvanyāloka 3.17)
Whether in a continuous composition or in a detached verse, a poet whose mind is intent upon the depiction of *rasa* and *bhāva* should exert supreme effort to avoid contradictions;
otherwise, not even a single verse consisting of *rasa* will be properly accomplished. (3.17)
What, then, are those contradictions that must be avoided by a poet with effort? It is said:

The employment of excitants (*vibhāva*) and other factors associated with a conflicting rasa, and the description of another object, even if it is elaborately developed [in the context]. (Dhvanyāloka 3.18)

An interruption at an inappropriate moment, manifestation at an inappropriate time, the repeated highlighting even of that which has already reached full development, and indeed impropriety of style— all these lead to the contradiction of rasa. (Dhvanyāloka 3.19)

In relation to the rasa under discussion, the inclusion of the excitants (vibhāvas), ensuants (bhāvas), and ensuants of change (anubhāvas) belonging to a rasa that is its opposite is possible as a cause for the contradiction of the rasa.

Among these, the inclusion of the excitants of a contrary rasa occurs, for example, when after describing the excitants of the *śānta* (quiescent) rasa—having been defined precisely as such excitants—one immediately proceeds to describe the excitants of *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) or other rasas.

The inclusion of the ensuants of a contrary rasa occurs, for example, when one attempts to appease amorous women who are angry due to a lovers' quarrel with their beloved by means of discourses on dispassion (*vairāgya*).

The inclusion of the *anubhāvas* (consequent manifestations) of a conflicting *rasa* is, for example, when the *nāyaka*, overcome by a fit of anger toward his beloved who remains displeased despite his affection, describes the *anubhāvas* of the *raudra-rasa* (fury).
Another cause of the disruption of *rasa* is the extensive description of some other matter, even if it is somehow connected, at the expense of the *rasa* under discussion;

as, for instance, when a poet, out of a fondness for employing ornaments such as *yamaka* (paronomasia), describes a mountain or similar object at great length while he had begun to describe a particular *nāyaka* within the context of the *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (love-in-separation).

Furthermore, this other cause of the disruption of aesthetic flavor (*rasa-bhaṅga*) should be understood: namely, an interruption of the flavor at an inappropriate moment, and the manifestation of the flavor at an inappropriate moment.

In that regard, an untimely cessation of the flavor is as follows: when the love-in-union (*śṛṅgāra*) of a certain hero has reached its highest state of development through a heroine with whom he is to have a desirable union, and their mutual passion is known, it would be improper to interrupt the contemplation of the means for their union.
Regarding the description of other activities independently, having abandoned the ongoing narrative,

and the manifestation of rasa at an inappropriate time— for instance, in a battle resembling the dissolution of a kalpa where various heroic deeds are already underway— the cause for the manifestation of the erotic sentiment of separation (*vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*) would not apply even to a hero who is like Lord Rāma himself.
Without propriety, there is no justification for introducing a description of the descent [of a deity] within an erotic narrative;

nor is being deluded by fate an acceptable excuse for the protagonist in such a context, because it is the composition of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) alone that rightly constitutes the primary motive for a poet’s undertaking.
It was stated previously—beginning with the verse, "Just as a person seeking light exerts effort toward the flame of a lamp"—that the description of the plot is merely a means to that end.

Therefore, since such lapses occur among poets when there is a primary focus on the mere description of historical events (*itivṛtta*) and when they compose *rasas* and *bhāvas* devoid of the relationship between the primary and subordinate elements (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*), it is appropriate that these works have as their ultimate purport (*tātparya*) the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) consisting of *rasa* and so forth;
thus, our effort has been undertaken for this reason, and not out of an obsession with merely propounding the theory of *dhvani*.
Furthermore, this other cause for the disruption of rasa (rasa-bhaṅga-hetu) must be understood: the repeated intensification of a rasa that has already reached its full development.
For a rasa that has been experienced and has attained its full development through its own causal complex (sāmagrī), when it is touched upon again and again, becomes like a withered flower.
Likewise, any impropriety (anaucitya) regarding conduct or worldly behavior is also a cause for the disruption of rasa.
For example, when a heroine expresses her own desire for sexual union with the hero in a manner that is inappropriate;

or when there is an *anaucitya* (inappropriateness), such as the employment of the *vṛttis* well-known to Bharata— namely the *Kaiśikī* and others— or those known from other treatises on poetic ornaments, such as the *Upanāgarikā* and others, in an unsuitable context—
that too is a cause for the disruption of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Thus, regarding these contradictions of rasa and others of a similar kind that may be conceived by oneself, good poets must remain vigilant in their avoidance.
And on this point, there are these summary verses: "For good poets, the primary objects of their activity are rasa and the like."
In their composition, which is to be contemplated, they must always remain vigilant.

A composition that is devoid of aesthetic flavor is a great verbal fault for a poet; because of it, he would be no poet at all, whereas by another [type of work], his status as a poet remains unchallenged according to the traditional definition.
In former times, poets were unrestrained in speech and attained great fame;
relying on their example, a wise person should not abandon this policy.
"And this method we have not presented is outside the intention of those renowned lords of poets, headed by Vālmīki and Vyāsa. (Dhvanyāloka 3.19)
But when the intended rasa has attained firm establishment, the mention of its opposites—whether they function as subordinates or are subject to suppression—is free from fault. (Dhvanyāloka 3.20)

However, when the intended rasa has attained full development through its own causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is no fault in the mention of those elements that are opposed to it—namely, elements belonging to a conflicting rasa—provided they have either become subordinate (*aṅga-bhāva*) to the primary rasa or are subject to suppression (*bādhya*).
For the state of being suppressed by a conflicting element occurs only when such elements are capable of being overcome, and not otherwise;
thus, their mention serves precisely to nourish the rasa under discussion.
Furthermore, for those things that have attained the status of being auxiliary members (*aṅga*), their very state of contradiction ceases.
For the attainment of the status of an auxiliary member by these things is either natural or produced through superimposition (*samāropa*).
In that regard, as for those whose [attainment] is innate (*naisargikī*), there is indeed no contradiction when they are stated.

Just as in the case of the *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment of separation), there is no fault in the presence of its constituent elements such as illness and so forth, nor in those [elements] which are indeed its constituents;
however, even when their status as constituents is possible, the mention of death is not superior [as a poetic element],
because upon the severance of the substratum, the rasa would reach a state of absolute cessation.

If it is argued that there will be a nourishment of the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*) in such a context, we say no; for that [pathetic sentiment] is not the subject at hand, and there would be an interruption of what is currently under discussion. However, where the pathetic sentiment itself constitutes the very purpose of the poem, there is no contradiction.

In the case of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), if death is possible with a non-prolonged recovery, its occasional depiction is not absolutely contradictory. However, if the recovery takes a long time, there is indeed an interruption in the flow [of the sentiment] in the interim; therefore, a poet whose primary concern is the composition of rasa should avoid such a narrative structure. In that regard, however, when the intended rasa has already established itself, there is no fault if the elements of a conflicting rasa are described as being subordinate (*bādhyatvena*), as for example:
Where is the reproach of the hare-marked moon, and where is my noble lineage? May she be seen once more;
alas, my learning has served only to quell my faults! Oh, even in anger her face was lovely.
What will those stainless ones of perfected intellect say? She is difficult to find even in a dream.
Attain composure of mind; for what fortunate youth indeed shall drink from this lower lip?
Or as in the description of the instruction given by the second young sage to Puṇḍarīka, whose intense passion for Mahāśvetā had already set in;
there is no fault when a natural state becomes a subordinate element (aṅga), as in: "Whirling, restlessness, and heaviness of heart..."
"The poison born of the serpent-cloud forcibly brings about dissolution, fainting, darkness, exhaustion of the body, and even death for women separated from their lovers"— thus it begins.
There is no contradiction even when [a subordinate element] is superimposed, as in the case of “pāṇḍu-kṣāmam” (pale and emaciated) and so forth.

Furthermore, this attainment of the status of a subordinate element is distinct [from the previous cases], in that when there is a single principal sentence-meaning due to its being the governing factor, two mutually contradictory *rasas* or *bhāvas* both attain the status of subordinates;
in that case too, there is no fault.
As it has been said: "Cast aside, yet clinging to the hand," and so forth.
If it is asked how there is no contradiction in that case, it is because both of those [statements] are established as being intended for something else.
If it is asked, "Even if they are directed toward another [purpose], how can there be a cessation of contradiction between two contradictory things?
it is said: The fault of the coexistence of contradictories lies in a positive injunction (*vidhi*), not in a restatement (*anuvāda*). For example: "Come! Go! Fall! Rise! Speak! Observe silence!"
"In this way, the wealthy play with supplicants who are seized by the planet of desire," and so forth.
For in such cases, there is no contradiction when both injunction and prohibition are present as mere restatements (*anuvāda*); likewise, it will be so here as well.
Indeed, in this verse, neither the object of the erotic sentiment of separation through jealousy (*īrṣyā-vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*) nor that of the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*) is being enjoined.

Since the extraordinary power of the enemy of Tripura constitutes the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), and since those two [the simile and the hyperbole] are established as subordinate elements (*aṅga*) to it;
nor can it be said that the technical distinction between injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*) does not exist regarding aesthetic flavors (*rasa*),
because they are accepted as being the meaning of sentences.
Who can prevent the injunctions and restatements that apply to the sentence-meaning and the expressed meaning from also applying to the aesthetic flavors (rasas) implied by them?
Furthermore, even by those who do not accept that the aesthetic flavors and so forth constitute the direct object of poetry,
it must necessarily be admitted that these [flavors] are at least the cause of that [poetic effect].
Nevertheless, there is no contradiction in this verse.

For, from the enjoined element—which has as its auxiliaries the restated subsidiary factors, the cause, both [the subsidiary and the cause], the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and the objective entity—there arises the cognition of a specific emotional state (*bhāva-viśeṣa*); therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Indeed, it is observed that a specific effect is produced from a cause that possesses two contradictory auxiliaries.
For it is contradictory for a single cause to simultaneously produce two opposing effects, but it is not contradictory for it to have two opposing factors as its auxiliaries.
If it is asked how a performance (*abhinaya*) can be employed with respect to such contradictory objects,
the same principle that applies to the subject matter of such a statement being restated will apply here as well.
Thus, by relying on the method of restating the injunction (*vidhi*), the contradiction in this verse is first resolved.

Furthermore, when describing the extraordinary power of some leader whose rise is to be celebrated, the sentiment of compassion (*karuṇa-rasa*) felt toward his adversaries does not cause dejection in discerning critics; on the contrary, it serves as a cause for an excess of joy.
Since it is said that [the emotion] "proceeds," because its power is blunted, there is no fault whatsoever in establishing a contradiction with it.

Therefore, it is logical to say that "that which contradicts the rasa" (rasavirodhin) refers to something that contradicts either the rasa or the bhāva that has become the primary meaning of the sentence,
but not to anything that is merely a subordinate element (aṅga).

Alternatively, even for some object of the sentiment of pathos (*karuṇa-rasa*) that has become the primary meaning of the sentence, its conjunction with an element of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-vastu*) by means of a particular stylistic turn serves solely to nourish that sentiment; for objects that are naturally sweet, when they have fallen into a state of lamentation, produce an even greater intensity of grief when their former states are recollected through their past playful charms. As it is said:
"This is he who used to pull up my girdle and press against my full breasts..."
"His hand touched her navel, thighs, and hips, loosening the knot of her garment"—
in such passages as these, the amorous Śambhu, whose offenses were fresh, behaved toward the young women of Tripura just as he did;
thus, even by this manner of expression, there is indeed no contradiction.
Therefore, however one examines this matter, in every way there is an absence of fault. And thus:
Treading upon the ground strewn with darbha grass, their feet—marked as if by fallen lac-dye from their tender toes wounded and bleeding—leave their faces washed by falling tears.
Terrified, with their hands grasped by the hands of their husbands, the lords of your enemies now wander about the forest fire as if they were entering into marriage once again.
In this manner, it should be understood that all such cases are indeed free from contradiction.
Thus, first of all, the distinction between the domains of the coexistence and non-coexistence of sentiments (rasa) and so forth with contradictory sentiments has been shown. (DhvA 3.20)
Now, in order to establish the proper sequence for arranging them within a single composition, it is said:
"Even though compositions are established as being based on various sentiments (rasa), one who desires their excellence must accept that a single sentiment is the primary one. (Dhvanyāloka 3.21)

Although it is well known that in literary compositions such as mahākāvyas or dramas, many aesthetic flavors (rasas) are composed in a scattered manner through the relationship of primary and subordinate elements, nevertheless, for one who desires a particular excellence of luster in those compositions, some specific intended rasa among them must be established as the predominant element (aṅgin).
Thus, this is the more logical path.

Anticipating the objection—"How is it not contradictory for a single rasa to be the predominant factor when many other rasas have attained full development?"—this is said: "The intrusion of other rasas does not impair the predominance of the rasa under discussion, provided that [the latter] manifests as the stable emotion (sthāyin). (Dhvanyāloka 3.22)

When a rasa that has been introduced at the very beginning of a composition is pursued again and again as the dominant sentiment (sthāyin), its interpenetration by other rasas occurring in the intervals— though pervading the entire work— does not detract from its status as the primary element. (Dhvanyāloka 3.22)
To demonstrate this very point, it is said:
"Just as a single effect is established as pervading a continuous sequence, so too in the composition of rasa, no contradiction whatsoever exists. (Dhvanyāloka 3.23)

Just as in the case of a literary composition consisting of parts such as the *saṃdhi*, a single effect is postulated that persists throughout and pervades it, yet it is not confused with other effects,
nor is its primacy diminished even when it is intermingled with them;
in exactly the same way, there is no contradiction whatsoever when a single *rasa* is introduced.
On the contrary, for those who possess discernment, who are engaged in contemplation, and who are sensitive-souled, an extraordinary rapture arises toward such an object. (Dhvanyāloka 3.23)

Now, in the case of those sentiments that are not mutually contradictory— such as the heroic and the erotic, the erotic and the comic, the furious and the erotic, the heroic and the marvelous, the heroic and the furious, the furious and the pathetic, or the erotic and the marvelous— let there be a relationship of primary and subordinate (aṅga-aṅgin) between them. But how could such a relationship exist for those which stand in a relation of mutual sublation (bādhya-bādhaka-bhāva)?

Anticipating the objection that this might apply to cases such as the erotic and the loathsome, the heroic and the terrifying, the tranquil and the furious, or the tranquil and the erotic, the following is stated:

"Whether a rasa is non-conflicting or conflicting with another rasa that serves as the primary element (aṅgin), it must not be allowed to reach full development; in that way, its non-conflict is maintained. (Dhvanyāloka 3.24)

When there is a primary sentiment (*aṅgin*), such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) or another, which is manifested through the composition (*prabandha-vyaṅgya*), a subordinate sentiment (*rasa*)—whether non-contradictory or contradictory—must not be brought to full development (*paripoṣa*). In that regard, the first avoidance of development is this: the non-contradictory sentiment must not be made excessively predominant relative to the primary sentiment, because even if their excellence were equal, no contradiction would arise between them. For example:
On one side his beloved weeps; on the other, the roar of the battle-trumpets.
By affection and by the passion for combat, the warrior’s heart is tossed to and fro.
Or as it is said:
Having cut the necklace from her neck and twirling it like a rosary in her hand,
she assumed the paryanka posture with her girdle-string as a serpent-king;
with her lips quivering as she muttered false mantras, she revealed an indistinct smile.
"May she, by whom the Goddess Sandhyā was seen there with jealousy and Paśupati was made to smile, protect you"— in this [verse],

the second [type of *sahokti*] consists in either the non-inclusion of a profusion of transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) that are incompatible with Aṅgiras, or, if they are included, their immediate subordination to a transitory emotion of Aṅgiras.

Furthermore, the third [type] consists of the repeated contemplation of the *rasa* that has become a subordinate element (*aṅga*), even as it is being brought to full development. Other varieties should also be inferred along these lines.
However, in the case of a conflicting *rasa*, its deficiency must be ensured in comparison with the *rasa* that serves as the subordinate element.
Just as when the *śānta* (tranquil) rasa is subordinate to the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic), or the *śṛṅgāra* is subordinate to the *śānta*.
If it is asked, "How can a rasa that lacks full development (*paripoṣa*) be considered a rasa?", it has been stated here that this is in relation to its status as a subordinate element (*aṅga*).
For the degree of full development that belongs to a rasa as a principal element (*aṅgin*) need not be applied to it when it is subordinate.
But who can prevent the natural development [of a rasa] that is possible by itself?

Furthermore, this state of being preeminent in relation to one particular rasa among many rasas in literary compositions— which even one who does not accept the relationship of primary and subordinate between rasas cannot deny— is, in this manner, not in conflict with those [other rasas] that are non-contradictory.
Furthermore, when conflicting rasas are integrated through the relationship of primary and subordinate (aṅga-aṅgi-bhāva), there is no contradiction within literary compositions (prabandhas).
This entire discussion is stated according to the view of those for whom one rasa may function as a transitory emotion (vyabhicārin) toward another rasa.
Even in other systems, the stable emotions (sthāyibhāvas) are designated by the word "rasa" figuratively; thus, their status as subordinate elements is entirely free from contradiction. (DhvA 3.24)

Having thus established the common means of non-contradiction regarding the immersion of both non-conflicting and conflicting [emotions] into the dominant rasa (aṅgin) which persists as a continuum, the following is now stated in order to explain that very same means specifically with respect to the domain of the conflicting:
"But that which is a conflicting emotion (sthāyin) sharing a single locus with another [emotion] is contradictory..."
That effect has a distinct substratum; thus, there is no fault even in its nourishment.
Opposition is of two kinds: that which is opposed by sharing a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇya*) and that which is opposed by contiguity (*nairantarya*).

Among these, when there is opposition with a single locus between the dominant stable emotion (*sthāyin*), which is the primary rasa, and its opposite—considering propriety—that opposition must be made to have different loci.
The locus of that hero should be placed upon the object that is his adversary, namely the opponent of the protagonist of the narrative.
This being the case, even the nourishment of that which is its opposite is faultless;
for when an excess of fear regarding the opposing side is described, the hero's excellence in statesmanship, valor, and so forth is all the more illuminated.
This has been clearly demonstrated by me in the context of Arjuna’s descent into Pātāla in my *Arjunacarita*.

Thus, it has been shown how there is no contradiction when a stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), which exists within a continuous narrative (*prabandha*) and opposes [other emotions] by virtue of sharing a single substratum (*aikādhikaraṇya*), attains the status of a subordinate element (*aṅgabhāva*) for the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Now, however, in order to demonstrate this for the second case, it is said:
"When they share a single locus (*ekāśrayatva*), there is no fault; but when they occur in immediate succession (*nairantarya*), there is contradiction."
A rasa may be suggested by a wise person through the intervention of another rasa. (Dhvanyāloka 3.26)

Furthermore, that which is non-contradictory when within the same context, yet contradictory in terms of immediate succession, should be introduced into the composition by means of an intervening rasa;
as for example, the *śānta* (peaceful) and *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasas are introduced in the *Nāgānanda*.
And the *śānta* rasa—characterized by the full development of the bliss of the destruction of craving—is indeed perceived there.
And so it has been said:
"Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is—
these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the bliss of the destruction of craving."

Even if it is true that this state does not fall within the range of experience for all people, it cannot on that account be rejected as a specific mental transformation characterized by extraordinary power that is common among those who have seen the light. Nor is it proper to include it within the category of the "hero" (vīra),
because that is established as being composed of conceit (abhimāna).

And since this [state] exists as having the singular nature of the subsiding of egoism (ahaṅkāra), if unity were to be postulated despite the existence of such a distinction between those two, then the same would follow for the heroic (vīra) and the furious (raudra) sentiments as well. Furthermore,
because specific mental states such as compassion-heroic (dayā-vīra) and others are entirely devoid of egoism, they are varieties of the peaceful sentiment (śānta-rasa).
Otherwise, however, if it were established that [the *śānta*] is merely a sub-variety of the *vīra*, there would be no contradiction.
Thus, the *śānta* rasa exists;
and because it is separated by non-conflicting rasas, it remains free from contradiction even when conflicting rasas are present within a literary composition (*prabandha*).
As has been demonstrated in the subject matter [already] shown.
To confirm this very point, it is said:
"For even when two sentiments reside within a single sentence, their mutual opposition ceases once they are separated by another sentiment. (Dhvanyāloka 3.27)
There is no doubt that the contradiction between two sentiments existing within a single composition is removed when they are separated by another sentiment;
for, according to the principle already stated, the contradiction between even two sentiments situated within a single sentence is likewise removed. For example:
[the limbs] smeared with the dust of the earth... the fresh *pārijāta*...
With their waists perfumed by the pollen from flower garlands, their arms were tightly embraced by female jackals, while the spaces between them were filled with the embraces of celestial nymphs.
They were fanned by the quivering wings of blood-drinking birds,
and were cooled by sprinklings of sandalwood water.
With fragrant garments from the wish-fulfilling vines.
Seated upon the couches within their celestial palaces,
they were at that time filled with curiosity as [the sights] were being pointed out by the fingers of the women.

"The heroes saw their own fallen bodies"— in such passages as these, the coexistence of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), or their respective subordinates (*aṅga*), is not contradictory because they are separated by the heroic sentiment (*vīra-rasa*). One should analyze contradiction and non-contradiction everywhere in this manner.
In particular, however, this [quality] is most delicate in the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).
A connoisseur should determine, in accordance with the characteristics as stated, the presence or absence of contradiction among all the *rasas* within a composition or elsewhere;
this is especially true for the *śṛṅgāra*.

For that [rasa], being essentially the nourishment of *rati*, and because *rati* can be shattered by even a slight cause, is the most delicate of all *rasas* and cannot tolerate even the slightest intrusion of a contradictory element.
A true poet, possessing an excellence of concentration, endures [the difficulties] in that very aesthetic flavor (rasa);
for any negligence regarding it is immediately perceived.
And regarding that very rasa, which possesses a preeminent delicacy superior to all other rasas, the poet should be attentive and diligent;
for if he is negligent therein, he will quickly become an object of contempt among the connoisseurs.
Indeed, because it is invariably an object of experience for worldly beings, the *śṛṅgāra* rasa is the most prominent of all rasas by virtue of its loveliness.
And this being the case:

"In order to attract those to be instructed, or for the sake of enhancing the beauty of the poem, there is no fault in the contact of a rasa opposed to that [intended rasa] with its constituent parts. (Dhvanyāloka 3.30)

The contact with a rasa incompatible with the erotic (śṛṅgāra), which belongs to the components of the erotic, does not constitute a fault not only when there is a connection characterized by non-contradiction, but it also does not constitute a fault when it is employed for the sake of the beauty of the poem in order to attract the disciples [to the teaching]. For once the disciples have been attracted by the components of the erotic rasa, they easily accept the instructions of discipline.
For dramatic assemblies and the like, which take the form of instruction in right conduct (*sad-ācāra*), were introduced by the Sages solely for the benefit of those to be trained.

Furthermore, because the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is delightful and captivating to the minds of all people, its inclusion as a constituent element in poetry nourishes an excellence of beauty; thus, by this reasoning as well, the inclusion of elements of the erotic sentiment is not contradictory even when it occurs within a conflicting sentiment.
And therefore:
It is true that women are enchanting; it is true that worldly splendors are delightful;
yet life is indeed as fickle as the flickering glance from the corner of an intoxicated woman's eye.

In such cases as these, there is no fault of incompatibility between the aesthetic flavors (rasas). Having thus understood the scope of compatibility and incompatibility among the flavors and other elements, a skilled poet, while composing poetry, is never deluded. (Dhvanyāloka 3.31)

Thus, by understanding through this manner just described the scope of both the mutual opposition and non-opposition among *rasas*, *bhāvas*, and their semblances (*tad-ābhāsas*), a skilled poet, endowed with an excellence of creative intuition (*pratibhā*),
does not falter anywhere while composing poetry.

Having thus established the utility of determining compatibility and incompatibility regarding rasa and the other elements, the same is now demonstrated for the determination of the suggester (vyañjaka), the suggested (vācya), and the signifier (vācaka) within that same domain:

"The employment of the signifieds and signifiers in accordance with propriety (*aucitya*) with respect to the domain of rasa and the rest—this is the primary task of the great poet. (Dhvanyāloka 3.32)

The primary task of a great poet is the appropriate application of the specific events to be expressed (*vācya*) and of the expressive words (*vācaka*) directed toward them, in relation to the aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) and other elements.

Indeed, this alone is the principal function of a great poet: to make the *rasas* and so forth the primary meaning of the poem by composing both words and meanings in a manner conducive to their manifestation.
And that the composition of poetry with a focus on *rasa* and the like is well-known even in the works of Bharata and others, he states in order to demonstrate:
The usage of both meaning and word based on their conformity with the aesthetic flavor (rasa) and other factors is what constitutes propriety;
these styles (vṛtti) thus established are of two kinds.
For "vṛtti" (mode) is said to be "vyavahāra" (conduct).

In this context, those modes such as Kaiśikī and the others are conduct based on the expressed meaning (*vācya*) that is either in harmony with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) or possesses propriety (*aucitya*);
while those such as Upanāgarikā and the others are based on the expressive word (*vācaka*).
For the stylistic modes (*vṛtti*), when arranged with a primary intent toward the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and so forth, bring about a certain luster to both drama and poetry;
for the aesthetic flavors and the like constitute the very life-force of both,
whereas the plot and such elements constitute merely the body.

On this point, some say: "The relationship of quality and qualified (guṇa-guṇi) between the aesthetic flavors (rasas) and so forth on one hand and the plot (itivṛtta) and so forth on the other is appropriate, but the relationship of soul and body (jīva-śarīra) is not;
for the expressed meaning (vācya) appears as consisting of the flavors and so forth, rather than as something distinct from the flavors and so forth."
To this it is replied: if the denoted meaning (*vācya*) were composed solely of rasa and so forth— just as the body is composed of whiteness—

then, just as whiteness necessarily appears to everyone when the body appears, so too would rasa and the rest appear to both the sensitive (*sahṛdaya*) and the insensitive (*asahṛdaya*) simultaneously with the denoted meaning.
But it is not so; this has already been established in the first chapter (uddyota).

It might be argued: "Just as the genuineness of gems is perceived through the excellence of the connoisseur, so too the nature of the expressed meanings as rasa and so forth is perceived [through the excellence of the appreciator].
This is not so.

For just as in the case of a gem appearing as a species of gem, its nature is perceived as being non-different from the very essence of the gem, so too the rasa and other aesthetic elements would have to be perceived as non-different from their denotable forms consisting of the excitants (vibhāva), ensuants (anubhāva), and the like. But this is not the case; for no one understands that the excitants, ensuants, and transitory emotions (vyabhicārin) themselves are the rasa.

For this very reason, the apprehension of rasa and the like is inseparable from the apprehension of the excitants (vibhāvas) and so forth; since these two apprehensions are established as being in a relationship of cause and effect, a sequence is necessarily present.
However, because of its extreme rapidity, that sequence is not perceived, and thus it has been said: "The suggested rasas and the like are indeed those whose sequence is imperceptible.

Now, one might object: since the word itself—delimited by context and other factors—produces the apprehension of both the expressed and the suggested simultaneously, what is the use of postulating a sequence in this case?
For it is not the case that the consideration of the cognition of the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) is the sole basis for the suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) of a word;
for instance, there is the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) even from words such as songs,
and yet there is no intervening consideration of the expressed meaning in those cases.

To this we reply: we certainly accept that words possess suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) through delimitation by context and other factors. However, that suggestiveness of theirs is sometimes based on a specific nature (*svarūpa-viśeṣa*) and sometimes based on expressive power (*vācaka-śakti*).

Among these, if for those whose [suggestiveness] is based on expressive power, that [suggestiveness] were accomplished merely through the cognition of their own form without the cognition of the expressed meaning, then it would not be based on expressive power.

Now, it follows as a matter of course that the cognition of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) occurs subsequent to the cognition of the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*vācya-vācaka-bhāva*), which is itself necessarily based on that [relationship].
If that sequence is not perceived due to its extreme rapidity (*lāghava*), what can be done?
Furthermore, if the cognition of rasa and so forth were produced by the word alone, as delimited by context and other factors, even without the cognition of the signified meaning; [then...]

This [suggestion] might occur for those listeners who have not ascertained the context and are themselves unlearned in the relationship between the signified and the signifier, solely upon hearing the poem; however, in that case,
the cognition of the signified would be useless for the coexistence [of suggestion].
Or, even in the case of utility, there is no simultaneity.

Even for those things whose nature as a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) consists in being the cause for the cognition of a specific form—such as songs and other sounds—there exists a sequence that necessarily occurs between the cognition of their own form and the cognition of the manifested object (*vyaṅgya*). However, this sequence of the priority and posteriority of actions in a word is not perceived in cases where the accomplishment of its result occurs rapidly, where it is not achievable by any other means, or where it does not conflict with the expressed meaning, as in the case of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and the like, which are distinct from other denotable objects.
In some cases, however, it is indeed perceived, as in the cognitions of suggested meanings (vyaṅgya) in the form of resonance (anuraṇana).
If it is asked how that is so, it is said: first, regarding the dhvani in which the suggested meaning in the form of resonance is rooted in the power of the sense (artha-śakti-mūla)...
Since the expressed meaning and the other meaning implied by its power are distinct from other expressed meanings,

the relationship of cause and effect between their two cognitions— which are themselves absolutely distinct— is impossible to deny; thus, the sequence of priority and posteriority therein is quite evident,
as in the verses cited in the first chapter (udyota) for the sake of establishing the suggested meaning (*pratīyamānārtha*).
In such a case, because the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya) are entirely distinct, it cannot be said that the cognition of one is identical to the cognition of the other. However,

in the case of *dhvani* where the suggestion takes the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana*) rooted in the power of words— as in the verse beginning “May the cows produce for you the highest and most boundless joy among purifying things”— when two meanings are cognized through the verbal process, the relationship of simile (*upamānopameya-bhāva*) between those two meanings is perceived.

Even when there is an absence of words expressing a simile, [the simile] is suggested by the power of the sense (*artha-sāmarthya*); even in that case, the sequence between the comprehension of the expressed meaning and the suggested ornament (*alaṃkāra*) is easily discernible. This is also true in the case of *dhvani*—where the suggested meaning takes the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana*) rooted in the power of the word (*śabda-śakti-mūla*) revealed by the words—regarding an adjective (*viśeṣaṇa-pada*) capable of being connected with both meanings.

Even in a case where there is no word serving as a connector (*yojaka*), the connection (*yojana*)—though not explicitly expressed by the words—is established through the sense; here too, as before, the sequence between the comprehension of the expressed meaning and the comprehension of the mere figure of speech (alaṅkāra) implied by its power is firmly established.

Furthermore, even this comprehension derived from the sense, in such a context, is produced by the power of the words capable of connecting both meanings, and is thus considered to be rooted in the power of the words (*śabda-śakti-mūla*).

In the case of *dhvani* where the expressed meaning (*vācya*) is not intended to be primary, however, there is a rule-governed sequence in which the manifestation of another meaning occurs only after the perception of a turning away from its own well-known domain.
Because the expressed meaning is not intended there, no investigation into a sequential perception of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) alongside the expressed meaning has been undertaken.

Therefore, just as between the cognition of the signifier (*abhidhāna*) and the signified (*abhidheya*), there is a rule-governed sequence due to the relationship of cause and effect (*nimitta-nimittibhāva*) between the cognition of the expressed and the cognition of the suggested.
However, according to the reasoning already stated, it is perceived in some cases and not perceived in others.

Thus, when the varieties of *dhvani* have been defined by way of their manifestors (*vyañjaka*), someone might ask: "What is this so-called 'manifestor-ness' (*vyañjakatva*)? Is it the illumination of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*)? But that is not manifestor-ness."

Furthermore, that suggestibility (*vyaṅgyatva*) of the meaning depends upon the establishment of the suggester (*vyañjaka*); and the establishment of suggestiveness depends upon the suggestible. Thus, because of this mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), there is no stable foundation.

[Objection: But surely the existence of a suggestible distinct from the expressed (*vācya*) has already been established; and since the establishment of the suggester depends upon that [establishment of the suggestible], what occasion is there for such an objection?
This is indeed true.
By the arguments previously stated, the existence of an entity distinct from the expressed meaning has been established;

however, why is that object designated specifically as "suggested" (*vyaṅgya*)? Furthermore, where there is no primary persistence [of the suggested], it is proper to designate it precisely as "expressed" (*vācya*).
Because the sentence is directed toward that [object],
the function of the sentence that reveals it is simply its denotative power (*vācakatva*).
What is the use of postulating another function for it?
Therefore, that object which is the focus of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is primarily what is denoted.

As for the intermediate cognition of another denotable object in such a case, it is merely a means (*upāya*) for the cognition of that [intended] meaning, just as the cognition of word-meanings is a means for the cognition of the sentence-meaning.

To this it is replied: where a word, while denoting its own primary meaning, causes another meaning to be understood, there exists both its capacity to denote its own primary meaning and its status as the cause for the understanding of that other meaning.
Between these two, there is either no distinction or there is a distinction.
First of all, they are not without distinction; for those two operations are indeed perceived as having different objects and different forms.
For indeed, the function of a word characterized as denotation has its own meaning as its object, whereas the function characterized as indication has another meaning as its object.
Furthermore, the linguistic usage regarding one's own [meaning] and another [meaning]— namely, that between the denoted and the indicated— cannot be denied,
because one is perceived as being directly related [to the word], while the other is perceived as being related to that which is related [to the word].

For the denoted meaning is directly related to the word, whereas the other [implied] meaning is brought forth by the power of the denoted meaning; it is related to that which is related [to the word].
If its status as being directly related to the word were [the case], then the very designation of it as a "different meaning" would not occur.
Therefore, the distinction between the objects of these two operations is well-established.
The distinction between the two forms is indeed well-established;
for the power of denotation is not the same as the power of comprehension,
since we observe that even non-denotative things, such as songs and the like, bring about the comprehension of objects characterized by aesthetic flavor (rasa) and so forth.
Moreover, it is well known that even non-verbal gestures and the like reveal specific meanings;
for instance, in the verse beginning with "With her face bent down from modesty," a particular gesture was indeed shown by the skillful poet as the cause for revealing the meaning.

Therefore, because they have different objects and different forms, there is a clear distinction between a word's function of denoting its own primary meaning and its function of being a cause for the comprehension of another meaning.
If it is a particularity (*viśeṣa*), then it cannot now be designated as "denotable" (*vācya*)—that is, as something whose status as denotable is implied by the capacity of the denoted object itself.
We certainly accept that it falls within the scope of the word's operation; however, that occurs solely through being suggested (*vyaṅgya*), not through being denoted (*vācya*).

Furthermore, since that other meaning is perceived through its fitness for a relationship with another well-known designation, it is only appropriate to speak of its "manifestation" when it is made the object of another word expressing its own primary meaning. Moreover, the logic of the word-meaning (*padārtha*) and the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) does not apply to the expressed (*vācya*) and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
For some scholars maintain that the cognition of word-meanings is indeed unreal;
even by those who do not accept its unreality, the analogy of the jar and its material causes must be accepted regarding the relationship between the sentence-meaning and the word-meanings.
Just as when a jar has been produced, its material causes are no longer perceived separately, so it is with the sentence.
Alternatively, once that meaning is understood, or when those words and their respective meanings are perceived as distinct at that time, the very cognition of the sentence-meaning would vanish.
However, this logic does not apply to the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya);
for when the suggested is being perceived, the cognition of the expressed does not vanish.
Because it is manifested through an inseparable connection with the appearance of the signified (vācya),
the principle of the jar and the lamp applies to these two;

for just as when the cognition of a jar arises by means of a lamp, the illumination of the lamp does not cease, so too the appearance of the signified does not cease during the cognition of that which is manifested by it.

As for what was stated in the first Uddyota, beginning with "just as [the meaning is conveyed] by way of the word-meanings" (1.10), that was intended to show their equality merely on account of being means [to the same end].
But surely, in this case, it follows that a sentence would possess two meanings simultaneously; and if that were so, its very status as a single sentence would be undermined.
Because that [coherence] is characterized by a single purpose;
this is not a fault,
since those two are established through the relationship of subordinate and principal.

For in some cases the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) is predominant while the expressed meaning (vācya) is subordinate, and in other cases the expressed meaning is predominant while the other is subordinate.
Among these, it has already been stated that when the suggested meaning is predominant, it is called *dhvani*;
however, when the expressed meaning is predominant, another variety will be described.

Therefore, it is established that even though poetry is intent upon the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), the suggested meaning does not possess the status of being the denoted (*abhidheya*), but rather possesses the status of being the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) alone.
Furthermore, when the suggested meaning is not intended as the primary focus, you yourselves must not admit that it is the denoted, because the word is not intent upon it (*atatpara*).
Thus, it remains a fact that there is indeed a certain domain of words that is suggested.

Even where that [expressive power] is predominant, why should its very nature be denied? Thus, first of all, the power of manifestation (*vyañjakatva*) is indeed distinct from the power of expression (*vācakatva*); furthermore, the power of manifestation is distinct from the power of expression because while the power of expression has the word alone as its locus, the other [power of manifestation] has both the word and the meaning as its locus, since the power of manifestation belongs to both word and meaning.
Because it has already been established [that the primary function does not apply here],
the operation of a quality (*guṇavṛtti*), however, may rely on both metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Nevertheless, suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) differs from that even further, both in terms of its essential nature and its object.
This, first of all, is the distinction between the two types of function: it is well known that a secondary function (*guṇavṛtti*) is an operation that is non-primary;
however, the function of suggestion (*vyañjakatva*) is the primary operation of the word itself.
For the cognition of the three types of suggested meanings [the literal, the indicated, and the suggested] which arises from the meaning is not perceived as being even slightly non-primary.

And this is another distinction regarding its essential nature: that which is called "denotative function" (*vācakatva*) is established as being non-primary in relation to the operation of qualities (*guṇa-vṛtti*);
however, "suggestive function" (*vyañjakatva*) is entirely distinct from denotative function.
And this has been demonstrated.

This is another distinction regarding form (*rūpa*): when an object, in the operation of its qualities (*guṇavṛtti*), indicates another object, it then becomes transformed into the very nature of that indicated object, as in the case of "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" and so forth. However, in the process of manifestation (*vyañjakatvamārga*), when an object illuminates another object, it is perceived as the illuminator of the other precisely while manifesting its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), like a lamp.
For example, as in "Pārvatī counted the petals of her play-lotus," and so forth.
Furthermore, if the conventional usage of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is applied only where a meaning whose own denotation is not set aside indicates another meaning,
then it follows that indication alone must be the primary function of a word.
For generally, sentences possess an appearance of a meaning that is their intended purport (*tātparya*), which is distinct from the literal meaning (*vācya*).
Now, even in your own view, when the meaning itself manifests the three types of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*), what kind of operation (*vyāpāra*) does the word have?

It is said: since such suggestiveness of the meaning occurs precisely through the power of the word as delimited by context and other factors, how can the utility of the word in that regard be denied?
The difference in scope between *guṇavṛtti* (the function of poetic quality) and *vyañjakatva* (suggestiveness) is indeed clear.

For the scope of suggestiveness consists of three things: aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) and the like, specific figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*), and the object (*vastu*) as delimited by its suggested form.
Among these, no one asserts—and it cannot even be maintained—that the cognition of *rasa* and the like constitutes *guṇavṛtti*.
The cognition of suggested figures of speech (*vyaṅgyālaṅkāra*) is likewise [to be understood].
That which is intended to be conveyed without being denoted by its own word for the sake of perceiving the beauty of a thing (*vastu-cārutva*) is the "suggested" (*vyaṅgya*).
And not all of that is the domain of secondary function (*guṇavṛtti*), because we observe the use of figurative words even in accordance with common usage (*prasiddhi*) and convention (*anurodha*).
As was stated previously:

even that which is the object of figurative function (guṇavṛtti) is so only by way of entering into the state of being a suggester (vyañjakatva). Therefore, there is an absolute difference between figurative function and suggestiveness.
Moreover, although that [suggestion] is distinct from the functions of denotation (*vācakatva*) and secondary indication (*guṇavṛtti*), it is established as being based on both of them;
for suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) is sometimes established by relying on denotation, as in the case of *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is intended as something other than the primary one.
In some cases, however, it occurs by relying on the function of secondary qualities (*guṇavṛtti*), as in the case of *dhvani* where the literal meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*).
Furthermore, precisely to demonstrate that it relies upon both of these, two primary divisions of *dhvani* were presented first.
And because it relies upon both of those, its identity with either one of them cannot be asserted.
For it is not exclusively of the nature of denotation, since in some cases it functions by resorting to indication (lakṣaṇā);
nor is it exclusively of the nature of indication, since in other cases it is established by resorting to denotation.
Nor does that [word] fail to possess each of those individual forms simply because it possesses both natures;
for it also lacks the nature of sound as defined by being devoid of the characteristics of denotativeness and so forth.
For instance, even musical sounds possess the capacity to manifest aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and other such objects.
Furthermore, neither their status as denoters (*vācakatva*) nor their function as indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is perceived in any way.
Since suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) is observed even in objects other than words, it is improper to claim that it is a mode of the properties of words such as denotative power.

Moreover, if suggestiveness were postulated as a mode [of words] despite its being distinct from well-known modes such as denotative power and indication, then that [suggestiveness] would belong to the word itself.
Why is it not postulated as a mode?
Thus, in verbal discourse, there are three modes: denotative power (*vācakatva*), metaphorical function (*guṇavṛtti*), and suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*).
Among these, when suggestiveness involves the predominance of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyaprādhānya*), that is *dhvani*.

Of that [dhvani], two varieties have been enumerated—namely, that whose expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣita-vācya*) and that whose expressed meaning is intended but subordinate to another (*vivakṣitānyapara-vācya*). These two have first of all been determined in detail.

Another might say: "Is it not true that what has been stated—that there is no operation of secondary function (*guṇavṛtti*) in the case of dhvani where the expressed meaning is intended but subordinate—is incorrect?
For, in a case where the comprehension of another meaning occurs preceded by the cognition of the expressed and the expressive, how can there be the designation of 'secondary function'?"
For when a word is superimposed upon another object by means of some cause through a figurative function (*guṇavṛtti*), its own primary meaning is completely set aside—

as in "The boy is fire" (*agnir māṇavakaḥ*) and so forth— or when, without entirely abandoning its own primary meaning, it extends to another object by way of its connection with that [primary] meaning; [in both cases, there is metaphorical usage].
As in the case of "a hamlet on the Ganges" and similar examples, the state of the expressed meaning being unintended (*avivakṣita-vācyatva*) is established.

For this very reason, in *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is intended for something else (*vivakṣitānyapara-vācya*), both the cognition of the essential forms of the expressed and the expressive, as well as the comprehension of the [deeper] meaning, are observed; thus, the designation of "suggestiveness" (*vyañjakatva*) is applied.
That which manifests its own form while simultaneously illuminating another is called a "manifestor" (*vyañjaka*);

in such a case, since the function of manifestation is nothing other than denotation (*vācakatva*), one cannot by any rule apply the conventional designation of "secondary function" (*guṇavṛtti*). How, then, is *dhvani*—in which the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*)—distinguished from secondary function?
Since its two-fold division is indeed characterized by the nature of the two-fold division of *guṇa* (poetic quality) and *vṛtti* (mode of operation),

this too is not a fault; for while *dhvani* whose literal meaning is unintended (*avivakṣitavācya*) may rely upon the path of *guṇa* and *vṛtti*, it does not consist solely of the form of *guṇa* and *vṛtti*.
For the operation of a poetic quality (*guṇa-vṛtti*) is observed even when devoid of suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*).
Moreover, suggestiveness does not establish itself without the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), which is the cause of the aforementioned beauty.

However, the operation of a poetic quality can exist in the form of a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), based either on the attributes of the expressed meaning (*vācya-dharma*) or solely on the suggested meaning.
As in "The boy is fire because of his sharpness," or "Her face is indeed the moon because of its loveliness," and so forth;
and as in "With a beloved person, there is no such thing as repetition," and so forth.

Even that function consisting of the characteristic (lakṣaṇa), form (rūpa), quality (guṇa), and operation (vṛtti) is indeed possible even without the cognition of a charming suggested meaning (vyaṅgya), by relying merely on the connection with the object to be indicated (upalakṣaṇīya),
as in cases such as "The platforms cry out.

However, where that [function] is the cause for the cognition of a charming suggested meaning, there too it occurs only through the entry of suggestiveness (vyañjakatva), just like denotative power (vācakatva).
Furthermore, where linguistic usage occurs with respect to an impossible object—

such as in the case of “the earth with golden flowers” and the like— it is precisely the cognition of the suggested beautiful form (*cāru-rūpa-vyaṅgya*) that serves as the motivator; thus, even in such a domain, when there is a secondary function of words (*guṇavṛtti*), it is only the designation of *dhvani* (suggestive poetry) that accords with logical reasoning.

Therefore, in *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣita-vācya*), the function of *guṇa* (poetic quality) and *vṛtti* (poetic figure) is indistinguishable from the specific nature of suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) in both varieties; it is not, however, of that same single form [as mere suggestion], because it is perceived as delighting the hearts of the connoisseurs, whereas elsewhere it is seen to be devoid of that form since it serves merely as a cause for cognition.

And although all of this has been indicated previously, it is stated again for the sake of even clearer understanding. Furthermore, that property of word and meaning characterized as "suggestiveness" (*vyañjakatva*) conforms to the well-known relationship [between them]; thus, it cannot be a subject of doubt for anyone. For the operation characterized as suggestiveness follows precisely that well-known relationship between word and meaning called the "signifier-signified relation" (*vācya-vācaka-bhāva*), due to its connection with a different set of causal conditions (*sāmagry-antara*).
It functions as something conditioned (*aupādhika*).
For this very reason, its distinction lies in its denotative capacity (*vācakatva*).

Indeed, denotative capacity is the fixed nature of a specific word, because it is established as being invariably concomitant with that [meaning] from the time of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) onward.
But that [meaning] is indeterminate, because it is conditioned by limiting adjuncts (upādhi);
for it is apprehended through delimitation by context and so forth, whereas otherwise it would not be apprehended.
Now, if it is indeed indeterminate, what is the use of examining its essential nature?
This is not a fault; for its indeterminacy pertains to the nature of the word itself.
But it is not so in its own domain, characterized by the suggested (vyaṅgya); and the logic of being a mark (liṅgatva) is observed for this state of being a suggester (vyañjakabhāva),
just as the state of being a mark has an indefinite appearance with respect to its substrata.
Because it is dependent on one's will,
and because it does not deviate from its own object;
this manifestation is exactly as has been shown.
Furthermore, because it is not restricted to the nature of the word itself, its status as a mode of denotation (*vācakatva-prakāratā*) cannot be postulated.
For if it were a mode of denotation belonging to that [word], it would necessarily be restricted to the nature of that word, just like the property of denotation itself.

And such a contingent (*aupādhika*) attribute of words, by one who knows the true nature of sentences and asserts that the relationship between word and meaning is innate (*autpattika*), while explaining the distinction between human and non-human sentences, [cannot be maintained].

For if that [intrinsic capacity] were not admitted, then even though the relationship between word and meaning were eternal, there would be no distinction between non-human (apauruṣeya) and human (pauruṣeya) sentences in their communication of meaning. But if it is admitted, then in the case of human sentences— which possess other adventitious functions superimposed in accordance with human intention— even while they do not abandon their own inherent connection to the denoted object, they may also have false meanings.

For it is observed that entities, even while not abandoning their own intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), can possess contradictory functions when they undergo other conditioned operations (*aupādhika-vyāpāra*) produced by the encounter with a different causal complex (*sāmagry-antara*).

To illustrate: it is well known that the rays of the moon and similar phenomena, while carrying a coolness that quenches the entire world of living beings, nevertheless cause intense heat (*santāpa*) when beheld by people whose minds are being consumed by the fire of separation from their beloveds.

Therefore, one who wishes to establish the falsity of human utterances— even while admitting that they possess an innate connection with their objects— must clearly state some adventitious form distinct from their denotative capacity (*vācakatva*).
And that [form] is none other than suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*).
For suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) consists in the manifestation of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
And human sentences primarily manifest the intention of the person [who composed them].
And that [intention] is indeed the suggested, but not the denoted (*abhidheya*).
Because there is no relationship characterized by the status of signifier and signified between that [word] and its co-utterance. [Objection:
But surely, by this logic, the conventional usage of the term "dhvani" would apply to all worldly sentences, since all of them are manifestors according to this principle.
This is true;
however, that suggestiveness which arises from the manifestation of the speaker’s intention is common to all worldly sentences without distinction.
Moreover, it does not differ from denotative power (*vācakatva*), for in that case, the suggested meaning is established as being invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyakatayā*).
But it is not by virtue of being intended [to be expressed].
However, that suggested meaning which exists by virtue of being intended is what constitutes suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*), which is the cause for the designation "suggestion" (*dhvani*).

On the other hand, that suggested meaning which consists of a specific intention and is manifested through both word and sense becomes "intended" when it is manifested as the primary purport (*tātparya*).
However, that alone is not the sole determinant for the application of the term *dhvani*, because it is not all-encompassing (*avyāpaka*).

Rather, everything—whether manifesting through its intended meaning (*tātparya*) in the form of the three types of distinctions previously shown, or whether it is of the nature of intention (*abhiprāya-rūpa*) or non-intentional—is the determinant for the application of the term *dhvani*. Thus, the definition of *dhvani* consists in the specific quality of suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) as described above.

There is neither over-extension nor under-extension [of the definition]. Therefore, according to the view of those who know the true nature of speech, the verbal operation characterized as manifestation (*vyañjakatva*) is not contradictory; on the contrary, it is observed to be entirely consistent.
