Since this discourse on *dhvani* proceeds by relying precisely upon the opinion of the wise who have attained the certainty of the flawless *Śabdabrahman*, why should one deliberate with them regarding contradiction or non-contradiction?

However, for those who know the reasoning and maintain that the relationship between word and meaning is artificial (*kṛtrima*), this manifesting capacity (*vyañjakabhāva*) of words— which is established by experience— is not subject to rejection, provided it is not in contradiction [with other facts], just as in the case of other meanings. Indeed, let the disagreements of the logicians (*tārkika*) proceed regarding the status of being a denoter (*vācakatva*).

Is this [meaning] inherent (*svābhāvika*) to words, or is it conventional (*sāmayika*), and so forth? But if [words] are manifestors (*vyañjaka*), then when that which follows upon them—which is common to other entities and already well-established in worldly usage—is being followed, what occasion is there for disagreements?
For all the disagreements of logicians (*tārkika*) proceed regarding supramundane (*alaukika*) matters, but not regarding mundane ones.

For indeed, regarding such realities as blue, sweet, and so forth—which fall within the range of the senses of all people in the world and are free from sublation—no mutual disagreements are observed.
Indeed, when one says "this blue is blue" in a manner free from sublation, one is not contradicted by another saying, "This is not blue; it is yellow.

In the same way, who can deny that which is established by the experience of everyone: namely, the capacity to manifest [meaning] belonging to expressive words, to non-expressive musical sounds, and to non-verbal forms such as gestures?
For in the assemblies of the discerning, various utterances and actions—whether formal or informal—that indicate a charming meaning even when it is not explicitly stated, are perceived;
what conscious person, wishing to avoid becoming an object of ridicule for themselves, would intentionally deceive them?
Now, he might say:

There is an opportunity for a refutation: the suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) of words is their capacity to convey meaning (*gamakatva*), and that is precisely their nature as a logical mark (*liṅgatva*).

Consequently, the cognition of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) is nothing other than the cognition of the object possessing the mark (*liṅgin*); thus, their relationship of the suggested and the suggester is simply the relationship of the marked and the mark, and nothing else.

Therefore, this must necessarily be understood: since you have just now established that suggestiveness depends upon the speaker’s intention (*vaktr-abhiprāya*), and the speaker’s intention is of the nature of an inferable object (*anumeya*).

To this it is replied: Even if this were so, what of it? What is lost to us? We accept that there exists a function of the word characterized as manifestation (*vyañjakatva*), which is distinct from the functions of denotation (*vācakatva*), quality (*guṇa*), and metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And even in this case, there is no impairment whatsoever of that [manifesting function].

Whether that quality of being a manifestor (*vyañjakatva*) be considered "being a logical mark" (*liṅgatva*) or something else, in any case, it possesses a character distinct from all well-known verbal modes and has as its object the operation of the word; thus, there is no dispute between us on this point. However, it is not an ultimate truth that being a manifestor is necessarily being a logical mark, nor that every cognition of a manifested object is necessarily a cognition of a logical consequence (*liṅgin*).

Furthermore, as for that which you have restated from our own statement in order to establish your own position—namely, that because the speaker’s intention is admitted to be the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), words possess the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*) only in its manifestation—that very point, as we have explained it, shall now be set forth in detail; listen: the object of words is twofold.
The object of inference (*anumeya*) is that which is to be established. In this context, the object of inference is characterized by the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*).
This intention is of two kinds: the desire to manifest the nature of the word itself, and the desire to manifest the meaning by means of the word.
Among these, the first is not a factor for verbal linguistic usage (*śābda-vyavahāra*),
for it has as its fruit merely the cognition of the quality of being a living being (*prāṇitva*).
The second, however, even though it is mediated by the determination of a specific word, is the basis for verbal linguistic usage which employs that word.

Both of these, however, are the inferable objects of words; but the object to be communicated is that meaning which has been made the focus of the speaker’s intention to communicate a meaning. And that is of two kinds: the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya).
For an agent sometimes intends to manifest an object by means of its own word, and sometimes, depending on a particular purpose, by way of its not being denotable by its own word.
Yet that twofold object to be communicated does not shine forth to words in its own form as something possessing an inferential mark (*liṅgin*),
but rather through another relation, whether artificial or natural.
For the state of being the object of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) is perceived of that meaning through its being indicated by words, but not its intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).

If the operation of words toward it were indeed by way of indication, then disputes regarding the correctness or falsity of that word-meaning would never arise, just as in the case of another inferable object inferred from a mark such as smoke.

Furthermore, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), being implied by the power of the expressed (*vācya-sāmarthya-ākṣiptatayā*), certainly becomes a relation of the word, just like the expressed meaning itself.
For whether a relationship is direct or indirect is irrelevant to its function;
moreover, it has already been demonstrated that suggestiveness (vyañjakatva) rests upon the relationship between the signified and the signifier (vācya-vācaka-bhāva).
Therefore, the operation of words with respect to the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) consists solely in their functioning as a logical mark (liṅga) for the speaker’s intention (vaktrabhiprāya).

But when that [meaning], whether in the form of an intention (*abhiprāya*) or not in the form of an intention, is made the object [of cognition] as that which is to be communicated (*pratipādya*), there is no operation [of the word] either through denotative power (*vācakatva*) or through another relation.
It is not first through denotative power, as was stated previously.
The capacity to manifest [an object] occurs through a different type of relation.
Furthermore, this capacity to manifest is not identical to the nature of being a logical mark (*liṅga*), because it is observed otherwise in cases such as light and so forth.
Therefore, the object to be communicated by words is related [to them] as something to be expressed (*vācya*), not as a logical mark (*liṅgin*).

For that object which is related to them as a probandum (*liṅgin*)— as it has been shown— is not perceived as something to be directly expressed (*vācya*), but rather as a qualifying attribute (*upādhi*).
Furthermore, if the object to be established were itself the probandum, it would follow as an absurd consequence that there could be no disagreements regarding that object made by ordinary people.
And this has already been stated:

just as when the correctness of a verbal object is apprehended through the accompaniment of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), even though that [object] falls within the domain of another means of valid cognition, there is no loss of its status as an object of the operation of the word—
this applies equally to what is manifested by it (*vyaṅgya*).

Furthermore, regarding the domain of poetry (*kāvya*), the determination of whether the cognitions of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) are true or false is simply irrelevant; thus, an examination of the operation of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein serves only as a source of ridicule.
Therefore, it cannot be asserted that the cognition of the suggested is everywhere identical to the cognition of an inferential mark (*liṅgin*).

As for the power of words to suggest (*vyañjakatva*) a suggested object in the form of an inferable (*anumeya*), that is not a factor that warrants the technical designation of "suggestion" (*dhvani*).

Rather, this has been set forth for the purpose of demonstrating that the function of words characterized as manifestation (*vyañjakatva*) must be accepted even by one who maintains that the relationship between word and meaning is innate (*autpattika*).

For that manifestation—whether through the form of an inferential mark (*liṅga*) or in some other form—is something that cannot be denied by any proponent, whether regarding words that are expressive (*vācaka*) or those that are non-expressive (*avācaka*); it is for this reason that we have undertaken this effort.

Thus, because it differs from word-types such as those denoting qualities (*guṇa*), functions (*vṛtti*), and so forth, suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) is necessarily distinct. Even if one were to insist that it is included within those [other categories], the elucidation of *dhvani*— which is its specific variety— is by no means superfluous when it is undertaken for the purpose of dispelling misconceptions or for the instruction of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*).

For it is not possible to reject the definitions of specific useful properties by means of a definition consisting of mere generality alone. If that were the case, once a definition consisting of mere existence (*sattā*) had been made, there would follow the consequence of redundancy for all definitions of existing things. Thus, that which was the object of dispute among the wise, whose true nature was constantly unknown—
This very variety of poetry, designated as *dhvani*, has thus been revealed.

Another type of poetry is seen in which the suggested meaning is subordinate (guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya), wherein the beauty of the expressed meaning attains excellence through its connection with the suggested meaning. (Dhvanyāloka 3.34)
It has been stated that when the suggested meaning—such as the beauty of a woman (*lalanā-lāvaṇya*) which has been explained—is predominant, there is *dhvani*.

However, when that same [suggested meaning] becomes subordinate (*guṇībhāvena*) due to the excellence of the beauty of the expressed (*vācya-cārutva-prakarṣe*), a distinct variety of poetry called *guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya* (that in which the suggestion is subordinated) is postulated.

In that case, when a mere fact (*vastu-mātra*) as the suggested meaning—which is perceived from those instances where the expressed is subordinated (*tiraskṛta-vācya*)—occasionally becomes subordinate in relation to the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) of the expressed form, there occurs the state of being *guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*.
Just as it is said:
"What indeed is this other ocean of loveliness here, wherein lotuses float together with the moon?"
Wherever there are the temples of elephants emerging, there also are other stalks of plantain trees and lotus fibers.

Even from words whose expressed meaning is not subordinated (*atiraskṛtavācya*), when the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*)—which is being perceived—is sometimes rendered subordinate (*guṇībhāva*) in view of the primacy of the expressed meaning and the aesthetic beauty (*cārutva*) of the poetry, there occurs the state of "subordinate suggestion" (*guṇībhūta-vyaṅgyatā*).
An example has been cited: “The twilight is full of passion,” and so forth.
In that very case, the subordination [of the suggestion] arises because its manifestation is brought about by the speaker’s own explicit statement.
As it has been illustrated:
"The mind at the time of convention," and so forth;
the subordinate status of the suggested form of rasa and the like has been shown in the *rasavat* ornament.
And in that case, their subordination (guṇībhāva) is in relation to the directly stated sentence (ādhikārika-vākya), like a king followed by servants engaged in marriage.
When the suggested figure of speech (vyaṅgyālaṅkāra) is subordinate, the scope is [figures] such as the Illuminator (dīpaka) and so forth. (Dhvanyāloka 3.34)
Likewise:
"Poetic compositions with clear and profound words bring happiness;
and in those cases as well, this very same method should be employed by one of keen intelligence. (Dhvanyāloka 3.35)

Furthermore, in all those poetic compositions—which, though possessing immeasurable forms, are delightful through their subject matter and bring joy to the discerning as they shine forth—this very type known as *guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya* (where the suggested meaning is subordinated) must be applied. For example:
"Lakṣmī is the daughter, Hari is the son-in-law, and Gaṅgā is his wife."
O dear ones, our children, oh, the family of the great ocean!
[Fortune is his daughter, Hari is his son-in-law, Gaṅgā is his wife, and the nectar and the moon are his two sons; oh, what a family the great ocean has! DhvA_3.35.
This class of verbal ornaments, when accompanied by a suggested element,
is generally observed in actual usage to possess a supreme luster.

This is the section on verbal ornaments (*vācyālaṅkāra*). When the suggested element—whether it be an ornament, a mere fact, or both—is appropriately present, it imparts a heightened brilliance; thus, almost all such ornaments, when examined according to their definitions, are observed in actual poetic instances (*lakṣya*) as being of that nature.
For instance, like *dīpaka* (illumination) and *samāsokti* (speech of brevity), other ornaments are generally seen to be in contact with other suggested ornaments or other facts.
For first of all, the inclusion of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) within every poetic ornament is possible;
and indeed, when it is employed by great poets, it nourishes a certain unique splendor of poetry.
For how could the application of hyperbole, when executed with propriety toward its own subject matter, not bring about excellence in poetry?
Bhāmaha also stated in his definition of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole):
"This is indeed all *vakrokti* (figurative expression); by it the meaning is brought to life.
The poet must exert effort in this; what ornament is there without it?"

In this regard, it should be understood that the meaning is as follows: whatever ornament *atiśayokti* presides over by virtue of the power of the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*), that [ornament] is endowed with an excellence of beauty (*cārutvātiśaya*), whereas any other [ornament] is merely an ornament.
Because it is capable of assuming the very body of all ornaments, it is figuratively treated as non-different from them;
thus, *atiśayokti* itself takes the form of all ornaments. This is the sense that must be grasped.
And its intermingling with other ornaments occurs sometimes as the expressed (vācya) and sometimes as the suggested (vyaṅgya).
Even when it is suggested, it is sometimes predominant and sometimes subordinate.
Among these, in the first case, there is the path of the expressed ornament (vācyālaṅkāra-mārga).
In the second case, however, there is inclusion within *dhvani*;
in the third, it takes the form of *guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion).
And this type exists for other poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) as well.
However, for those [other figures], there is no universal scope;

whereas for *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), it is possible even to have all figures as its scope—this is the distinction. Furthermore, in those figures where the apprehension of reality occurs by way of similarity, such as *rūpaka*, *upamā*, *tulyayogitā*, *nidarśanā*, and so forth.

Among those [figures], that similarity which exists precisely by way of the suggested (gamya) element is what possesses the excellence of beauty; thus, all of them, being endowed with a preeminent charm, are the domain of *guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion) alone.

In cases such as *samāsokti*, *ākṣepa*, and *paryāyokti*, however, because their very establishment depends on the inseparable connection with the suggested portion, their status as *guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya* is beyond dispute.

In that regard, concerning the state where the suggested meaning is subordinate (*guṇībhūta-vyaṅgyatā*), there is a restriction for certain figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) in that they must contain a specific figure within them;
for example, the restriction that *vyāja-stuti* (feigned praise) must contain the figure *preyas* (the lovely).
For others, there is a restriction that they must contain merely a figure of speech.
Just as doubt (*sandeha*) and other figures possess the nature of being "pregnant with" (*garbha*) a simile (*upamā*),
it is also possible for certain figures to be mutually pregnant with one another,
as in the case of the lamp (*dīpaka*) and the simile.
In this context, the *dīpaka* (lamp) is well known for having the *upamā* (simile) as its core;
yet sometimes the *upamā* follows the shadow of the *dīpaka*,
as in the case of the *mālopamā* (garland simile).
For instance, in such examples as "the lamp [is] like a flame with great radiance," the shadow of the *dīpaka* (lamp-illustration) is clearly perceived.

Thus, when there is contact with a suggested element (*vyaṅgyāṃśa*), all poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) such as metaphor (*rūpaka*) and the rest—which possess an excellence of beauty—constitute the path of *guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya* (where the suggestion is subordinated). And this state of being *guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya* is the common characteristic of all such ornaments, whether they have been explicitly mentioned or not.
In this definition, all these [figures] become well-defined.

However, by means of stating the specific nature of each one individually—devoid of a general definition—it is impossible to ascertain them in their true essence through a word-for-word recitation alone, due to their infinity.
For the conceptual variations of speech are infinite, and the figures of speech are of those very same types.
Furthermore, that which possesses a subordinate suggestion (*guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*) indeed has as its domain the characteristic of being followed by a suggested meaning through another mode as well.
Therefore, this second subject matter of great poets, consisting of the outflow of *dhvani*, is exceedingly delightful and should be characterized by connoisseurs.
In every respect, there is no variety of poetry that captivates the hearts of connoisseurs wherein there is not a certain charm through contact with a suggested meaning.
Therefore, this supreme secret of poetry should be contemplated by the wise:
"Even among the words of great poets that bear ornaments, it is this suggested shadow that is the true ornament, like modesty is for women. (Dhvanyāloka 3.37)
By means of this [poetry], even a well-known matter is rendered somewhat desirable; for example:
"Those certain particular playful gestures of the lovely-eyed one, arising from confidence in the execution of the commands of Love."
Those [qualities] should be cultivated continuously by one who, standing in solitude, contemplates them with an unimpaired and exclusive mind.

In this passage, by the phrase "some [say]," which expresses the literal meaning (vācya) in an indistinct manner while imparting an unobstructed and infinite suggested (pratīyamāna) reality, what kind of aesthetic splendor has not been produced? (DhvA 3.37)
And this apprehension of another meaning through intonation (kāku) which is observed, that occurs when the suggested sense is subordinate, relying upon this particular mode. (Dhvanyāloka 3.38)

Furthermore, when this perception of another meaning through intonation (*kāku*) is observed, it relies upon that variety of poetry characterized by subordinated suggestion (*guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*), because the suggested meaning has attained a subordinate status.
For example: “The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra remain at ease while I live. Or, for instance:
“Ah! You are untruthful; desist, O devoted wife! Your character has not been sullied by you.”
How much more so for the common people—why should we not desire that barber as our own wife?

For it is the power of the word itself—assisted by the intonation (kāku) implied by the capacity of its own denotation—that is the cause for the comprehension of a specific meaning, and not intonation alone;
because such a comprehension of meaning is impossible from mere intonation produced according to one's own whim in another context.

And that meaning, although mounted upon the operation of the word assisted by a particular intonation, is nonetheless obtainable through the capacity of the meaning itself; thus, it is of the nature of the suggested (vyaṅgya).

However, when there is a cognition of the expressed meaning as qualified by that [suggested sense] precisely through the accompaniment of its denotative power (*vācakatva*), then the designation of such poetry—which illuminates an object of that kind—is made on the basis of its having a subordinated suggestion (*guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*).
For it is the state of having a subordinated suggestion that belongs to that which expresses an expressed meaning qualified by the suggested.
And the scope of this particular variety is that which is perceived through reasoning.
Therefore, sensitive critics should not apply the concept of *dhvani* in that case.
For indeed, a certain mixed path is observed among the poetic specimens (*lakṣya*) of both *dhvani* and that wherein the suggested meaning is subordinate (*guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*).
In such cases, designation should be made according to that [element] which possesses the support of logical reasoning;
it is not necessary that *dhvani* must prevail everywhere. For example—
Having had her feet dyed by her friend, who said with a playful jest, "Touch the crescent moon on your husband's head with this," she was granted a blessing.
He struck her with a garland until she was speechless.
And as it is said:
"When the proud woman was addressed by her lover with the name of a rival wife while she was plucking flowers high up,"
She said nothing at all; with eyes clouded by tears, she merely traced figures upon the ground with her foot.

In this instance, because the suggested meaning—namely, that he "struck down the etymological definition" (or "uttered nothing at all")"—is expressed by way of negation, its subordination (*guṇībhāva*) alone is appropriate, as it has been brought within the scope of verbal expression. When the suggested meaning is understood through the primary purport (*tātparya*) without recourse to *vakrokti* (indirect or figurative speech), then it possesses predominance (*prādhānya*). As in the verse beginning with "While the divine sage was speaking thus... and so forth.
In this case, however, because there is a repetition by way of a stylistic turn (*bhaṅgī*), the expressed meaning (*vācya*) also possesses primacy.
Therefore, the designation of *dhvani* as "suggestion consisting of a resonant after-effect" (*anuraṇana-rūpa-vyaṅgya-dhvani*) should not be applied here. (DhvA 3.39)

This variety, although it is of the nature of *guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*, again assumes the form of *dhvani* through a thorough consideration of its ultimate intent (*tātparya*) as being directed toward rasa and so forth. (Dhvanyāloka 3.40)

Even a type of poetry where the suggested meaning is subordinate (*guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*) becomes *dhvani* itself when one considers its ultimate intent to be the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), emotion (*bhāva*), and so forth—
as in the two verses just cited above, and as in:
"O fortunate one, Rādhā is difficult to propitiate, since even by this [effort] of yours..."
"Your tears have fallen upon the garment of your lord's hips;
that heart of a woman is hard—enough with these pretenses, desist!
"May Hari bring you prosperity! Thus was he addressed by her as she offered her entreaties.

This being the case, although the words specified in the verse beginning with "For this indeed is an insult" (*nyakkāro hy ayam eva*) convey a denoted meaning qualified by the suggested sense, their status as suggestors (*vyañjakatva*) is stated in relation to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) that constitutes the meaning of this sentence. One should not, therefore, entertain the misconception that these words constitute *arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya* suggestion (*dhvani*).
Because their expressed meaning is intended to be conveyed,

for in those cases it is the expressed meaning that is perceived as being qualified by the suggested meaning, rather than the expressed meaning having undergone a transformation into the form of the suggested.
Therefore, in such instances, the sentence itself is *dhvani*.
The words, however, possess subordinated suggestion (*guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*).

Moreover, it is not only words with subordinated suggestion that are the suggestors (*vyañjaka*) of *dhvani* with imperceptible sequence (*alakṣya-krama-vyaṅgya*), but also those whose literal meaning is transferred to another sense (*arthāntara-saṃkramita-vācya*), which are forms of the varieties of *dhvani*.
Just as in this very verse, the word "Rāvaṇa" functions as a suggestor (*vyañjaka*) of a different specific form [of the suggested meaning].

However, in a sentence where there is no primary intent toward rasa and so forth, even if it is illuminated by words whose suggested meanings are subordinate (*guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*), the status of being a sentence with subordinate suggestion (*guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*) remains the property of the whole. For example:
"They serve even a king; they consume even poison."
"And virtuous men indeed take delight together with women," and so forth.
A supreme effort must be made in discerning the predominance and non-predominance of the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya),
by which the unmixed domains of *dhvani*, *guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*, and the poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) may become well understood.
Otherwise, however, confusion arises regarding the very domain of well-known ornaments, as in the following example:
"The expenditure of the wealth of beauty was not reckoned; great hardship was undertaken;
the fire of anxiety was kindled for people living at their own will."
This poor girl too has been destroyed by her own lack of a suitable lover; what purpose did the Creator have in his mind when he fashioned the slender body of this delicate woman?
(Dharmakīrti, *Kuvalayāvalī* 100)
In *Aucityavicāracarcā* 11 and *Subhāṣitaratnakośa* 814, it was explained by someone that the figure of speech here is *vyājastuti* (ironical praise); however, that is not correct,
because this subject matter does not harmonize well if it is restricted solely to the nature of that particular figure of speech.

For this is not, first of all, the conceptual construction of anyone who possesses passion (*rāgin*), because for such a person, an expression such as "this poor woman too is ruined by herself alone due to the absence of a compatible lover" would be untenable. Nor is it [the construction] of one free from passion (*nīrāga*);
Because its sole function is the avoidance of such conceptual constructions as these,
and because this verse is not heard to occur within any specific literary work (*prabandha*) from which its meaning might be inferred as following from that context.
Therefore, this is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).

For it is revealed that through this expressed meaning— which is subordinate in nature— this is the lamentation of one who, puffed up by a mass of extraordinary qualities, suffers from the fever of envy in others produced by the excellence of his own greatness, and sees no one else at all as a connoisseur of himself.
And thus there is a well-known tradition that this verse belongs to Dharmakīrti; moreover, it is highly probable that it is indeed his,
because—
My thought, whose depth cannot be fathomed even by one of no small intellectual power, and whose ultimate reality has not been seen even through great efforts,
finds no worthy recipient in this world.
It will undergo decay within its own body, like the water of the ocean.
By this verse as well, such an intention is indeed revealed;
and in the case of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), that which is expressed may sometimes be intended [as the primary meaning] and sometimes not intended.
Sometimes there is the state of being intended or not intended; this is the threefold shadow of bondage.
Among these, "intendedness" is as follows:
he who experiences suffering for the sake of others is sweet even in his defeat.
If indeed the transformation of all things here is accepted,
yet that [transformation] does not reach full maturity because it has fallen upon a barren field—
is this the fault of the sugarcane, and not rather of the desert soil which lacks its virtues? (22)
[*22] Or as it was said by me myself: "Are not these who are seen here truly of beautiful form? Is there not fruitfulness..."
When these [senses] have come within the range of their objects,
alas, how is it that this eye alone has now become equal to all [the senses] in a world devoid of light? Or rather, it is not equal to the other limbs.
For in these two verses, the sugarcane and the eyes are not intended as their literal natures (*svarūpa*), nor are they the subject at hand;

rather, the purport of both verses is to describe the nature of someone who possesses great qualities, who has not fallen into the range of [ordinary] objects, and who has not yet attained the supreme state. As for their being unintended [as literal objects]: [example follows].
"Who are you, sir? "I am a wretched man, cursed by fate; know me to be a śākhoṭaka tree.
"You speak as if out of world-weariness.
"It is well understood; why is this being asked?"
There, travelers resort with their whole being to that banyan tree on my left; yet not even its shade performs a service for others, even though it stands right by the path.

For since a dialogue consisting of question and answer is not possible with a particular tree, it is understood that the intended meaning of this verse is, by its very nature, the lamentation of a certain wise but impoverished man living near a prosperous but wicked person; thus, the literal sense of the words is made subordinate to this underlying purpose.
Regarding the state of being intended or unintended to be expressed:
"O traveler, by providing sustenance to the jujube tree— which has grown on a wrong path, is unlovely, and is devoid of fruit, flowers, and leaves— you will be laughed at!"
For here, the expressed meaning is neither entirely possible nor entirely impossible;
therefore, the predominance and subordination of the expressed and the suggested meanings must be carefully determined. (Dhvanyāloka 3.40)
Since the suggested meaning is thus established through its primary or subordinate status in poetry, that which is other than these two is called "the extraordinary" (citra).
Poetic embellishment (citra) is established as being of two kinds according to the distinction between word and meaning;
among these, some is word-embellishment (śabdacitra), and that which follows is meaning-embellishment (vācyacitra).
When the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) is predominant, it is the type of poetry designated as *dhvani*; when it is subordinate, it is *guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*.

Other than these, there is that poetry which lacks the primary intent of rasa, bhāva, and so forth, and which is devoid of the power to manifest any particular suggested meaning; composed solely by relying on the variety of the expressed (*vācya*) and the expressive (*vācaka*), it is like a mere painting (*ālekhyaprakhya*).
That which merely appears [as poetry] is a painting;
it is not primary poetry,
for it is but an imitation of poetry.
In that regard, some [poetry] is "word-ornamented" (*śabda-citra*), such as difficult *yamaka* (paranomasia) and the like.

"Meaning-ornamented" (*vācya-citra*) is other than that word-ornamented; it is devoid of contact with a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*), exists primarily as the literal sentence-meaning, and is devoid of the intended purpose of rasa and so forth—such as *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) and the like.
Now, what is this that is called "ornamentation"?
Where there is no contact with a suggested meaning—

since a suggested meaning has already been shown to be of three types— that alone may indeed be considered the province of Citra (the pictorial). In that case, there exists neither a suggested object nor another poetic figure.
However, that variety of poetry in which rasa and the other [elements] are not objects of experience is simply impossible;
for it is not logically tenable that poetry should lack contact with reality (vastu).
And every reality within the world necessarily becomes an auxiliary element of some rasa or bhāva, at least by way of being a determinant emotion (vibhāva).
For rasa and the other aesthetic elements are indeed specific modifications of mental activity (*citta-vṛtti-viśeṣa*);

and there is no object whatsoever that does not produce such a specific modification of mental activity, for if it did not produce one, it would not even be an object of poetry. Furthermore, an object of poetry is defined as something characterized by its manifoldness (*citratayā*).
To this it is replied: True, there is no such type of poetry in which rasa and the like are not perceived.

However, when a poet composes a verbal ornament (śabdālaṅkāra) or a semantic ornament (arthālaṅkāra) devoid of the intention (*vivakṣā*) to express rasa, bhāva, and so forth, then—relative to that lack of intention—the meaning is considered to be devoid of rasa and the like;
for in poetry, the meaning of words is precisely that which has ascended to the level of the poet's intention.

Alternatively, even in the absence of the poet’s intention, when the cognition of rasa and so forth arises in such a subject solely by the power of the expressive capacity of the words, it becomes extremely weak; thus, by this method as well, its lack of rasa is determined, and it is established as having the *citra* (variegated) mode as its domain.
This is what has been stated:
When there is an absence of the intention to express objects such as rasa (flavor) and bhāva (emotional state),
that composition of figures of speech is considered to have *citra* (pictorial poetry) as its subject matter.
But when there is an intention regarding rasa and so forth that possesses *tātparya*,
then that poetry does not exist at all where it is not within the scope of *dhvani*.

And this [distinction] has been postulated by us because we observe that for poets whose speech is unrestrained, there is an engagement in poetry even without regard for the primary aim of rasa and so forth;
however, when the proper system of poetic theory is now being established, there is indeed no variety of poetry apart from *dhvani*.
For the very activity of mature poets does not shine at all in the absence of an orientation toward rasa and the like.
And when the primary aim is rasa and so forth, there is simply no such thing as an object that, being brought into the service of a desired rasa, does not become effective.

For even insentient entities—whether by serving as the appropriate excitants (*vibhāva*) of a rasa or by being linked to the experiences of sentient beings—are certainly not those that fail to become limbs of rasa.
Thus it is said:
In the boundless universe of poetry, the poet alone is the Lord of Creation;
as it pleases him, so does this entire world transform.
If the poet is possessed of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), the world becomes composed of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) within his poetry;
if he is devoid of passion, all of that becomes utterly flavorless.

Just as a skilled poet, through his independence, employs entities—even those that are insentient—as if they were sentient, or sentient as if they were insentient, according to his own will in his poetry; so too does [the Lord] employ them in worldly discourse.
Therefore, there is simply no such thing as an entity that, when intended by a poet whose primary aim is rasa, does not—by his will—assume the status of a constituent of that intended rasa;
nor, even if so depicted, does it fail to nourish an excellence of beauty.
And all of this is observed in the poems of the great poets.

We too have demonstrated this accordingly in our own poetic compositions. And this being the case, every variety of poetry does not transcend the nature of *dhvani* when considered in relation to rasa and the like; for even that variety characterized as having a subordinate suggested meaning (*guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*) assumes the status of a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to that [rasa], as was stated previously.

However, when rasa and the other elements are established as subordinate members within flatteries or hymns to the deities, or when they appear as the predominant element in certain heart-touching verses of wise poets where the suggested sense is distinguished from the expressed, that too is merely a manifestation of *dhvani* within the category of *guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*, as was stated previously.

Thus, when instruction on the principles of contemporary poetry and poetics is being given, it is established that for beginners seeking practice, there may at most be engagement with *citra* (poetic figures), whereas for those who have attained maturity, *dhvani* alone is poetry.
This is the summary here:
That in which either rasa or bhāva is manifested through its primary intent, or where, by way of conventional usage, a thing or even an ornament is expressed; [that is the subject matter].

In the path of poetry (*kāvyādhvan*), *dhvani*—which is based solely on the predominance of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*)—is to be understood by sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*) as the subject throughout that [path]. (DhvA 3.42)

Together with its own subdivisions—those in which the suggested meaning is subordinate (saguṇībhūta-vyaṅgya) and those accompanied by figures of speech (sālaṅkāra)—it shines forth again in many ways through both commingling (saṅkara) and combination (saṃsṛṣṭi). (Dhvanyāloka 3.43)

And when the classification of that sound (dhvani) through its own subdivisions, as well as through its mixture and combination with *guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya* and expressed poetic figures (*vācyālaṅkāra*), is being established, a great multiplicity of varieties is observed in actual literary examples (*lakṣya*). For instance: [it may be] mixed with its own subdivisions, combined with its own subdivisions, mixed with *guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*, combined with *guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*, or mixed with other expressed poetic figures.

Suggestion (dhvani) manifests in many ways: as mixed with other verbal ornaments (*vācyālaṅkāra*), as combined with mixed ornaments (*saṃsṛṣṭālaṅkāra*), and as mixed with mixed ornaments (*saṃsṛṣṭālaṅkāra-saṃsṛṣṭa*).
Among these, its combination with its own sub-varieties sometimes occurs through the relationship of the assisted and the assister (*anugrāhyānugrāhaka-bhāva*).

For example, in passages such as “When the divine seer had spoken thus,” etc., here a specific variety of suggestion with imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya-dhvani*) is perceived as being supported by a specific variety of suggestion consisting of resonance arising from the power of the meaning (*artha-śakty-udbhava-anuraṇana-rūpa-vyaṅgya-dhvani*).
Likewise, sometimes there is doubt due to the convergence of two varieties. For example—
O brother, this momentary guest has been said something by your wife; she is weeping in the side-chamber of the house—please go and console this poor woman.
"This guest for a moment, your brother-in-law, has been said something by your wife; he weeps in the empty upper-room, let this poor fellow be consoled.

For here, the word "be consoled" (anunīyatām) is intended through the transfer of the expressed meaning to another sense (arthāntara-saṅkramita-vācya), and it is also possible that it possesses another suggested meaning (vyaṅgya).
Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for determining one side [or the other] exclusively.

However, the state of being suggested (*vyaṅgyatva*) through the entry of a single suggester (*vyañjaka*) is generally possible for that which is suggested with imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya*), in relation to its own internal subdivisions;
as, for example, in the verse beginning with "snigdha-śyāmala" and so forth.
And the state of being mixed with its own subdivisions is as in the previous example;
for here there is a mixture of the "denoted meaning transferred to another" (arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya) and the "completely set aside denoted meaning" (atyantatiraskṛtavācya).
The state of being mixed with the "subordinate suggested" (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya) is as in “This indeed is my humiliation that enemies [survive],” and so forth.
Or for example:
"The arrogant one who was the author of the deceits of gambling, who set fire to the lacquer house,
and who was skilled at stripping away Draupadī’s hair and upper garment— he whose servants were the Pāṇḍavas."
"Where is that King Duryodhana—the teacher of Duḥśāsana and his hundred younger brothers, and the friend of Aṅgarāja? Tell me; we have come here not out of anger, but to see him."

For here, there is a commingling of the suggestion whose sequence is imperceptible—which has become the meaning of the sentence—with words that express the literal sense as qualified by that suggestion.

Precisely for this reason, even though there is a commingling of *guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion) when it rests on the meaning of individual words (*padārtha*) and of *dhvani* when it rests on the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), there is no contradiction, just as in the case of its own internal subdivisions.
For just as the various subdivisions of *dhvani* intermingle with one another and are not contradictory by virtue of resting on either the meaning of words or the meaning of sentences.

Furthermore, while the relationship of primary and subordinate is contradicted when multiple [figures] have a single manifested entity as their substratum, it is not contradicted with respect to the distinction between the manifestations themselves;
therefore, there is no contradiction in this case either.

Moreover, this conventional usage of "confusion" (*saṅkara*) and "commixture" (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) should be understood as being entirely without contradiction even in the relationship between the manifested and the manifestor, just as it is in the relationship between the expressed and the expressor when many [elements] reside in a single [locus].

However, where certain words have meanings that are not intended to be expressed (avivakṣita-vācya) or where their expressed meanings consist of a resonant suggestion (anuraṇana-rūpa-vyaṅgya), there is a coexistence (saṃsṛṣṭatva) of Suggestive Poetry (dhvani) and Poetry of Subordinated Suggestion (guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya).
For example, in the verse beginning with "teṣāṃ gopa-vadhū-vilāsa-suhṛdām" and so forth.

Here, indeed, the words "vilāsa-suhṛdām" and "rādhā-rahaḥ-sākṣiṇām" take the form of varieties of Suggestive Poetry, while the words "te" and "jāne" take the form of Poetry of Subordinated Suggestion.

The state of being intermingled with verbal figures of speech is well-established everywhere in poetry possessing rasa and figures, in relation to that where the suggestiveness has an imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya*).
Even among other varieties [of suggestion], such intermingling certainly occurs at times;
as in my own work:
Relying upon both that certain novel vision of poets which is active in savoring aesthetic flavors (rasas), and that scholarly insight which unfolds the realm of established meanings—
we who incessantly contemplate the entire universe by means of these two— [we proceed].
O You who recline upon the ocean, though we were exhausted, we did not obtain any happiness equal to devotion to You.

Thus, in this instance, there is a commingling (*saṅkīrṇatva*) of the variety of suggestion (*dhvani*) in which the expressed meaning is transmuted (*arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya*) with the figure of contradiction (*virodhālaṅkāra*). Furthermore, the state of being conjoined with an expressed figure (*vācyālaṅkārasaṃsṛṣṭatva*) pertains specifically to the words themselves; for in such cases, some words possess expressed figures while others are endowed with varieties of suggestion. For example:
Where, at dawn, the cry of the cranes— sweet with intoxication and prolonged— becomes pungent with its friendship toward the fragrance of blossoming lotuses,
and where that breeze, flowing along the limbs, removes the exhaustion of women after lovemaking.
Like a most beloved lover, the breeze from the Siprā river utters flattering words of entreaty.

For here, in the word "maitrī" (friendliness), there is suggestion (*dhvani*) where the literal meaning is not intended; in the other words, there are other figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*). This is a case of suggestion mixed with other figures of speech that are themselves combined, as for example:
Upon your body, which was covered with dense horripilation, the female lioness, her heart filled with passion, bestowed tooth-marks and gashes made by her claws.
They were gazed upon even by sages who had conceived a longing for them.

For here, there is the manifestation of a *dhvani*—whose suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) has its sequence unperceived (*alakṣyakrama*)—which is intermingled with the figure of speech *virodha* (contradiction) that is itself commingled with *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation).
This is because, in the ultimate sense, the *dayāvīra* (heroism of compassion) constitutes the primary meaning of the sentence.
And the manner in which the *dhvani* is commingled with commingled figures of speech is as follows:
On days that resound with the cries of fresh clouds and appear darkened by travelers,
the dancing of flocks of peacocks with their necks outstretched is beautiful.
For here, there is a commingling (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of the *dhvani*—which consists of a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) arising from the power of words—with both simile (*upamā*) and metaphor (*rūpaka*).
Thus, by whom could the varieties of *dhvani* and the further subdivisions of those varieties be enumerated? We have stated only a mere indication (*diṅmātra*) of them. (Dhvanyāloka 3.44)
For the varieties of sound are indeed infinite; only a mere indication of them has been stated here for the instruction of those with aesthetic sensitivity.

Thus, that *dhvani* which has been defined above should be diligently investigated by the virtuous who are earnestly devoted to either composing or correctly understanding excellent poetry. (DhvK 3.45)
For true poets and connoisseurs, who are indeed skilled in defining the nature of sound as previously described, certainly attain the highest state of excellence regarding the subject of poetry.
Since this essence of poetry, as it has been described, manifests in an indistinct manner, the *rītis* (styles) were introduced by those unable to explain it fully. (Dhvanyāloka 3.46)

Because this essence of poetry (kāvyatattva), though determined by the operation of this Suggestion (dhvani), was not clearly manifest and could not be fully explained [by others], the styles (rītis)—namely Vaidarbhī, Gauḍī, and Pāñcālī—were introduced. It appears that for those who formulated the definitions of these styles, this essence of poetry remained only slightly manifest due to its lack of clarity; therefore, there is nothing [to be gained] from any other definition of style presented here with such clarity. (DhvA 3.46)
When this definition of poetry is understood, certain functions (vṛtti) based on the essence of words and others connected with the essence of meaning also become manifest. (Dhvanyāloka 3.47)

When this definition of poetry, which consists of an analysis of the relationship between the suggested (vyaṅgya) and the suggester (vyañjaka), is understood, then whatever well-known styles (vṛttis) there may be— such as the Upanāgarikā and others based on the essence of words, and those connected to the essence of meaning such as the Kaiśikī and others—
they properly enter the path of the term "rīti."
Otherwise, these functions, like those whose purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*), would be merely untrustworthy and not established by experience.

Thus, the nature of this *dhvani* must be clearly defined as that wherein certain words and meanings possess a quality perceivable only by a specific cognizer, similar to the innate excellence of particular gems.

As for the definition of *dhvani* stated by some— that it is the usage of the term *dhvani* when an indescribable beauty (*cārutva*) shines forth in poetry— that is incorrect and does not deserve to be accepted as a definition;
for, first of all, the nature of words consists in their being employed without difficulty, provided they are not unestablished usages.

The distinction, however, is that [in the case of suggestion], clarity (*prasāda*) rests upon the expressive words, and it constitutes suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*). Furthermore, the distinction is that the manifestation of meanings with clarity consists in their being directed toward the suggested (*vyaṅgyaparatva*) and being characterized by the element of the suggested (*vyaṅgyāṃśaviśiṣṭatva*).
These two distinctions can be explained, and they have been explained in many ways.
However, the possibility of a specific quality that is distinct from those [qualities] and yet indescribable is rooted solely in the failure of discrimination (*viveka*).

This is because "indescribability" cannot possibly belong to anything by virtue of being beyond the range of all words; for ultimately, it is possible to designate even that [indescribable thing] by the very word "indescribable."

Furthermore, that which is sometimes called "ineffability"— namely, the state of being manifest while remaining beyond the scope of conceptualization and words that touch upon generalities— is also impossible in the case of specific poetic works, just as it is with specific jewels;
for their forms have been fully described by the authors of treatises on poetics.

Furthermore, it is observed that the determination of the value of various specific jewels occurs precisely through a general estimation; for both of these types of objects, there certainly exists a state of being perceivable by a qualified cognizer. Indeed, it is only the jewel-merchants who truly know the reality of jewels.
For who would have any disagreement that it is only those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*) who are knowers of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of poems?
As for the well-known Buddhist doctrine that all defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are inexpressible (*anirdeśya*), we shall examine that position in another work.
However, in this context, we do not proceed with it, as merely illuminating a fragment of what is heard in other works would only cause distress to those with aesthetic sensitivity.
Or, just as the definition of perception and so forth is according to the Buddhist view, so too shall our definition of *dhvani* be.
Therefore, since no other definition can be formulated and because [the others] do not constitute the meaning of the word, the definition of *dhvani* already stated is indeed superior.
This has been said:
The state of being illuminated by an inexpressible portion [of meaning] due to the suggestiveness (*dhvani*) of sound is not its definition; rather,
its superior definition is as it has been stated.
Thus ends the third chapter of the *Dhvanyāloka*, composed by the venerable teacher Rājānaka Ānandavardhana.
The Fourth Radiance.
Having thus explained *dhvani* along with its manifold varieties (*saprapañca*) for the purpose of dispelling misconceptions, another purpose for this exposition is stated:

"The path of *dhvani*, including that in which the suggested sense is subordinate (*saguṇībhūtavyaṅgya*), which has been demonstrated—by means of this [explanation], the quality of the poets' creative intuition (*pratibhāguṇa*) attains infinity. (Dhvanyāloka 4.1)
The further fruit of this path of *dhvani* and *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* which has been illuminated is the infinity of the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*).
If one asks how so,
it is because [the poetic work], adorned by even one of these modes, [attains such excellence].
Speech attains novelty even when it possesses a connection with previously expressed meanings.

Therefore, when speech is adorned by even one of the aforementioned varieties of *dhvani*, it attains a sense of novelty (*navatvam*), even when it touches upon a theme already composed by ancient poets. For instance, the novelty of *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣita-vācya*) arises through recourse to its two varieties, even while following a prior theme, as in:
"A slightly charming smile; the power of her gaze, tremulous and sweet..."
The movement of her words is as fresh and charming as waves of playful grace; the onset of her gait is fragrant with budding coquetry—
indeed, what is there that is not delightful about a fawn-eyed maiden as she touches upon youth?
Thus,
to whom are these amorous women not dear— women whose tremulous eyes break into playful smiles, whose speech falters, and who move with the languid gait of heavy hips?

Even though such verses as these exist, through the reliance on suggestion where the expressed meaning is subordinated (*tiraskṛta-vācya-dhvani*), a state of unprecedentedness (*apūrvatva*) alone appears. Likewise, consider this:
"He who is the first is indeed the first; for he is a lion among the hosts of beasts of prey, devouring the abundant flesh of slain elephants—who could possibly humiliate a lion?"—of this [verse].
By whom else can one whose greatness is purchased by his own splendor be surpassed?
Is a lion ever overcome even by great elephants?
In these and other such verses, there is novelty by virtue of relying on *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is transferred (*saṅkramita-vācya*).
There is also novelty for that which has an intended expressed meaning other than the literal (*vivakṣitānyapara-vācya*) by relying on the aforementioned modes, as in:
"The young bride, placing her face upon the face of her lover who feigned sleep..."

Though her passion for the kiss was suppressed by the fear of discovery, she remained restless with longing; yet, fearing he might turn away out of embarrassment, she desisted from further effort— and thus, even toward him who had ceased his advances,
her heart reached the ultimate height of erotic fulfillment through that very act of expectant withdrawal.
Regarding this verse and others:
having observed that the dwelling was empty, she rose slightly from her bed and, approaching slowly under the pretext of sleep, gazed for a long time at the face of her husband.
Having kissed her confidently and seeing her cheek flushed with horripilation, the young woman, her face bowed in shame, was kissed for a long time by her laughing beloved.
Even though such verses as these exist, there is novelty;
or, for example, the verse beginning with "taraṅgabhrūbhaṅgā" is distinct from the verse beginning with "nānābhaṅgibhramadbhrūḥ. (DhvA 4.2)
By this reasoning, the extensive range of rasa and the other elements should be pursued;
for it is by relying upon them that the path of poetry attains mutual infinity.

This path, characterized by aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), emotion (*bhāva*), their semblances (*tad-ābhāsa*), and their subsidence (*tat-praśama*), is very extensive according to its respective varieties of determinants (*vibhāva*) and consequents (*anubhāva*), as previously stated.
All of it should be followed by means of this method.

Since this path of poetry has been traversed in many ways by thousands or even innumerable ancient poets on account of these aesthetic flavors and the rest, though it is measured, it attains infinity.

For each of the aesthetic moods (*rasa*), emotional states (*bhāva*), and so forth, is infinite by virtue of its dependence upon a multitude of determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*). Even with respect to a single variety among these, when the activities of the world are depicted by skilled poets, they manifest quite differently from how they actually exist, according to the poet’s own will. This has already been established in the discussion on the nature of the marvelous (*citra*).
And on this point, a verse has indeed been composed by the great poet:
"That speech which causes specific meanings—though not existing as such—to appear as if they were so situated within the heart, triumphs; it is the domain of the formidable poet."
Thus, the infinity of the meanings of poetry based on rasa, bhāva, and so forth has been well demonstrated.
To further establish this very point, it is said:
"For even objects previously perceived, through their inclusion within the *rasa* in poetry..."
All appear as if new, like trees in the month of honey.

For instance, novelty arises when intended meanings rely on a mode of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) produced by the power of words (*śabda-śakti*), specifically in the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana*) that is not the literal meaning (*aparavācya*).
An example is: “Now you, O Śeṣa, are the upholder of the earth,” and so forth.
[The double meaning is: “Śeṣa” is the Snowy Mountain (Himālaya) and you; both are great, venerable, and steadfast.
For they, whose boundaries are not transgressed, support the earth even as it quakes.
Even though such [factors] as these exist,
its novelty arises by relying on a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) that takes the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana*) produced by the power of the meaning itself;
as, for example, in the verse beginning with “*evaṃ-vādini devarṣau*.”
When an excellent conversation has been conducted, the maidens,
their faces bowed with inward shame, indicate their longing through the bristling of their hair.

In such cases as these, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), which arises from the power of the sense (*artha-śakti*) and takes the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana*), possesses novelty because its body is constructed through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet.
For example, in the verse beginning with “The fragrant month prepares [everything],” beautiful things suddenly manifest when the season of *surabhi* has arrived.
The longing of those filled with passion arises together with the buds of the mango tree.
Even when such [conventional meanings] exist, there is indeed a sense of novelty (*apūrvatva*).

The suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), which takes the form of a resonance arising from the power of the sense (*artha-śakti*), possesses a freshness because its body is produced solely through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of a speaker composed by the poet.
This is as in the case of the meaning of the verse beginning with "The ivory for trade... and so forth.
"My son, who was as formidable as a female elephant and capable of piercing with a single arrow,
has been killed by his wife in such a way that the quiver is overflowing."
"My son, who could slay with a single arrow,
has been made by his slain daughter-in-law such that he carries a quiver of arrows"—
in the presence of such meanings, there is indeed no "tasting" (of the poetic figure). (Dhvanyāloka 4.4)

Just as the novelty of the meanings of poetry arises in *dhvani* by relying on the various types of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*), so too does it arise by relying on the various types of the suggester (*vyañjaka*).
However, that [latter] is not written here for fear of excessive prolixity in the text.
This should be inferred by sensitive readers for themselves.
Furthermore, although it has been stated again and again, this is said once more because of its essential importance:
"Even though these various types of the relationship between the suggested and the suggester are possible..."
A poet should be attentive toward a single [poem] composed of rasa and the other elements.

Although this manifold relationship of the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) among words— which serves as the cause for the infinity of meaning— is possible, the poet, seeking the attainment of unprecedented meaning, should apply himself with effort to that single relationship of the manifested and the manifestor which consists of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and the like.

For when the manifested takes the form of *rasa*, emotion (*bhāva*), or their semblances (*ābhāsa*), and the manifestors consist of the phonemes, words, sentences, compositions, and literary works as previously described, everything becomes unprecedented for the poet whose mind is focused upon them.
Thus poetry is perfected.
And so, in works such as the *Rāmāyaṇa* and the *Mahābhārata*, even though battles and other events are described again and again, they appear ever-new.
Furthermore, in a literary composition, when a single dominant sentiment (*rasa*) is presented, it nourishes the attainment of specific meaning and fosters an excellence of aesthetic luster.
If one asks, "In what [work]?"—it is as in the *Rāmāyaṇa* or as in the *Mahābhārata*.

For in the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the sentiment of pathos (*karuṇa-rasa*) was personally indicated by the Primordial Poet himself through such words as, "Grief has attained the state of verse" (*śokaḥ ślokatvam āgataḥ*).
And that very sentiment was brought to its full realization by him while composing his own composition, culminating in the absolute separation from Sītā.

In the *Mahābhārata* as well, the Great Sage— by concluding with a finale that imparts despondency following the tragic end of the Vṛṣṇis and Pāṇḍavas, while conforming to the shadow-form of both scripture and poetry— demonstrates that the primary intent of his composition is to engender dispassion (*vairāgya*). Thus, he indicates that the human goal characterized by liberation (*mokṣa*) and the sentiment of tranquility (*śānta-rasa*) are his principal subjects of expression.
And this has already been explained in part by other commentators;
it has also been uttered by the Lord of the World himself, who, desiring to uplift the world submerged in the surging great delusion, bestows the light of exceedingly pure knowledge:
"In whatever way the worldly system revolves, it is devoid of essence."
In that very way, detachment arises here; there is no doubt about this.

Thus, as he speaks at length in this manner, it becomes clearly manifest that the intended purport of the *Mahābhārata* is as follows: the sentiment of peace (*śānta-rasa*), characterized by liberation (*mokṣa*), which is the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*), is the primary element (*aṅgin*) when it is sought to be expressed as such, being followed by other human goals and other sentiments as its subordinate elements.
The relationship of part and whole (*aṅgāṅgi-bhāva*) among the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) has already been established in the same manner.

From the perspective of the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*), which is independent of [lower] principles, it is not contradictory for even a *rasa*—which is like a limb of the body—to possess beauty through its own primacy, just as the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) does.

Now, one might object: "In the *Mahābhārata*, everything that was intended to be expressed has been enumerated in the table of contents (*anukramaṇī*); yet this [fact regarding the *rasas*] is not seen there."

On the contrary, in that very section, it is perceived through the explicit words of the text itself that the Mahābhārata is the cause for awakening all human goals (puruṣārtha) and contains the essence of all aesthetic sentiments (rasa).

To this, it is replied: It is true that in the Mahābhārata, the sentiment of tranquility (śānta-rasa) alone holds the status of the primary aesthetic flavor (aṅgin), and liberation (mokṣa) is the most preeminent among all human goals; however, this is not shown by the table of contents (anukramaṇī) as something denoted by its own explicit words, but rather as something suggested (vyaṅgya)—as seen in the sentence: “And the eternal Lord Vāsudeva is celebrated herein.”

For by this [verse], this meaning is intended to be suggested: that whatever account of the Pāṇḍavas and others is celebrated here in this *Mahābhārata*, all of it is ultimately insipid and is merely a manifestation of ignorance (*avidyā-prapañca*);
rather, it is the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva who is celebrated here as the nature of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*).
Therefore, let your minds be devoted solely to that Supreme Lord, the Blessed One.
Let there not be those whose minds are entirely and utterly fixed upon these various powers—which are devoid of essence—or upon certain qualities such as policy, discipline, and prowess;
for one who perceives the worthlessness of cyclic existence ahead of them, this very point shines forth clearly, and the word, aided by its suggestive power, manifests it.
The subsequent verses, beginning with “For he is the Truth,” appear to demonstrate this very meaning which has been thus internalized.
And this hidden, delightful meaning was perfectly clarified by that very creator-poet Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, who brought the Mahābhārata to its conclusion with the description of the Harivaṃśa;

and by means of this meaning—which instills an excess of devotion toward the ultimate reality transcending worldly existence—the entire mundane course of affairs is revealed in its full detail as being merely a prima facie position.

Furthermore, the description of the extraordinary power of deities, sacred fords, asceticism, and so forth, is intended solely as a means for attaining that very Supreme Brahman and as manifestations of His glory— including specific deities and others.
Likewise, even the narration of the life-stories of the Pāṇḍavas and others has the purpose of generating dispassion (*vairāgya*), and since dispassion is the root of liberation (*mokṣa*).

Since liberation is shown in the Gītā and other texts to be the primary means for attaining the Blessed One, it is [the goal] through which the Supreme Brahman itself becomes the means of attainment by way of a lineage. Furthermore, the Supreme Brahman—the locus of immeasurable power—is intended here as that which is designated by names such as Vāsudeva; it is well-known in various passages of the Gītā and elsewhere by those very names, and its entire essential nature is intended to be represented by the manifestation at Mathurā.
But it does not refer exclusively to the portion concerning the manifestation at Mathurā, because of its being qualified by the word "sanātana" (eternal);
furthermore, in the Rāmāyaṇa and other texts, we observe the usage of this name for other forms of the Blessed One.
And this matter has been determined by those who know the true nature of words.

Thus, it has been well demonstrated that by means of the introductory verse—which reveals the impermanence of everything other than the Blessed One—the single supreme human goal characterized as liberation is intended to be the primary theme (*aṅgin*) of the Mahābhārata according to the system of the Śāstra; and according to the system of poetry, the *śānta* rasa, characterized by the nourishment of the bliss of the destruction of craving, is intended as the primary theme.
Furthermore, because it constitutes the ultimate essence (*atyanta-sāra*), this meaning is shown solely as the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) and not as the directly expressed (*vācya*).
For an essential meaning, when manifested by not being denoted by its own word, brings forth a far greater beauty.
And this is indeed a well-known convention in the assemblies of refined scholars: that a most cherished object is revealed through suggestion, rather than by being the direct denotation of a word.

Therefore, this is established: when poetry is composed by relying on rasa and other elements that constitute its primary components (*aṅgin*), there is the attainment of a new meaning and a great splendor of composition (*bandha-chāyā*) is achieved.

For this very reason, even in the absence of other formal ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), one observes in actual literary works a connection with a particular meaning that accords with the *rasa*, which possesses an excellence of luster. As for example:
"The sage, the lord of yogins, the great-souled one born from a water-jar, is victorious."
"In which a single cup was seen those two divine fish and tortoise," and so forth.

For here, the sight of the fish and tortoise in a single cup, being consistent with the marvelous sentiment (*adbhuta-rasa*), nourishes an excellence of poetic luster (*chāyātiśaya*). For in that case, even though the entire ocean is present in a single cup, the sight of the divine fish and tortoise is more consistent with the marvelous sentiment because it remains unimpaired.
For an object that has already been experienced through worldly convention does not produce wonder, even if it is extraordinary.
Nor is an unexperienced object suitable for being depicted only in accordance with the marvelous rasa (*adbhuta-rasa*), but rather for any rasa whatsoever. For example:
"He perspires, his hair stands on end, and he trembles on the street like one on the tip of a scale."
O fortunate one, even today that side of her by which he passed away remains beautiful.
"He perspires, his hair stands on end, and he trembles on the street like one on the tip of a scale;
O fortunate one, even today that side [of the body] by which he passed remains so for her.
From the contemplation of the meaning of this verse, there arises a realization of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Upon touching you, she perspires, her hair stands on end, and she trembles—such meanings as these are not perceived even slightly from the literal sense [of the words].
Thus, it has been demonstrated how the novelty of poetic meanings arises by relying on the various divisions of *dhvani*.

Furthermore, regarding *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (poetry where the suggested meaning is subordinate), its various modes—in relation to the three types of suggested meanings—also certainly result in the novelty of poetic subjects by relying upon them.
However, because that would result in excessive prolixity, it has not been illustrated here; it should be inferred for oneself by those of sensitive taste.
Thus, by virtue of the existence of both *dhvani* and poetry where the suggested meaning is subordinate (*guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*),
there is no cessation of the aesthetic purpose of poetry, provided that the quality of creative intuition (*pratibhā*) is present.
Even though there exist compositions by ancient poets, if one possesses the quality of creative intuition (*pratibhā*), then [one may succeed];
but in its absence, there is no subject matter whatsoever for a poet.

Even the "shadow of composition"—the arrangement of words that conforms to both the literal meaning and the intended sense—how could it be possible in the absence of creative intuition regarding the subject matter?
The mere composition of syllables that disregard the specific meaning is but the shadow of poetic composition (*bandha-chāyā*); this is not close to the hearts of the sensitive (*sahṛdaya*).
For if that were the case, the designation "poetry" would apply even to the composition of clever and sweet words that are independent of meaning.

If it is asked, "If poetry consists of the union of word and meaning, how can there be the status of poetry in such a subject [where only the form is considered]?"—[the answer is: in the composition of a meaning fashioned by another.
Just as there is the conventional usage of the term "poetry" for that [work], so too it applies to such compositions of poetry.
And it is stated in order to demonstrate that the infinity of meaning does not depend solely on the suggested sense (*vyaṅgyārtha*), but extends even to the expressed sense (*vācyārtha*):
"Even through the particularities of state, place, time, and so forth, the expressed meaning itself becomes infinite by its very nature, even in its pure form. (Dhvanyāloka 4.7)
Even for a pure expressed meaning (*vācya*) that does not depend on a suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*), infinity arises by its very nature.
For this is the inherent nature of all things—whether sentient or insentient—that they become infinite due to differences in state, place, time, and individual characteristics.

And when these things, existing in such conditions, are composed even through the figure of speech known as *svabhāvokti* (description of nature), which consists in following their well-known manifold natures, the subject matter of poetry becomes truly limitless.

For instance, there is a novelty arising from differences in state (*avasthā-bheda*), as in the *Kumārasambhava* regarding the Blessed Lady Pārvatī. Although her description of form was already fully completed at the outset through such statements as "by means of a collection of all comparable objects" (*sarvopamā-dravya-samuccayena*) [Ku.Saṃ.
1.49], she is described once again as she comes within the range of the eyes of the Blessed Śambhu: "wearing ornaments of spring flowers" (*vasanta-puṣpābharaṇaṃ vahantī*) [Ku.Saṃ.].

[3.53] That very same [beauty], described by means of a different artifice as an accessory to the god of love, and again having her form being perfected at the time of her new wedding with such expressions as "having seated that slender maiden there facing the east," is depicted with its physical excellence revealed in a truly fresh manner.

Furthermore, those various modes of description repeatedly employed by that poet in one and the same place do not appear redundant, nor do they seem merely filled with ever-new meanings; rather, they manifest as distinct.
And this has already been shown in the *Viṣamabāṇalīlā*: "Neither does their limit appear, nor are they seen to be repeated in any way."
I am the wandering bee for the lotuses that are beloved women, or for the white-lotuses that are eloquent speeches.
Neither does a limit apply to them,
nor are they ever seen to be redundant— those delusions of beloveds or the meanings found in the speech of great poets.

This is another variety of the classification of states: that all insentient things possess a second, sentient form, well-known as their "egoistic nature" (*abhimānitva*), such as that of the Himavat, the Gaṅgā, and so forth.
And when this [sentient form] is depicted through its association with the essential nature of a fitting sentient subject, it becomes something entirely different;
as, for example, in the *Kumārasambhava*, the description of the Himavat mountain in its true nature as a sentient being.
Furthermore, in the pleasant utterances of the Seven Sages, that which was demonstrated with respect to the nature of consciousness appears truly unprecedented.
And this is the well-known path of great poets;
moreover, this method has been shown in detail within the *Viṣamabāṇalīlā* for the sake of the poet’s proficiency.
Furthermore, the difference between conscious beings according to their various stages, such as childhood and so forth, is well known even to great poets.
Even when there is no difference in the general stage of consciousness, there is a multiplicity due to differences in intermediate states;
for example, among young maidens whose hearts have been pierced by the flower-arrowed god [Kāma], and others who are not so affected.

Even there, if one were to describe individually the specific nature of each of those things—whether disciplined or undisciplined, and including even insentient entities—that are distinguished by the various states of their commencement and so forth, they would simply result in infinity. As it is said:
"In the cries of swans, [one might distinguish] those swallowed by which the warbling [birds] are affected..."
Another kind of gurgling, faltering movement arises from the rolling in their throats, which are still choked with phlegm;
now, in the lotus ponds, there have emerged the tips of the lotus bulbs, rivaling the tender sprouts of the tusks of young elephants.
[*23] Srk 284, Skm 1309 (attributed to Kamalāyudha):
Thus, in other cases as well, one should proceed according to this direction.
First, there is diversity among insentient things due to differences in location.

Just as it is well known for winds moving through various directions and regions, and for other things such as water and flowers, so too among sentient beings— such as humans, animals, birds, and the like— who are nourished by villages, forests, water, and so forth, a great diversity is indeed observed.
And when this diversity is analyzed and described according to its specific instances, it likewise results in infinity.

For instance, who among mortals is able to reach the end of the various distinctions found in the social dealings and activities of even human beings alone—distinctions divided by direction, location, and so forth?
This is especially true for women.
Yet all of this is depicted by skilled poets exactly according to their creative intuition (*pratibhā*).
And there is diversity due to the difference in time,

just as there is for insentient things such as the directions, the sky, and water according to the change of seasons; and for sentient beings, states such as longing and so forth are well known to depend upon specific times.
Furthermore, it is well known that the basis for all things existing throughout the entire world is their specific characteristics (*svālakṣaṇya*).
Even when these are described exactly as they exist, they bring about an infinite expansion of the poetic subject matter (*kāvyārtha*).
On this point, some might say: "Things attain the status of being expressed (*vācyatā*) in their general form, not in their particular form."

For those [poetic works] are composed by superimposing the nature of pleasures and their causes as personally experienced onto other things, relying solely upon a commonality (*sāmānyamātra*) consisting of the forms experienced by oneself and others;
for they do not perceive—as yogins do—the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the past, future, or present, such as those previously familiar to them.
And that commonality of the object of experience and the experience itself is shared by all cognizers, yet because it is limited, it has become the domain of the ancients alone.
Because it is untenable for that [universal] to be an object [of cognition].
Therefore, the mere conceit of those moderns who perceive that particular mode as something new is nothing more than an illusion; there is here only a variety produced by verbal expression.

To this it is replied: as for what was said—that poetic activity proceeds by relying solely on universals, and since these are limited and have already been made the object of experience, there is no novelty in the subjects of poetry—[that is not so].
That is incorrect;

for if poetry proceeds by relying merely upon the universal (sāmānya), then what is the excellence of the poetic themes composed by great poets? Or rather, there would be no designation of "poet" for anyone other than Vālmīki, because there would be no poetic theme existing apart from the universal.
