And since the general [definition] has already been demonstrated by the first poet himself,
if it is argued that this is not a fault because of the variety of expression (*ukti-vaicitrya*), then what is this "variety of expression"?
For expression is speech that conveys a specific object of expression (*vācya*).
If there is such variety in that [meaning], why should there not be a corresponding variety in the expression?

For the signifier (vācaka) functions through an inseparable connection with the signified (vācya). Furthermore, the form of the signifieds as they appear in poetry is perceived precisely through their non-difference from the specific objects of apprehension.
Therefore, even by one who speaks of the variety of expressions, the variety of the objects expressed must necessarily be admitted, even if not desired.
This is the summary here:
if there were even a single person other than Vālmīki...
In the case of the objects of intuition, that respective infinity is held to be inexhaustible.
Furthermore, that variety of expression which is said to be the basis for the ever-newness of poetry is entirely consistent with our position;

for whatever variety of means previously shown causes the infinite diversity of poetic meaning all attains a twofold increase through the variety of re-expression (*punarukti-vaicitrya*). Moreover, this well-known class of ornaments such as simile (*upamā*) and paronomasia (*śleṣa*), when composed through the variety of phrasing (*bhaṇiti-vaicitrya*), itself becomes limitless and branches out into hundreds of forms.

Furthermore, speech, being established through the distinctions of its own various languages, brings about another infinity of poetic meanings by being the basis for the diversity of objects within the specific scope of each particular language; as in my own verse:
"Saying 'maha maha' (give me, give me), the time of people passes away."
May that King Janaka not become an object of pursuit for my mind.
"Though people spend their time saying 'mine,
mine,' nevertheless, the god Janārdana does not become an object of their minds."
In this way, however one examines them, no end to the meanings of poetry can be found.
However, this is said:
[it is] the composition of expressed meanings differentiated by circumstances and so forth.
That which was previously demonstrated— that [the object] is perceived by the whole (bhūman) alone when it is the target of perception— cannot be set aside.
But that [suggestion] shines forth by virtue of its dependence on rasa.
This is now stated here in brief for the instruction of good poets:

If the course of a subject matter—connected with aesthetic flavor (rasa), emotion (bhāva), and so forth—is followed according to propriety, even when it is differentiated by place, time, and other factors; [then it is successful]. (Dhvanyāloka 4.9)
What count can there be of other poets whose powers are limited?
Even by thousands upon thousands of Vācaspatis striving with effort, that [work] cannot be exhausted, just as the nature of the worlds [remains inexhaustible]. (Dhvanyāloka 4.10)

For just as the nature of the world, though it possesses a manifold proliferation of diverse objects manifested throughout a succession of past kalpas, cannot now be said to have its power to create other objects exhausted;
even so, this state of poetry, though enjoyed by infinite poetic minds, is not diminished today.
On the contrary, it increases through ever-new insights;
even this being the case,
confirmations nonetheless frequently occur for those of superior intelligence.
For it is established that the intellects of the wise are indeed in agreement;
however,
all of them should not be considered by the discerning person as being of a single form.
If it is asked how this is so:

"For correspondence is indeed similarity with another; that, moreover, is like a reflection, like the form of a painting, and like [the likeness] of embodied beings to other embodied beings. (Dhvanyāloka 4.12)
For "correspondence" (saṃvāda) is said to be the similarity of the subject matter of a poem with another poetic subject;
that, moreover, is established in three ways: like a reflection of embodied beings, like a painted form, and like a counterpart of a living being.
For some poetic subject is like a reflection of another subject that possesses a body.
One [form] is like a painting; another is similar to an embodied being by virtue of its likeness.
Among these, the former has no self-nature other than itself, while the latter immediately following it has a void nature.
But the third [type of *sāmānyamala*], which consists of a well-known self-nature, the wise poet should not abandon its lack of similarity with anything else.
In this regard, first of all, the subject matter of poetry that is like a reflection must be abandoned by one of sound intelligence,
because it lacks a non-different essence and is empty of a real body.
Immediately after that, that which resembles a painting— similar to something else and though joined with another form— must be discarded as being essentially void.
Thirdly, however, even when there exists a distinct and beautiful body [of the plot], the poet must not abandon the subject matter of the poem even if it involves a repetition;
for it cannot be said that one embodied being is the very same as another, even if they are similar. (Dhvanyāloka 4.13)
To establish this very point, it is said:
"Even an object that conforms to its prior state appears all the more [vividly] when something else exists besides itself, like the moon-like face of a slender woman. (Dhvanyāloka 4.14)

When the Self, which is the essence of reality, exists, even another object that follows its former state appears exceedingly beautiful; for an object graced by the luster of ancient charm attains supreme splendor like a living body,
and does not appear as a mere tautology.
The face of the slender maiden is like the luster of the moon.
Thus, the boundaries of sentence-meanings that consist of aggregates and are accompanied by corroboration have been distinguished.

Now, it is stated in order to demonstrate that there is indeed no fault in poetic subjects that take the form of word-meanings and resemble other existing things: "Where the arrangement of a subject matter from antiquity is joined together like an arrangement of syllables and so forth..."
When a new poetic subject matter flashes forth, it is indeed evident that she (the poetic figure) is not at fault. // DhvK_4.15 //
For even by Vācaspati, no letters or words that are unprecedented can be fashioned;
rather, it is those very same [words] that have been composed, and they do not contradict the novelty found in poetry and the like.
In the same way, the forms of word-meanings consisting of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and so forth are the true essence of meaning. Therefore—
Whatever that may be, it is also delightful... the body of poetry... wherein there is something for the world.
When whatever appears to the world arises with the cognition, "This is a manifestation," a sense of wonder arises in those of aesthetic sensitivity that "this is some kind of manifestation."
Even when a thing is followed by its previous shadow, a skilled poet who composes it in such a way does not incur censure. (Dhvanyāloka 4.16)

Even an object that follows from that [previous context] may, when composed by a skilled poet through the "shadow of the composition"— which consists of a verbal arrangement capable of conveying both the intended suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) and the expressed meaning (*vācya*)— in such and such a manner, never incur censure.
Thus, it stands as follows:
Let the words, which possess the nectar-like flavor of various signified meanings, be understood; poets should not succumb to despondency regarding their own faultless domain.
There are ever-new poetic themes; yet, when composing upon a subject already fashioned by another, there is no merit whatsoever for the poet—considering this, one should proceed.
For one whose mind is free from the desire to take another's property, this blessed Sarasvatī herself arranges the substance of a good poet according to her will.
The divine Sarasvatī fulfills the subject matter according to her will for that good poet whose mind is free from the desire to appropriate the property of others.

For those good poets whose activity proceeds by the power of the ripening of the practice of former merits, and who are devoid of longing to adopt meanings composed by others, their own labor is of no use whatsoever;
that very same divine Sarasvatī herself manifests the intended meaning.
This indeed is the true greatness of great poets—so be it!

Thus, because the desired subject matter, which bears the splendor of qualities and ornaments appropriate to its basis in unblemished aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), is attained in its entirety by those of virtuous deeds; [this work is thus completed].

In this garden of the wise called Kāvya, which is the abode of all happiness, this very Dhvani has been revealed; may it, possessing a majesty equal to the wish-fulfilling tree, be enjoyed by those of noble soul.
That which had long been as if dormant within the minds of those of mature intellect— concerning the path of the principles of true poetry—
he has now expounded for the sake of securing the welfare of connoisseurs.
He whose renowned name was Ānandavardhana.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Dhvanyāloka composed by the venerable teacher Rājānaka Ānandavardhana.
